findings.title: proxy.ts revalidates every request against GoTrue with no rate limiter, and an attacker-forged cookie is enough — unauthenticated cross-tenant auth outage
findings.boundary: Unauthenticated internet -> the shared Supabase Auth (GoTrue) quota of the single production project, which every customer organization depends on. Also the middleware/route-handler boundary: middleware runs before every limiter in the application.
findings.precondition: None. No account, no session, no credential. The attacker needs only to send HTTP requests to the deployed app with one static, self-authored Cookie header. The value is not secret and does not need to be valid.
findings.affected_actor: Every tenant simultaneously, plus every prospective user. Sign-in, password reset, invitation acceptance and mid-session token refresh all traverse the same GoTrue endpoint from the same egress IP.
findings.exploit:
1. proxy.ts:127-132 matches `/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)` — i.e. every path including /api/live and any nonexistent URL. Confirmed present in the shipped artifact via functions-config-manifest.json's `/_middleware` matcher.
2. proxy.ts:121 calls `await supabase.auth.getUser()` unconditionally on each matched request. There is no rate-limit check in proxy.ts; all 45 limiters in the codebase are inside Server Actions and Route Handlers, which execute AFTER middleware.
3. auth-js `_isValidSession()` accepts any object where the keys access_token, refresh_token and expires_at merely EXIST. No signature verification, no type check.
4. The attacker sends `Cookie: sb-<projectref>-auth-token=base64-<base64url of {"access_token":"forged","refresh_token":"forged-refresh","expires_at":1}>`. expires_at in the past forces __loadSession into _callRefreshToken().
5. Each such request costs the app exactly one outbound `POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=refresh_token`. The attacker replays it at whatever rate they like.
6. GoTrue's own abuse protection keys on the caller IP as GoTrue sees it — the app's single Railway egress IP — so the attacker does not need to exhaust a global quota, only to get the app's own egress address throttled. At that point legitimate auth traffic from every tenant fails too, and because proxy.ts is on every request, so does session refresh.
findings.evidence:
proxy.ts:121  `  await supabase.auth.getUser();`
proxy.ts:132  `    "/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)",`
Grep of proxy.ts for `.check(` / `createInMemoryRateLimiter`: no matches — zero limiters in the middleware layer.

auth-js 2.112.4, GoTrueClient.js `_isValidSession`:
```
_isValidSession(maybeSession) {
    const isValidSession = typeof maybeSession === 'object' &&
        maybeSession !== null &&
        'access_token' in maybeSession &&
        'refresh_token' in maybeSession &&
        'expires_at' in maybeSession;
    return isValidSession;
}
```

LIVE PROBE (isolated; a throwaway in-process http listener stands in for GoTrue — no database, no Supabase instance, nothing shared was touched). Script at <scratchpad>/probe-proxy-amplify.mjs builds the same @supabase/ssr createServerClient proxy.ts builds, feeds it the forged cookie, and calls getUser(). Exact output:
```
cookie name tried: sb-127-auth-token
  outbound requests made by getUser(): ["POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=refresh_token"]
  user: null  error: stub
cookie name tried: sb-127.0.0.1-auth-token
  outbound requests made by getUser(): []
  user: null  error: Auth session missing!
```
The first line is the finding: three attacker-chosen strings produce a real GoTrue round trip. (The second line is the control — a cookie under a name the client does not look for produces no call, confirming the first result is the cookie doing the work.)

Artifact reachability, next-server.js:1080-1083 in .next/standalone/node_modules:
```
if (this.dev || functionsConfig?.functions?.['/_middleware']) {
    return require(join(this.distDir, 'server', 'middleware.js'));
}
```
and .next/standalone/.next/server/functions-config-manifest.json contains `"/_middleware"` with `"originalSource": "/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)"`.
findings.why_controls_fail: The rate-limiting design places every limiter at the Server Action / Route Handler boundary — 45 of them, all correctly wired, all correctly gating. Middleware sits in front of all of them, so none is in the path. The prior passes verified that limiters exist, execute and cannot be bypassed by the E2E flag; none asked which requests reach GoTrue WITHOUT passing a limiter at all. Separately, proxy.ts's own doc comment treats the getUser() round trip as purely a security virtue ('getSession() only reads the possibly stale cookie... getUser() always makes a real Auth server round-trip') and never considers that an unauthenticated caller controls whether that round trip happens. get-client-ip.ts's hardening is irrelevant here because no key is ever computed. rate-limiter.ts's maxKeys ceiling is irrelevant because no limiter is consulted.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated, single-source, low-cost denial of authentication against all tenants at once. For a CBAM compliance platform the availability window is not fungible: reporting periods have statutory deadlines, and an outage that blocks sign-in and invitation acceptance during a filing window is a regulatory exposure for every customer, not an inconvenience. It also degrades quietly — the symptom is GoTrue 429s on legitimate traffic, which will read as a Supabase problem rather than as an attack.
findings.recommendation: Rate-limit the middleware itself before the getUser() call, keyed by getClientIp(), with a budget appropriate to normal page-load volume; the existing createInMemoryRateLimiter is reusable as-is. Better, short-circuit the round trip when the request carries no plausible session at all, and treat an unparseable or structurally-invalid session cookie as 'no session' locally rather than handing it to GoTrue — clear the cookie and return the signed-out response without a network call. Longer term this is the same argument the rate-limiter header already makes for a shared store: a per-process in-memory limiter in front of a shared, project-wide external quota does not bound what that quota actually sees.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: /auth/callback adopts any access_token/refresh_token pair from the URL fragment on GET, with no click and no identity warning — session fixation on a live, orphaned endpoint
findings.boundary: The authentication boundary: who this browser is. The endpoint lets a third party choose the identity a victim's browser holds.
findings.precondition: Any Snowkap account (self-signup is enabled: supabase/config.toml `[auth] enable_signup = true`), from which the attacker obtains their own access_token/refresh_token pair — trivially, by calling GoTrue's /auth/v1/token?grant_type=password with the public anon key. Plus getting the victim to open one link. The victim need not be signed in and need not click anything on the page.
findings.affected_actor: Any user who opens the link — importer/declarant and producer staff alike. Downstream, the organization whose data that user then enters or exposes.
findings.exploit: Send the victim `https://<app>/auth/callback#access_token=<attacker>&refresh_token=<attacker>&type=invite`. app/auth/callback/page.tsx runs its effect on mount (line 100), finds no error params, reads the fragment (lines 178-195), and calls establishSessionAction(accessToken, refreshToken) — a Server Action that calls setSession() on the SERVER client (app/auth/callback/actions.ts:48,57), so the attacker's session is written as real Set-Cookie headers the browser cannot refuse. It then router.replace(next) (line 235) into the app. The victim is now signed in as the attacker with no prompt, no confirmation, and no notice of whose account they are in. Anything they subsequently enter — shipment lines, evidence uploads, emissions figures — lands in the attacker's organization, and the attacker reads it at leisure.
findings.evidence:
Code, not live-reproduced (see could_not_test). app/auth/callback/page.tsx:100 `useEffect(` — runs on mount, unconditionally; lines 178-195 read access_token/refresh_token from window.location.hash and call establishSessionAction; line 235 `router.replace(next)`. There is no getUser() call, no signed-in check, and no confirmation UI anywhere in the file. app/auth/callback/actions.ts:48-57 `establishSessionAction` -> `supabase.auth.setSession({access_token, refresh_token})` on getServerSupabaseClient().

The endpoint is orphaned but live: all four Auth email templates now link to /auth/confirm, not /auth/callback — supabase/templates/{invite,confirmation,recovery,magic_link}.html each hardcode `{{ .SiteURL }}/auth/confirm?token_hash={{ .TokenHash }}&type=...`. So no legitimate email produces a /auth/callback URL any more, while the route, the client component and the Server Action all still ship.
findings.why_controls_fail: The project already built the exact control this endpoint lacks — and applied it only to the other one. tests/architecture/auth-confirm-get-is-inert.test.ts:46-59 forbids `useEffect`, `setSession` and `exchangeCodeForSession` in app/auth/confirm/**, precisely so a GET cannot establish a session; app/auth/confirm/page.tsx additionally renders "You are currently signed in as X. Continuing will sign you out of this browser and sign you in as the account this link was sent to." /auth/callback/page.tsx contains all three forbidden constructs and shows no such warning. The same test file's third case reads app/auth/callback/page.tsx and asserts only that it does not contain `verifyOtp` (lines 122-131) — which passes while the file auto-establishes sessions by a different mechanism, so the suite gives affirmative comfort about this exact file on a property it does not check. Next.js Server Action origin checking does not help: the action is invoked from the app's own page, in the victim's own browser. The httpOnly hardening does not help either — it is what makes the injected cookie stick (establishSessionAction's own doc comment explains that moving setSession server-side was done because the client-side write silently failed).
findings.impact: Zero-click account confusion on the product's own trusted origin. A victim doing real work inside an attacker-controlled tenant is a data-exfiltration channel for whatever they type or upload; combined with finding 5 (password change requires no re-authentication) the reverse direction is worse, since an attacker who can inject a session can then also lock the account. That the endpoint has no remaining legitimate producer makes this pure attack surface.
findings.recommendation: Delete the route. Nothing emails it any more; app/(auth)/actions.ts:268, app/(auth)/forgot-password/actions.ts:121 and app/team/actions.ts:645 pass a redirectTo pointing at it that GoTrue's templates never use. If it must stay for links already in flight, give it exactly what /auth/confirm has: inert on GET, an explicit Continue press, and the signed-in-as warning — and extend tests/architecture/auth-confirm-get-is-inert.test.ts's forbidden-construct list to cover app/auth/callback/page.tsx rather than only checking it for verifyOtp.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The Annex II sector lookup fails open in three ways: swallowed query errors, absence treated as "not Annex II", and a silent arbitrary pick among candidates
findings.boundary: Regulatory-treatment selection inside the trusted calculation path -- the point where the engine decides whether indirect emissions enter the CBAM figure.
findings.precondition: Any ACTUAL-method line. Two of the three mechanisms are reachable by an ordinary member with no special rights; the third needs a cbam_goods dataset containing two TRADE_GOOD rows for one code.
findings.affected_actor: Own tenant and the filing: the persisted figure silently changes treatment, and the row records nothing about which treatment was chosen or why.
findings.exploit: (a) src/application/calculations/calculate-line.ts:122 destructures only `data` from the shipments lookup and drops `error` entirely; src/application/calculations/reproduce-calculation-result.ts:170-179 does the same for the cn_code lookup. Any transient failure returns null, the Annex II gate does not fire, and indirect emissions are added to an iron/steel line -- a wrong authoritative number produced by a swallowed error, with no trace on the row. (b) A member can force the same null deterministically: set the shipment's release_date outside the goods' effective window, or set a cn_code that is in no cbam_goods row (only a regex constrains it). (c) calculate-line.ts:141 is `return candidates[0]?.sector ?? null;` over a query with no ORDER BY and `.limit(10)` (src/infrastructure/regulatory/supabase-regulatory-repository.ts:724-746). For the identical candidate list the domain's own src/domain/shipments/classify-good.ts returns AMBIGUOUS for length > 1 and never picks.
findings.evidence:
Both member-reachable forcings, run as `authenticated` (uid be92879e, role MEMBER) in one BEGIN ... ROLLBACK, script area4_controls.sql, verbatim output:

  --- C5: can a MEMBER change the shipment release_date the sector lookup uses? ---
  before: release_date = 2026-03-01
  UPDATE 1
  after : release_date = 2025-06-01
    cbam_goods rows for 72061000 as-of 2025-06-01 = 0  => resolveGoodSectorForActualLine returns NULL => Annex II gate does not fire
  --- C6: can a MEMBER set a cn_code that is in no cbam_goods row at all? ---
  UPDATE 1
    line cn_code now = 99999999, cbam_goods rows for it = 0
  ROLLBACK
  === rolled back. release_date = 2026-03-01, line cn_code = 72081000

Why both succeed: policy shipments_update_own_org_not_terminal has USING `org_id in (select app.user_org_ids()) and status <> all (ARRAY['LOCKED','VOID'])` with no column restriction and no BEFORE UPDATE trigger on release_date (only prevent_org_id_change); shipment_lines_update_parent_not_terminal is the same shape. All 170 TRADE_GOOD rows carry active_from = 2026-01-01, active_to = NULL:
  select coalesce(active_from::text,'NULL'), coalesce(active_to::text,'NULL'), count(*) from cbam_goods where record_level='TRADE_GOOD' group by 1,2;
  -> 2026-01-01|NULL|170
And a real line already carries an unmatchable code today: shipment_line 27023f49-882a-4aa4-badd-b3c62e0f7f24 has cn_code 72081000 while `select count(*) from cbam_goods where trade_code='72081000'` returns 0.

Engine confirmation that null is not neutral, from running the real engine (direct 1, indirect 9, qty 100):
  good_sector IRON_STEEL -> COMPUTED 100
  good_sector null       -> COMPUTED 1000
  good_sector 'iron_steel' (case differs) -> COMPUTED 1000
ANNEX_II_SECTORS is a case-sensitive Set, so any sector string that is not exactly 'IRON_STEEL'/'ALUMINIUM' silently disables the gate.
findings.why_controls_fail: The engine's doc comment says the null-sector case is deliberate -- "a good whose sector could not be resolved is unknown, not Annex II, and the engine does not guess in either direction". It does guess: unknown resolves to the include-indirect branch, which is a different number, not an abstention, and calculateLine persists it as authoritative. That is the exact pattern CLAUDE.md forbids ("never treat 'no value' as 'value is zero'" / ambiguity must surface). calculate-line.ts's own doc comment calls the not-found case "an unexpected-data-drift case, not a normal outcome" and then returns null for it anyway, and the same comment does not mention that the `error` channel is discarded at all. For (c), CLAUDE.md states plainly: "Silently pick among ambiguous candidates -- ambiguity must surface as AMBIGUOUS/UNRESOLVED, never an arbitrary choice." cbam_goods has no uniqueness constraint on trade_code (pg_constraint shows only a PK on id), so duplicates are schema-permitted; today's dataset happens to have 170 codes for 170 rows, which is why this is latent rather than live.
findings.impact: A regulated treatment worth the entire indirect-emissions component is selected from state a member controls and from a query whose failure is indistinguishable from a legitimate answer. In the swallowed-error case an infrastructure hiccup silently changes a compliance number and the row keeps no evidence it happened. In the duplicate-candidate case the number becomes non-deterministic across runs, which also makes the reproduction proof meaningless for those rows.
findings.recommendation: Return a discriminated outcome from resolveGoodSectorForActualLine rather than `string | null`: RESOLVED(sector) / NO_MATCH / AMBIGUOUS / LOOKUP_FAILED. Stop discarding `error` in both that function and resolveCnCodeForLine. Have calculateLineEmissions refuse (PARAMETER_DATASET_UNAVAILABLE, which types.ts still names for exactly this) on anything but RESOLVED, instead of computing under the include-indirect branch. Replace `candidates[0]` with the same length check classifyGood already applies. Add ORDER BY to findCbamGoodsByCode regardless, and raise rather than truncate at the limit. Independently: freeze release_date (a shipment's declared release date drives classification effective-dating and should not be editable in place), which also makes reproduce-calculation-result.ts:264's claim true instead of false.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: 32 of the 50 CBAM headings in the platform's own dataset cannot be declared at all, and the product tells the declarant 'That code isn't a CBAM good'
findings.boundary: Classification boundary — CN/TARIC code to cbam_goods. The dataset expresses many goods at HS4/HS6 heading level, but classification and resolution both require exact equality against an 8- or 10-digit TRADE_GOOD row.
findings.precondition: None. Any importer declaring a line for one of the affected codes — which includes essentially all flat-rolled steel and almost all aluminium products.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant, who is affirmatively told the good is out of scope, and through them the regulator and the filing.
findings.exploit: Enter CN 72081000 (hot-rolled flat steel), 72085100, 76011000 (unwrought aluminium), 76061200, or 73089098 on a shipment line. validateCnCodeFormat passes (8 digits). findCbamGoodsByCode filters record_level='TRADE_GOOD' and returns zero rows. classifyGood returns UNSUPPORTED_CODE. The UI renders 'That code isn't a CBAM good.'
findings.why_controls_fail: The control that should exist is hierarchical resolution CN8 -> HS6 -> HS4. The types anticipate it: ResolutionReason includes EXACT_HS6_MATCH and EXACT_HS4_MATCH, codeLevelPriority ranks all four levels, and cbam_goods.parent_good_id is populated for 60 rows. None of it is wired up — matchesCode is string equality and a line's cn_code is always 8 or 10 digits, so the HS4/HS6 branches are unreachable from any production caller. `grep -rn parent_good_id` over src/ and app/ returns nothing outside the loader and the migration. classify-good.ts:59-65 argues no record_level filtering is needed because digit length determines level, which is true but sidesteps the question of whether a shorter code should cover a longer one — the exact question cnScopeCoversCnCode answers 'yes' for emission data scopes, in the same codebase, with the same CN8/TARIC10 reasoning.
findings.impact: The single largest CBAM import categories cannot be entered. Worse than a refusal: the product states as fact that the code is not a CBAM good, which invites the declarant to leave it out of the declaration entirely. That is an under-report by omission, induced by the product. Also 5,921 REFERENCE_REQUIRED rows sit at HS4/HS6 level, so the resolver's REFERENCE_REQUIRED branch never fires for any declarable good either.
findings.recommendation: Either implement hierarchical resolution — which per CLAUDE.md and R5 of ANNEX_II_APPLICABILITY_DATASET_REQUIREMENTS.md needs a written, cited matching rule in REGULATORY_RESOLUTION_RULES.md with its own rule id before any code is written, not an inference from the data's shape — or, at minimum and immediately, change the message. 'That code isn't a CBAM good' must become something like 'This platform cannot yet determine emissions for this code — do not omit it from your declaration.' A false out-of-scope statement is worse than an honest inability.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Spelled-out magnitude-prefixed and non-metric denominators are accepted as tonnes: tCO2e/kilotonne computes identically to tCO2e/t
findings.boundary: Unit boundary in unitMatchesQuantityBasis — the only thing standing between a free-text producer-entered emission_unit and the arithmetic.
findings.precondition: An emission_data record whose emission_unit is written out rather than abbreviated. emission_unit has no CHECK constraint and no application validation; the form's own placeholder invites free text ('e.g. tCO2e/t').
findings.affected_actor: The regulator and the filing, in either direction depending on the prefix.
findings.exploit: Record actual emissions with emission_unit 'tCO2e/kilotonne' (or TCO2E_PER_KILOTONNE, tCO2e/megatonne, TCO2E_PER_MILLITONNE, tCO2e/short tonne, tCO2e/long tonne). The numerator regex /^TCO2E?(?:\/|_PER_|$)/ passes, and the denominator test normalized.includes('TONNE') passes because 'KILOTONNE' contains 'TONNE'. The value is multiplied by a quantity in tonnes as if it were per-tonne.
findings.evidence:
Real engine, run under node_modules/.bin/tsx against src/domain/calculations/calculate-line-emissions.ts, 1000 t line, direct_specific 1.000:
  tCO2e/t                    COMPUTED         1000
  tCO2e/kilotonne            COMPUTED         1000
  TCO2E_PER_KILOTONNE        COMPUTED         1000
  tCO2e/megatonne            COMPUTED         1000
  TCO2E_PER_MEGATONNE        COMPUTED         1000
  TCO2E_PER_MILLITONNE       COMPUTED         1000
  tCO2e/long tonne           COMPUTED         1000
  tCO2e/short tonne          COMPUTED         1000
  tCO2e/kt                   UNIT_UNSUPPORTED
  kgCO2e/t                   UNIT_UNSUPPORTED

Live DB acceptance of the unit string (sandbox, rolled back):
  insert into public.emission_data (... emission_unit ...) values (..., 'tCO2e/kilotonne', ...) returning emission_unit;
  -> tCO2e/kilotonne   (INSERT 0 1)
And accepted end-to-end onto a 2026 line: 'accepted: 2031-period, tCO2e/kilotonne unit, on a 2026 line | tCO2e/kilotonne'.

file:line — src/domain/calculations/calculate-line-emissions.ts:180-186.
findings.why_controls_fail: The guard was hardened twice and both fixes were denominator-blind to spelled-out prefixes. The numerator check (added after the P13 kgCO2e/t incident) is anchored — /^TCO2E?(?:\/|_PER_|$)/ correctly rejects KGCO2E/T, KTCO2E/T, MTCO2E/T. The denominator check is not: `normalized.includes('TONNE')` is a bare substring test, and the anchored `/\/T(?![A-Z0-9])/` alternative only covers the slash-abbreviated form. The golden fixture tests/golden/fixtures/engine-1.3.0/emission-units.json pins 'tCO2e/kt is refused' with the note 'a kilotonne denominator would understate by a thousand' — the class was identified and only the abbreviated spelling was tested, while TCO2E_PER_TONNE, the codebase's own dataset spelling convention, makes the spelled-out form the more natural thing for a producer to type. A passing fixture suite is not evidence the class is closed.
findings.impact: tCO2e/kilotonne over-reports 1000x; TCO2E_PER_MILLITONNE under-reports 1000x; short tonne under-reports 9.3% and long tonne over-reports 1.6% — the non-metric ones being the realistic case for a US or UK operator. No warning, no trace annotation; the number simply is what it is, and record_declaration_filed freezes it.
findings.recommendation: Do what the function's own doc comment says is the real fix and has said since P6: an allow-list on emission_data.emission_unit at entry, as a DB CHECK mirroring default_emission_values' own {'TCO2E_PER_TONNE','TCO2_PER_MWH'} constraint, so the engine stops sniffing free text. Until then, at minimum anchor the denominator the way the numerator already is (require the tonne token to start the denominator, not merely appear in it) and add golden fixtures for the spelled-out prefixes and for short/long tonne.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: EU-origin, EFTA-origin and entirely unknown origin codes all resolve to a third-country default value, so out-of-scope goods get a positive CBAM figure
findings.boundary: Scope boundary — whether a good is subject to CBAM at all. There is no such gate; origin handling has only MAPPED and UNLISTED, and both roads lead to the Other Countries and Territories fallback.
findings.precondition: None. A shipment line with origin_country 'DE' (or NO, IS, LI, CH, or a nonsense 'XX'). shipment_lines_origin_country_check accepts any two uppercase letters.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant, who is handed a CBAM liability for goods that carry none, and the regulator, who receives a filing asserting in-scope status for out-of-scope goods.
findings.exploit: Set a line's origin_country to DE. mapCountry('DE') queries countries by iso2 and finds nothing (EU member states are absent from the table). resolutionCountryName returns the synthetic '(unlisted origin: DE)'. resolveDefaultValue finds 0 records for that name and falls through to the Other Countries and Territories geography. A value resolves, RESOLVED / OTHER_COUNTRIES_FALLBACK.
findings.evidence:
SQL (sandbox):
  select country_type, active, count(*) from countries group by 1,2;  ->  OTHER_TERRITORIES t 1 ; COUNTRY t 121
  select iso2, name from countries where iso2 in ('DE','FR','IT','NL','BE','PL','US','CN','IS','NO','LI','CH','GB');
Output: only CN China, GB United Kingdom, US United States. No EU member state, no EFTA state.

Real resolver (tsx, src/domain/regulatory/resolve-default-value.ts, records for CN 26011200 pulled from the sandbox):
  (unlisted origin: DE) => RESOLVED OTHER_COUNTRIES_FALLBACK total=0.686 TCO2E_PER_TONNE sheet=_Other Countries and Territorie
  (unlisted origin: NO) => RESOLVED OTHER_COUNTRIES_FALLBACK total=0.686 ...
  (unlisted origin: IS) => RESOLVED OTHER_COUNTRIES_FALLBACK total=0.686 ...
  (unlisted origin: XX) => RESOLVED OTHER_COUNTRIES_FALLBACK total=0.686 ...

file:line — src/domain/emissions/types.ts:45-53 (the gap, documented); src/application/emissions/resolve-line-emissions.ts:158-165 (resolutionCountryName); supabase migration 20260828150000, shipment_lines_origin_country_check (any ^[A-Z]{2}$).
findings.why_controls_fail: This is disclosed as a KNOWN OPEN GAP in types.ts:45-53 and MASTER_PLAN §41, pending an owner decision — so it is not hidden. But disclosure is not a control, and the product is a release candidate that files declarations. UNLISTED conflates three materially different things: a genuine third country absent from the dataset (fallback is correct), an EU member state (out of scope entirely), and a code that is not a country at all ('XX' resolves silently, which is the protected zone's own 'never treat no value as a value' rule being violated at the origin layer rather than the emissions layer). The explanation panel says 'Origin not individually listed -- Other Countries and Territories used', which is honest about the mechanism and silent about scope.
findings.impact: A positive embedded-emissions figure, and eventually a certificate liability, for goods of EU or EFTA origin that carry none — over-reporting, but also an invalid filing. Equally, a typo'd or invented origin code produces a confident number rather than an error, which is the exact failure mode the resolver's AMBIGUOUS/UNRESOLVED discipline exists to prevent one layer down.
findings.recommendation: At minimum, before shipping: reject an origin_country that is not a known country as an explicit UNRESOLVED reason rather than resolving it, so 'XX' stops producing a number. The full fix is the versioned in-scope/out-of-scope dataset §41 already calls for — CLAUDE.md's facts-as-datasets rule forbids a hardcoded EU/EFTA list — and the resolution outcome needs a third case (OUT_OF_SCOPE) alongside MAPPED and UNLISTED so the distinction survives into the frozen snapshot.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Cross-tenant denial of service: an importer can permanently destroy a producer's ability to correct its own verified emissions record by squatting emission_data.predecessor_id
findings.boundary: Cross-tenant. An attacker in org A writes a value into their own row that permanently constrains what org B can write into org B's rows, through a global unique index. No read of B's data is required beyond what B already deliberately shared.
findings.precondition: MEMBER role in an organization that holds an ACTIVE sharing grant over the victim's installation — i.e. an ordinary counterparty that the producer chose to share with. The attacker needs the victim's emission_data.id, which the sharing grant itself hands over: emission_data_select_own_org's second disjunct exposes the full ACTIVE+VERIFIED row, and the id is also embedded in the grantee's own frozen determination snapshot and in record_shared_data_consumption payloads. No privileged access, no guessing.
findings.affected_actor: The producer/operator organization. It loses, permanently and silently, the ability to issue a corrected version of a verified emissions record — the exact operation CBAM compliance requires when a figure turns out to be wrong.
findings.exploit: 1. The producer shares an installation with the importer (a normal ACTIVE grant). 2. The importer's plain MEMBER reads the shared record and notes its id. 3. That member INSERTs an ordinary emission_data row in their OWN organization, for their OWN installation, but sets predecessor_id to the victim's emission_data id. The FK to emission_data(id) is checked by the system, not under RLS, so it resolves happily across the tenant boundary; nothing checks that the predecessor belongs to the same org, installation, or lineage. 4. The unique index emission_data_predecessor_id_uq is now occupied for that id. 5. When the producer later records a correction, recordEmissionData computes predecessor_id as the id of the latest row in its own lineage — that same id — and the INSERT fails with a unique violation, surfaced to the producer as PERSIST_FAILED. The producer cannot see the squatting row (no cross-org SELECT), cannot delete it (emission_data has no DELETE policy for authenticated at all), and cannot work around it, because the predecessor id is derived, not chosen.
findings.evidence:
Realistic chain, single transaction, rolled back:
  -- setup: victim rev-vic shares installation b2000000-… with importer rev-atk via an ACTIVE grant
  set local role authenticated; set local request.jwt.claims='{"sub":"aaaa0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003","role":"authenticated"}';
  STEP 1 - grantee MEMBER legitimately reads the shared record and learns its id:
    b3000000-0000-4000-8000-00000000000b  direct=2.500
  STEP 2 - grantee MEMBER squats that id as its OWN row's predecessor_id:
    insert into emission_data(id,installation_id,entered_by_org_id,...,version,predecessor_id)
     values('ac000000-…','a2000000-…'(attacker's own installation),'a0000000-…'(attacker's own org),...,2,
            (select id from emission_data where installation_id='b2000000-…'));
    INSERT 0 1
    squat ok
  STEP 3 - producer OWNER issues a genuine correction (v2) of its own verified record:
    set local request.jwt.claims='{"sub":"bbbb0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",...}';
    insert into emission_data(installation_id,entered_by_org_id,...,version,predecessor_id)
     values('b2000000-…','b0000000-…',...,2,'b3000000-0000-4000-8000-00000000000b');
    ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "emission_data_predecessor_id_uq"

The index, from pg_indexes:
  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX emission_data_predecessor_id_uq ON public.emission_data USING btree (predecessor_id) WHERE (predecessor_id IS NOT NULL)
Note it is NOT scoped by org, installation or dataset. The FK:
  emission_data_predecessor_id_fkey :: FOREIGN KEY (predecessor_id) REFERENCES emission_data(id) ON DELETE SET NULL

The same FK is also a cross-tenant existence oracle. Real cross-org id -> INSERT 0 1 (above). Random uuid, same statement shape:
  ERROR:  insert or update on table "emission_data" violates foreign key constraint "emission_data_predecessor_id_fkey"
  DETAIL:  Key is not present in table "emission_data".

Victim-side derivation confirming step 5 is the app's normal path, not a contrivance: src/application/emissions/manage-emission-data.ts:252-305 selects the latest row in the (installation, entered_by_org_id, period) lineage and sets `predecessorId = latestRecord.id` unconditionally.
findings.why_controls_fail: emission_data_insert_own_org's WITH CHECK constrains exactly two things: that entered_by_org_id is one of the caller's orgs, and that installation_id belongs to that org. predecessor_id is not mentioned, so the policy's name (`insert_own_org`) is honoured for the row's tenancy while one of its columns reaches straight out of the tenant. Foreign-key validation in Postgres runs as the referenced table's owner and is not subject to RLS, so the FK confirms the victim's row exists without the attacker ever being able to SELECT it — this is the classic RLS/FK asymmetry and there is no compensating check anywhere. app.prevent_emission_data_fact_change does pin predecessor_id, but only on UPDATE, so it cannot help at INSERT. emission_data_predecessor_id_uq was introduced (per the comment at manage-emission-data.ts:262-264) as a DB-level backstop against same-org lineage forking; it was never scoped for a hostile writer from another tenant, and being global it converts an integrity aid into a cross-tenant resource that can be claimed first.
findings.impact: An importer — including one acting in bad faith after a commercial dispute, or one merely compromised — can permanently prevent a producer from correcting a specific verified emissions figure. The producer's only visible symptom is a generic PERSIST_FAILED; they cannot see the cause, cannot see the offending row, and cannot remove it, because emission_data exposes no DELETE policy to authenticated at all. Recovery requires service-role intervention against a row the producer cannot identify. In a compliance system where correcting a wrong figure is the primary remediation path, that is a durable, targeted denial of the remedy. The secondary effect is a cross-tenant existence oracle for any emission_data id.
findings.recommendation: Add a WITH CHECK conjunct to emission_data_insert_own_org requiring the predecessor to be in the caller's own tenant and lineage — an EXISTS against emission_data p WHERE p.id = predecessor_id AND p.entered_by_org_id = emission_data.entered_by_org_id AND p.installation_id = emission_data.installation_id AND p.reporting_period_* matches — mirroring the pattern app.declaration_predecessor_matches already uses correctly for declarations (it pins prior.org_id = p_org_id and the whole reporting period). Then narrow emission_data_predecessor_id_uq to include entered_by_org_id (or installation_id) so it can no longer be claimed across tenants even if the policy is later loosened. Audit the other cross-tenant FKs for the same shape while you are there — suppliers.linked_operator_id has it too (reported separately).
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: filed_reference is unbounded end to end, so a long filing reference makes any declaration unfileable — same abort, no size threshold needed
findings.boundary: UI form input -> Server Action -> SECURITY DEFINER RPC transaction
findings.precondition: Any ADMIN/OWNER of an IMPORTER_DECLARANT org with any READY declaration. Requires only typing or pasting a long string into the filing-reference field.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant organization. Self-inflicted rather than adversarial, but trivially reachable — a paste of a long confirmation blob from a customs portal is the obvious real case.
findings.exploit: 1. Take a READY declaration with as few as 2 member shipments. 2. Submit the filing form with a filed_reference of ~9000 characters. 3. record_declaration_filed passes its own EMPTY_FILED_REFERENCE check (it only tests for blank, deliberately does not trim, and writes the value verbatim), builds the audit payload with 'filed_reference', p_filed_reference, and the CHECK aborts the transaction.
findings.evidence:
Live, two-member declaration in p14_review_sandbox:
  psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "set local role authenticated; set local request.jwt.claims = '{\"sub\":\"11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111\",\"role\":\"authenticated\"}'; select * from public.record_declaration_filed('77777777-7777-7777-7777-777777777777', repeat('A',9000));"
  ->  ERROR:  new row for relation "audit_events" violates check constraint "audit_events_payload_size_ck"

No length bound exists at any layer:
  - app/(importer)/declarations/actions.ts:561 — `z.string().min(1)` (no .max())
  - src/application/declarations/record-declaration-filed.ts:107 — only `filedReference.trim().length === 0`
  - DB: `\d declarations` shows only `declarations_filed_reference_not_blank_ck CHECK (filed_reference IS NULL OR btrim(filed_reference) <> ''::text)` — no length constraint, unlike audit_events' own `aggregate_id_length_ck` and `correlation_id_length_ck` which both cap at 200.
findings.why_controls_fail: Three layers each validated the property they cared about and none owned length. Zod checked non-empty. The application service checked non-blank. The database checked non-blank. The one constraint that does bound this value is on a different table, applied to a payload the author of the filing form never sees. The neighbouring columns in audit_events (aggregate_id, correlation_id) are both explicitly length-capped, which shows the pattern was known — it just was not applied to the free-text field that flows into the same payload.
findings.impact: A declarant can put their filing into a permanently unfileable state through ordinary data entry, with a generic RPC_FAILED and no server-side diagnostic. It also lowers the shipment threshold in the previous finding: a 300-character reference costs roughly seven shipments of headroom.
findings.recommendation: Bound filed_reference at both walls: `z.string().min(1).max(200)` in the action, and a `length(filed_reference) <= 200` CHECK on declarations, matching the existing aggregate_id/correlation_id caps. Independently, do not embed the raw reference in the audit payload if it is already a column on the row the event points at.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The application emits no logs, no request ids, and no security events — an operator has nothing to diagnose an incident with
findings.boundary: Operations / incident response (cuts across every trust boundary)
findings.precondition: None. This is the steady state of the release candidate.
findings.affected_actor: The operator of the platform, and by extension every tenant whose incident cannot be diagnosed.
findings.exploit: Not an exploit — a capability that does not exist. Reproduce by taking any failure in the product (a failed filing, a rejected RLS write, a rate-limit trip, an auth failure, a swallowed list query error) and looking for evidence of it in stdout. There is none, for any of them.
findings.evidence:
Exhaustive grep over the whole source tree (excluding tests):
  grep -rn "log(\|createRequestId" --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx app/ src/ components/ | grep -v "\.test\."
  -> app/api/health/route.ts:241        (the only log call site in the product)
     src/infrastructure/observability/logger.ts:65,80,97   (the definitions themselves)
     components/ui/confirm-dialog.tsx:79 (a false positive: `export function ConfirmDialog(`)

  grep -rn "console\." --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx src/ app/ components/ | grep -v "\.test\."
  -> src/infrastructure/observability/logger.ts:50,80  (the sink)
     app/error.tsx:52  (client-side only)

The single production log line is a health-check database failure (app/api/health/route.ts:225-250). Nothing else in the application logs anything, ever.

Request ids are dead code:
  grep -rn "createRequestId" --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx . --exclude-dir=node_modules
  -> src/infrastructure/observability/logger.ts:97   (definition)
     src/infrastructure/observability/logger.test.ts:11,226,232,243,245  (its own test, only)

Correlation ids do not correlate a request either. The only producer is a locally-generated randomUUID() inside the calculation itself (src/application/calculations/calculate-line.ts:266), not threaded from any request:
  select count(*) total, count(correlation_id) with_corr from audit_events;  ->  2346|25

logger.ts:88-97 states the intent explicitly — "A short, sufficiently-unique per-request identifier for threading a request through logs, audit events ... see MASTER_PLAN §21/§28 ('Request IDs on every action, threaded into logs and audit events')". Neither half is implemented.
findings.why_controls_fail: The logger exists, is well built (field-name redaction, reserved keys, structured JSON) and is tested — which is exactly what made it look done. A passing logger.test.ts is not evidence anything calls the logger. Separately, src/application/audit/record-audit-event.ts:90-113 documents the decision not to log from the application layer (correctly, on layering grounds) and defers threading a request id through the Server Actions to post-release, with the honest note that "a warning on three of a dozen paths would be worse than none". The result of that deferral is none on all twelve. And listAuditEvents' own doc comment says outright that nothing about a query error "(message, code) is logged here" and that callers should inspect it at the infrastructure boundary — but no caller does, and no infrastructure boundary logs.
findings.impact: For any production incident — the filing blocker above, a partial outage, a suspected cross-tenant read, a credential-stuffing run against sign-in — there is no server-side evidence beyond Postgres' own logs. No request id means no way to correlate a user's report with anything. No security events means an authentication or authorization anomaly is undetectable. For a compliance product this also weakens the audit trail's standing: the audit_events table records successful mutations only, and nothing anywhere records attempts, refusals, or failures.
findings.recommendation: Before release, at minimum: generate a request id at the Server Action / route boundary, pass it into recordAuditEvent as correlationId on every call site (the parameter already exists), and log one structured line per Server Action failure including that id and the underlying error. Log rate-limiter denials and auth failures as security events. Then delete or wire up createRequestId — a tested helper with no callers reads as implemented and is worse than an absent one.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The audit screen tells an auditor "No audit events recorded yet" when the audit query failed
findings.boundary: Data access failure -> UI assertion (own-tenant, but the affected reader is an auditor or regulator)
findings.precondition: Any error on the audit_events query — transient database failure, connection exhaustion, a PostgREST error, a schema problem. No attacker needed.
findings.affected_actor: Anyone reading the audit trail to answer "what happened in this organization": an internal reviewer, an external auditor, a regulator.
findings.exploit: 1. Cause the audit query to error (any transient DB failure). 2. listAuditEvents catches it and returns []. 3. The page sees events.length === 0 with no filter params and sets emptyState = "no-events". 4. The table renders the positive claim: "No audit events recorded yet -- every mutation in this organization from here on is appended to this trail." There is no error state at all — the component's only three branches are no-events, no-matches, and rows.
findings.why_controls_fail: "Fail closed to an empty list" is the right convention for a dashboard widget and the codebase applies it consistently (the doc comment cites listSharedDataStatus and others as precedent). It is the wrong convention for an audit trail, because for an audit trail the empty result is itself a substantive claim — "nothing happened here" — and the screen states that claim in words rather than merely showing zero rows. The convention was applied uniformly without asking whether this one screen's empty state means something different from the others'. And because nothing is logged (previous finding), the failure leaves no trace anywhere: the auditor is told there is no activity, and the operator never learns the query failed.
findings.impact: An auditor or regulator can be shown, in plain English, that an organization has no recorded activity when in fact the query failed. That is the worst possible failure mode for the one screen whose entire purpose is evidentiary. The same false statement is on both the importer audit screen and the producer activity screen.
findings.recommendation: Give listAuditEvents a discriminated result — `{status:"OK", events} | {status:"UNAVAILABLE", reason}` — matching this codebase's own stated convention that expected outcomes are `{status, reason}` unions. Add an explicit error state to AuditEventTable that says the trail could not be loaded and must not be read as absence of activity. Log the underlying error. The audit trail should never render silence as a fact.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: A plain MEMBER can withdraw an ACTIVE, VERIFIED emission record that importers have already frozen into determinations — unaudited, un-gated, and invisible to the importer
findings.boundary: Producer-org member -> cross-org data integrity (grantee importers) and the domain lifecycle -> database
findings.precondition: Any active MEMBER (not ADMIN, not OWNER) of the organization that entered an emission_data row, using the Supabase JWT and anon key the app already ships to their browser. No elevated role, no stolen credential.
findings.affected_actor: Cross-tenant: every importer org that consumed the record through a sharing grant, plus the producer org itself (whose own audit trail is silently wrong). Ultimately the regulator, who receives a declaration built on a withdrawn figure.
findings.exploit: 1. As a plain MEMBER of the producer org, issue a direct PostgREST UPDATE on an ACTIVE + VERIFIED emission_data row setting status='DISCARDED'. The RLS UPDATE policy requires only org membership; enforce_emission_data_verification_gate is keyed on verification_status changes and on ACTIVE->DRAFT, and this statement is neither; prevent_emission_data_fact_change explicitly permits `status` to change. 2. The row is now DISCARDED. Grantee importers lose visibility (emission_data_select_own_org's grantee branch requires status='ACTIVE'). 3. On the importer's screens, checkActualSnapshotStaleness receives null for the current row and returns "CURRENT" — so the line keeps its green "Actual data" badge and its frozen "VERIFIED" status with no warning of any kind. 4. record_declaration_filed never re-checks emission_data, so the declaration files on the withdrawn figure. 5. No audit_events row is written by any of it.
findings.evidence:
Live in p14_review_sandbox. Setup — a plain MEMBER of the owning org:
  insert into auth.users (id,email,email_confirmed_at,aud,role) values ('99999999-...','p14rev-prodmember@example.test',now(),'authenticated','authenticated');
  insert into memberships (org_id,user_id,role) values ('97034b42-1e01-49e3-b94c-6451bd07fff2','99999999-...','MEMBER');
  select 'before', status, verification_status from emission_data where id='0f401852-a2c0-4a72-8f9b-98052720d586';
  ->  before|ACTIVE|VERIFIED

The attack, as `authenticated` with that member's claims:
  set local role authenticated;
  set local request.jwt.claims = '{"sub":"99999999-9999-9999-9999-999999999999","role":"authenticated"}';
  update emission_data set status='DISCARDED' where id='0f401852-a2c0-4a72-8f9b-98052720d586' returning id, status, verification_status;
  ->  0f401852-a2c0-4a72-8f9b-98052720d586|DISCARDED|VERIFIED
     UPDATE 1

Verified after, in a separate session:
  select 'after', status, verification_status from emission_data where id='0f401852-...';
  ->  after|DISCARDED|VERIFIED

No audit event was produced:
  select count(*) from audit_events where aggregate_id='0f401852-a2c0-4a72-8f9b-98052720d586';  ->  0

Supporting source:
  - Domain forbids it: src/domain/emissions/emission-data-lifecycle.ts:160-170, DISCARD requires status === 'DRAFT'.
  - DB permits it: app.prevent_emission_data_fact_change lists status among the columns that MAY change; app.enforce_emission_data_verification_gate's own comment states "DISCARD and SUPERSEDE are unaffected because they do not change verification_status".
  - Policy has no role check: emission_data_update_own_org USING/WITH CHECK is `entered_by_org_id IN (SELECT app.user_org_ids())` plus an evidence-ownership clause — no app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of anywhere.
  - Grantee loses sight: emission_data_select_own_org grantee branch requires `status = 'ACTIVE' AND verification_status = 'VERIFIED'`.
  - Importer sees no change: src/domain/emissions/check-actual-snapshot-staleness.ts:53-55, `if (currentEmissionData === null) { return "CURRENT"; }`; and src/application/emissions/list-actual-determined-lines.ts:455, `staleness: stalenessByLineId[line.id] ?? "CURRENT"`.
  - UI asserts it: app/(importer)/shipments/[id]/emissions-cell.tsx:210-224 renders `<Badge tone="success">Actual data</Badge>` and the warning badge only when staleness === "STALE".
  - Filing does not re-check: `select prosrc from pg_proc where proname='record_declaration_filed'` contains zero occurrences of `emission_data` (grep -c -> 0).

This write COMMITTED in p14_review_sandbox (the disposable database only — never the `postgres` database, never a hosted project). Exact restore for that row:
  psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "update emission_data set status='ACTIVE' where id='0f401852-a2c0-4a72-8f9b-98052720d586';"
(prior verified state: status='ACTIVE', verification_status='VERIFIED', version=1, entered_by_org_id='97034b42-1e01-49e3-b94c-6451bd07fff2', installation_id='d46f9150-7353-4010-86cb-9a013b2c0631'.)
findings.why_controls_fail: P14 hardened this trigger against un-verification, ACTIVE->DRAFT regression, and evidence removal, and its comments give the exact right reason each time — "Importers may already have frozen its evidence set into a determination." That reasoning applies with equal force to discarding the record outright, and the trigger explicitly excludes that case. The domain lifecycle is the only thing enforcing DRAFT-only DISCARD, and the domain is not a boundary a raw PostgREST write passes through. Meanwhile the staleness check is built to detect exactly one thing — a strictly higher version on a currently-ACTIVE row — and its own doc comment names withdrawal and revocation as cases it deliberately reports as CURRENT, choosing "the quieter result" to avoid false alarms. That trade is defensible for a revoked grant; it is not defensible when the answer is "the producer withdrew this figure", because CURRENT is not silence, it is a claim.
findings.impact: A producer-side member can invalidate figures that counterparty importers are relying on, with no admin approval, no audit record, and no signal to anyone. The importer continues to see a green, verified, apparently-current determination and can file a CBAM declaration on a figure its own source has withdrawn. The producer's audit trail shows the record as last ACTIVATED, contradicting the row's actual state — so even a diligent operator reconstructing events from the audit log gets the wrong answer.
findings.recommendation: Two independent fixes, both needed. (1) In app.enforce_emission_data_verification_gate (or a sibling), refuse `old.status = 'ACTIVE' AND new.status = 'DISCARDED'` outright — the domain has no such transition, so nothing legitimate breaks; supersession is the supported path. Gate any remaining status transition on app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of(entered_by_org_id), matching the verify/reject gate. (2) Split ActualSnapshotStaleness into three states — CURRENT, STALE, UNKNOWN — and return UNKNOWN when no current row is visible. The UI must render UNKNOWN as a warning ("source no longer available — cannot confirm this is current"), never as success. Consider also having record_declaration_filed re-check that each ACTUAL determination's source is still ACTIVE and visible, folding a failure into the existing INCOMPLETE path.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Migrations are neither atomic nor idempotent: re-applying 20260829580000 permanently drops two `shipment_lines` RLS policies and aborts before recreating them
findings.boundary: Migration application / partial-application recovery. Only 1 of 74 migration files declares its own transaction (`20260827110000` is the sole file with a `begin;`).
findings.precondition: Any repeated or interrupted apply of the migration set — an interrupted `supabase db push` re-run, a `supabase migration repair` followed by a re-apply, the two-pass fresh-rebuild recipe in DEPLOYMENT.md 'Rebuilding on a fresh database', or a manual `psql -f` recovery. No attacker.
findings.affected_actor: Every importer organization: with no INSERT and no UPDATE policy on `shipment_lines`, no shipment line can be created or edited by any user, in any organization.
findings.exploit: Apply the migration set, then apply `20260829580000_p13_review_shipment_line_determination_forgery_fix_v3.sql` a second time. Its lines 198-199 unconditionally `drop policy shipment_lines_insert_parent_not_terminal` and `drop policy shipment_lines_update_parent_not_terminal`; execution then reaches line 637 `create trigger shipment_lines_validate_emission_determination_trg`, which fails because the trigger already exists; the recreations at lines 654 and 668 are never reached. Because the file carries no BEGIN/COMMIT, the drops are already committed.
findings.evidence:
Isolated reproduction on p14rev_fresh:
  BEFORE re-run:
    select cmd from pg_policies where tablename='shipment_lines' order by 1;
    -> DELETE / INSERT / SELECT / UPDATE
  psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f supabase/migrations/20260829580000_p13_review_shipment_line_determination_forgery_fix_v3.sql
    -> psql:...20260829580000_...sql:640: ERROR:  trigger "shipment_lines_validate_emission_determination_trg" for relation "shipment_lines" already exists
  AFTER re-run:
    select cmd from pg_policies where tablename='shipment_lines' order by 1;
    -> DELETE / SELECT

File evidence: supabase/migrations/20260829580000_...sql:198-199 (unguarded drops), :637 (the failing CREATE TRIGGER), :654 and :668 (the never-reached recreations).

Scale of the non-idempotency: re-applying all 74 files to an already-migrated database gave ok=36, fail=38. Transaction discipline: `grep -c '^begin;'` across supabase/migrations/*.sql -> 1 of 74.

Same class in the PENDING set, with a realistic trigger: 20260903180000 does `alter table public.calculation_results drop constraint if exists calculation_results_numeric_format_ck;` (line 50) then `add constraint ... check (...)` (lines 52-65) with no transaction. Its own header states 'Verified before applying: all 21 existing rows LOCALLY are non-negative'. If any production row violates the new stricter predicate, the ADD fails and production is left with NO numeric-format constraint on calculation_results at all — strictly worse than before the migration ran.
findings.why_controls_fail: Nothing in the repository asserts per-file atomicity; I grepped docs/ and .github/ for any such claim and found none. The 20260829580000 header explains WHY the policies are dropped early ('to clear the dependency on the old 2-arg function') but the file is written as if it will only ever run once on a database in one specific prior state. The comparator catches the resulting missing INSERT policy, but only when someone runs it — and, per finding 7, it does not catch the missing UPDATE policy at all.
findings.impact: A recovery or rebuild that re-applies the set can leave the production schema silently unable to accept or edit shipment lines — the primary importer workflow — with no error surfaced anywhere. The 20260903180000 variant would silently retire an invariant that was added as a P14.1 security fix.
findings.recommendation: Wrap every migration file in `begin; ... commit;`, as 20260827110000 already does — 73 files, mechanical, and it converts every partial-application failure into a clean no-op. At minimum wrap the ones that drop before recreating (20260829500000, 20260829540000, 20260829580000, 20260903130000, 20260903180000). Independently, verify 20260903180000's predicate against production data before promoting it, not against the 21 local rows.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: `compare-database-posture.mjs` prints POSTURE MATCHES for a restored database containing none of the application's data
findings.boundary: Disaster recovery acceptance. BACKUP_RESTORE.md names 'compare-database-posture.mjs returning POSTURE MATCHES' as the outstanding acceptance criterion for the real hosted restore drill.
findings.precondition: A restore that recreates the schema but loses, truncates or fails to load the data — a schema-only dump, a `--schema-only` flag, a restore whose COPY phase failed after DDL succeeded, or a restore into the wrong target.
findings.affected_actor: Every tenant and the regulator, at the worst possible moment: the operator running the drill concludes recovery succeeded.
findings.exploit: Compare a fully-populated source against a schema-identical but empty target and read the verdict.
findings.evidence:
Row counts, source vs target, at the time the comparator reported every check [MATCH]:
  organizations       sandbox=688  fresh=2
  memberships         sandbox=502  fresh=2
  shipments           sandbox=517  fresh=1
  shipment_lines      sandbox=515  fresh=1
  declarations        sandbox=27   fresh=0
  emission_data       sandbox=92   fresh=1
  calculation_results sandbox=436  fresh=0
  audit_events        sandbox=2347 fresh=2
  evidence_files      sandbox=13   fresh=1
  sharing_grants      sandbox=87   fresh=0
Comparator verdict on that pair: [MATCH] on all 13 source-vs-target checks and [OK] on all 9 self-checks (only `schemas` differed, over two unrelated scratch schemas).
And standalone: `node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs --check <that database>` -> `RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES`.
None of the 22 queries in the file (CHECKS at :56-233, SELF_CHECKS at :241-430) reads a row count, a checksum, or any table's contents. The regulatory dataset is not exempt: nothing asserts that an ACTIVE regulatory_datasets row exists or that default_emission_values holds 12,540 rows.
findings.why_controls_fail: The 2026-08-29 drill did check row counts and md5 digests per table (BACKUP_RESTORE.md:328-340). The 2026-09-03 re-drill then declared 'The acceptance test is no longer a checklist a human reads. It is scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs' and did not carry the content checks into the script or restate them alongside it. The correction to one blind spot removed the coverage the previous procedure had.
findings.impact: The one gate standing between a hosted restore and 'recovery confirmed' cannot distinguish a complete restore from an empty schema. Combined with findings 1 and 2, POSTURE MATCHES is compatible with: no data, no integrity triggers, and `authenticated` holding TRUNCATE.
findings.recommendation: Add a content check: per-table row counts source-vs-target, plus the per-table column-list md5 the 2026-08-29 drill already used, plus an absolute self-check asserting exactly one ACTIVE `regulatory_datasets` row with 12,540 `default_emission_values` rows (the invariant `/api/health` already checks). Keep it in the same script so the acceptance test stays one command.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The comparator is blind to the entire `storage` schema — the evidence-file access-control surface — and a reconstruction differing there by three policies and a bucket still reports MATCH
findings.boundary: Disaster recovery acceptance vs. the evidence-file authorization surface (`storage.objects` RLS, the `evidence` bucket's size/MIME limits from 20260829510000).
findings.precondition: Any restore or rebuild. BACKUP_RESTORE.md's own scope table already says 'Storage objects (evidence files) | NO', so storage is out of the backup's scope by design — but the acceptance test then reports success without noting that it examined nothing there.
findings.affected_actor: Every producer and importer relying on verification evidence; evidence files are what makes a VERIFIED emission record admissible.
findings.exploit: Compare two databases that differ by every storage policy and by the evidence bucket definition, and read the verdict.
findings.evidence:
select schemaname||'.'||tablename||' | '||policyname||' | '||cmd from pg_policies where schemaname='storage';
  sandbox -> (zero rows)
  fresh   -> storage.objects | evidence_storage_delete_own_org | DELETE
             storage.objects | evidence_storage_insert_own_org | INSERT
             storage.objects | evidence_storage_select_own_org | SELECT
select id, file_size_limit from storage.buckets;
  sandbox -> NONE
  fresh   -> evidence limit=20971520
select relrowsecurity from pg_class ... where nspname='storage' and relname='objects';
  sandbox -> true (RLS on, zero policies => deny-all)
  fresh   -> false (RLS OFF, three policies => inert)
Comparator verdict on that pair: [MATCH] on all thirteen source-vs-target checks; [OK] tables_without_rls; [OK] rls_without_policies.

Every query in the file is scoped to public/app — scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs lines 72, 87, 102, 118, 131, 146, 164, 178, 193, 207, 219, 296, 420 (`in ('public','app')`) and lines 321, 334, 351 (`= 'public'`). The `schemas` check verifies only that a namespace named `storage` exists.

Context that makes the divergence real rather than an artifact of my shim: .github/workflows/ci.yml states that four storage-touching migrations 'were marked applied via `supabase migration repair`' on the developer's host because `[storage] enabled = false`, and that their storage.objects policies are, quoting the repo, 'shim-verified only'. The sandbox — the copy of the candidate — carries zero of them.
findings.why_controls_fail: The file's stated lesson is 'the text of every policy, the exact grant set, and whether the references those policies make actually resolve'. It applies that lesson to two schemas and silently exempts the third, which happens to be the one holding regulatory evidence. `tables_without_rls` and `rls_without_policies`, the two checks that would have caught `storage.objects` with RLS off or with RLS on and no policies, are both hardcoded to `nspname = 'public'`.
findings.impact: A restored or rebuilt database can have every evidence-file policy missing, or present-but-inert with RLS off, and the recovery gate says the posture matches. In the RLS-off-with-policies state my reconstruction produced, any role holding table grants on `storage.objects` reads and writes every organization's evidence files.
findings.recommendation: Extend the schema filter to include `storage` for policy_definitions, effective_grants, rls_enabled and constraints, and extend `tables_without_rls` / `rls_without_policies` to `storage.objects`. Add a self-check asserting the `evidence` bucket row exists with its 20 MB limit and MIME allowlist. Separately, resolve the four `migration repair`-ed storage migrations before release — the candidate's own database does not carry them.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Two unauthenticated Server Actions in app/auth/callback/actions.ts have no rate limiter, and each forces a GoTrue call from the platform's single egress IP against a bucket shared by every tenant
findings.boundary: Unauthenticated internet -> the application's auth surface -> the shared Supabase GoTrue project, whose per-IP rate-limit buckets are keyed on the app server's one egress IP and are therefore common to all customers.
findings.precondition: None. No account, no session, no cookie. The attacker needs only the action ID, which is published in a world-readable static chunk, and the ability to send an HTTP POST.
findings.affected_actor: Every signed-in user of every tenant simultaneously. This is cross-tenant: one anonymous attacker degrades authentication for all customer organisations at once, including during a CBAM filing deadline.
findings.exploit:
1. Fetch the public client bundle and read the action IDs (no auth required for /_next/static/*). establishSessionAction = 601b1b6dc3ebf94923f3cc5f67f4856fef4d7b3935, exchangeCodeForSessionAction = 401186c0850b3d136d3b6b8d37e5b8aa0a62b3cee4.
2. POST a Server Action invocation with that Next-Action header and a locally crafted, unsigned JWT as access_token whose `exp` is in the past (or absent entirely), plus any string as refresh_token. The JWT is only base64-decoded, never verified, so it costs nothing to make.
3. In GoTrueClient._setSession, `hasExpired` is initialised true and stays true when payload.exp is absent or past, so control reaches `await this._callRefreshToken(currentSession.refresh_token)` -- a real POST to GoTrue /token?grant_type=refresh_token. (If instead you supply a future exp, control reaches `this._getUser(access_token)` -- also a real GoTrue network call. Both branches egress.)
4. Repeat ~150 times per 5 minutes -- 0.5 requests/second, one host, no account. supabase/config.toml documents token_refresh as 'Number of sessions that can be refreshed in a 5 minute interval per IP address' = 150. Because every one of these calls originates from the Railway container, GoTrue sees a single IP for the entire platform, so that 150 is the whole platform's budget.
5. Legitimate users' session refreshes -- issued server-side by proxy.ts on every request -- now fail. Their access tokens expire, RLS denies everything, and they are silently signed out. exchangeCodeForSessionAction gives the same egress amplification via the PKCE branch, plus unlimited one-time-code guessing.
findings.why_controls_fail: The two-key build-time/runtime bypass guard is intact and I verified it holds -- but it protects limiters that were never applied here. The in-memory limiter cannot help either: it is keyed on the CLIENT's IP, whereas the resource being exhausted is keyed on the SERVER's egress IP, so even a perfectly enforced per-client limit places no ceiling on aggregate egress. Every sibling auth path was given a limiter (signIn 10/5min, signUp 5/10min, requestPasswordReset 5/10min, updatePassword 5/10min, confirmEmailLink 30/10min) -- app/auth/confirm/actions.ts:56-72 even wraps the directly analogous verifyOtp call in confirmEmailLinkLimiter. These two actions were simply missed. docs/runbooks/INCIDENT_RESPONSE.md:191-199 tells responders that ineffective rate limiting means 'check whether the service is scaled to more than one instance', which will send them down the wrong path entirely for this failure.
findings.impact: Platform-wide authentication denial of service for every tenant, from an unauthenticated attacker, at roughly half a request per second from a single host. On a regulatory-filing product this is an outage during the window customers cannot miss. Secondarily, exchangeCodeForSessionAction offers unmetered guessing against one-time PKCE authorization codes with no application-layer ceiling.
findings.recommendation: Add a limiter to both actions, matching the shape used at app/auth/confirm/actions.ts:56-72 (a shared AUTH_CALLBACK_RATE_LIMIT keyed on getClientIp(), checked as the first statement, returning the existing {status:'error', code:'over_request_rate_limit'} shape). That closes the unauthenticated per-client hole. It does NOT close the shared-egress problem underneath it -- for that, a single global counter across all GoTrue-calling paths is needed, sized below the hosted project's token_refresh / sign_in_sign_ups values, which must first be read off the dashboard and recorded in docs/architecture/ENVIRONMENT.md. Until that global counter exists, the app cannot bound its own GoTrue egress at all.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Per-client-IP limiters cannot bound project-wide GoTrue budgets, and the production Auth rate-limit values are recorded nowhere
findings.boundary: Any one tenant (or one anonymous caller) -> the shared Supabase Auth project's rate-limit budgets, which are either project-wide (email) or per-IP against the app's single egress IP (sign-in/sign-up, token refresh, OTP verification).
findings.precondition: For the email budget: one ordinary account with permission to invite, or unauthenticated access to the password-reset form. For the sign-in budget: three or four distinct source IPs, since the app's own limiter allows 10 sign-ins per 5 minutes per client IP.
findings.affected_actor: Every tenant. One customer's normal bulk activity, or one attacker, consumes a budget that all customers share.
findings.exploit:
Sign-in path: the app permits 10 sign-in attempts per 5 minutes per client IP (SIGN_IN_RATE_LIMIT). GoTrue permits 30 sign-in/sign-up requests per 5 minutes per IP, and because signInWithPassword runs on getServerSupabaseClient() -- server-side -- GoTrue sees one IP for the whole platform. Three client IPs x 10 attempts = 30 = the entire platform's budget consumed within the app's own limits, without ever tripping a single limiter. Every customer then receives over_request_rate_limit on sign-in.

Email path: email_sent is documented as a per-hour PROJECT-WIDE count, not per-IP. The app allows inviteMemberAction 20 per 10 minutes per IP and requestPasswordResetAction 5 per 10 minutes per IP -- budgets set far above whatever the project-wide hourly email cap is. One user issuing invitations at the rate the application explicitly permits exhausts the platform's hourly email allowance, after which no other tenant can send an invitation or a password reset until the hour rolls over.
findings.evidence:
supabase/config.toml:292-302:
  email_sent = 100          # 'Number of emails that can be sent per hour' (project-wide)
  token_refresh = 150       # 'per IP address' in a 5 minute interval
  sign_in_sign_ups = 30     # 'per IP address' in a 5 minute interval
  token_verifications = 30  # 'per IP address' in a 5 minute interval

and the file's own admission at supabase/config.toml:288-291:
  # THIS IS A LOCAL CLI TEST FIXTURE WITH NO HOSTED COUNTERPART. The
  # hosted project's Auth rate limits are dashboard settings; this value
  # has no effect on them, must never be presented as a production change,
  # and the production limits remain an owner-recorded item.

The app's own limits, all keyed on getClientIp() alone:
  app/(auth)/actions.ts:98-101   SIGN_IN_RATE_LIMIT   limit 10 / 5 min
  app/(auth)/actions.ts:117-120  SIGN_UP_RATE_LIMIT   limit  5 / 10 min
  app/team/actions.ts:68-71      INVITE_MEMBER        limit 20 / 10 min
  app/(auth)/forgot-password/actions.ts:39-42          limit  5 / 10 min

All of these call GoTrue server-side: app/(auth)/actions.ts:176-181 uses `await getServerSupabaseClient()` then `supabase.auth.signInWithPassword(parsed.data)`.

Search for a recorded production value returns nothing -- docs/architecture/ENVIRONMENT.md contains no Auth rate-limit entry; the only acknowledgement anywhere is docs/runbooks/AUTH_EMAIL_SMTP.md:156 ('Likewise leave Supabase's Auth rate limits at their defaults or higher.'), which is advice, not a recorded setting.

This was already raised and left open: docs/plans/P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:966 -- 'GoTrue rate-limit buckets are project-wide ... HIGH RISK ... No, but it degrades for everyone at once; owner must record and raise the hosted limits'. I re-derived it independently rather than accepting that entry, and the remediation it names has not happened.
findings.why_controls_fail: The in-memory limiter is per-client-IP by construction (src/infrastructure/rate-limit/rate-limiter.ts, keyed by the string the call site passes, always getClientIp()). It has no global counter and no notion of aggregate egress, so it is structurally incapable of bounding a resource that is shared across all clients. Every configured app-side limit is well above the shared GoTrue budget it feeds, so the limiters permit the exhaustion rather than preventing it -- they are not misconfigured, they are measuring the wrong thing. The one document that would have caught this, ENVIRONMENT.md, does not carry the production values at all.
findings.impact: A single tenant's permitted activity, or one attacker, causes platform-wide authentication and email failures for all customers. The failure is silent from the app's side: the app's own limiters report everything as within limits while GoTrue returns over_request_rate_limit.
findings.recommendation: Two separate actions, neither of which is code-only. First, read the hosted project's actual Auth rate limits off the dashboard and record them in docs/architecture/ENVIRONMENT.md as a deployment invariant, so the app's own limits can be sized against real numbers instead of CLI defaults. Second, add a process-global counter in front of every GoTrue-calling path (sign-in, sign-up, password reset, invitation, both callback actions from finding 1) sized below those recorded values, so the app fails one caller's request rather than exhausting the shared budget. Note that a global in-process counter is still per-replica; if the service is ever scaled past one instance this needs the shared store that master plan section 41 already lists as an open owner decision.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: A plain MEMBER can write arbitrary forged events into their organization's permanent, undeletable audit log, naming aggregates their org does not own
findings.boundary: Authenticated org member -> the organization's audit record, which is also the organization's only evidence of who did what
findings.precondition: A MEMBER seat in any organization, and the ability to reach the database or PostgREST with their own session JWT -- which is what the browser client already holds. No admin role and no elevated capability.
findings.affected_actor: The organization, its owners and admins, and any auditor reading the trail. Also, indirectly, counterparties named in forged payloads.
findings.exploit: As MEMBER be92879e in org 8eb4367f, insert audit_events rows directly. The policy audit_events_insert_own_org_as_self checks only three things: actor_type='USER', actor_user_id = auth.uid(), org_id in the caller's own orgs, and event_type in a 39-entry catalog. It does not check that the event corresponds to any real mutation, that aggregate_id names an existing row, that the row belongs to this org, that aggregate_id is even a UUID, or that the actor held the capability the event implies. So a member can insert: `emission_data.verified` naming e862d928 -- an emission_data row owned by a DIFFERENT organization (c7b4fb24) -- with a payload naming someone else as verifier; `membership.role_changed` claiming a promotion from MEMBER to OWNER; `declaration.marked_ready` with aggregate_id 'not-even-a-uuid'. All three committed. The forged rows are then unremovable: `delete from audit_events where org_id=<own org>` affects 0 rows, because the table has no DELETE policy -- so neither the forger, nor an admin, nor an owner can clean up. Because components/audit/audit-event-view.ts renders payloads with a deliberately generic `key: value, key: value` summarizer rather than per-type templates, a forged row is visually indistinguishable from a real one in the audit screen. Volume is unconstrained at this layer: the application's rate limiter (src/infrastructure/rate-limit) is in-process and is bypassed entirely by writing to the API directly.
