Rendering: components/audit/audit-event-view.ts summarizePayload -- generic `key: value` join, no per-event_type validation.
findings.why_controls_fail: record-audit-event.ts's doc comment states the design intent plainly: the policy's WITH CHECK "makes a plain client-side insert safe from forgery", which is why every mutation site shares one client-side helper instead of a per-mutation SECURITY DEFINER RPC. That claim is half right. It makes ACTOR forgery impossible -- I confirmed that, along with SYSTEM impersonation, cross-org writes, backdating, non-catalog types, UPDATE and DELETE, all correctly refused. But it makes no attempt at CONTENT integrity, and the whole architecture rests on the stronger reading. A policy can only see the row being inserted; it has no way to know whether the mutation the row describes actually happened, so a client-side insert can never be forgery-proof in the sense the comment needs. The catalog restriction narrows the vocabulary but does not help: every one of the 39 permitted types is a claim worth forging. Append-only, which is a genuine defence against tampering with real events, becomes an amplifier here -- it guarantees the forgeries are permanent.
findings.impact: The audit log is the compliance record and the organization's own evidence in a dispute. A member can fabricate entries that read as a verification that never occurred, a role change that never happened, or a declaration readiness on a nonexistent aggregate -- and can do so at volume, permanently, with no one able to remove them. That defeats the trail in both directions: it can be used to manufacture false evidence, and it can be used to bury real evidence in noise. Combined with the audit-suppression blocker above (a member can delete-by-omission what they do), a member has both halves of full control over what the organization's audit history says about them.
findings.recommendation: Move the audit write behind the mutation rather than beside it. Two workable shapes, both already present in this codebase: write the audit row inside the same SECURITY DEFINER function that performs the mutation, the way create_organization_with_owner() and record_declaration_filed() already do; or, where that is too large a change, add a per-event-type SECURITY DEFINER RPC that re-derives aggregate_id and payload from the actual row rather than trusting the caller, and then revoke INSERT on audit_events from `authenticated` entirely. As an interim mitigation that is much cheaper: keep the client-side insert but add a policy predicate requiring aggregate_id to name a row visible to and owned by the caller's org for the aggregate_type given -- that alone would have blocked FORGED-1 and FORGED-3. Whatever is chosen, note that revoking direct INSERT is the only change that actually closes the class.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Observability is effectively absent: one log call site in the entire application, request IDs never generated, no security events, and no signal on any failure path
findings.boundary: The product -> the operator responsible for diagnosing and responding to an incident
findings.precondition: None. This is the shipped state.
findings.affected_actor: Whoever is on call. Also every tenant, since an incident that cannot be diagnosed cannot be bounded or disclosed accurately.
findings.exploit: Not an exploit -- a measured absence, which is what makes the two blockers above silent. Four measurements: (1) `log()` is imported at exactly one place in the entire codebase, app/api/health/route.ts:13, and is called once, inside that route's catch block. No Server Action, no application service, no mutation, no auth flow, no error path logs anything server-side. (2) `createRequestId()` (src/infrastructure/observability/logger.ts:97) has zero call sites -- the master plan's §21/§28 commitment to "Request IDs on every action, threaded into logs and audit events" is entirely unimplemented. (3) Correlation coverage in audit_events is 1.4%: of 1734 rows, only the 25 `calculation.computed` rows carry a correlation_id, and that value comes from a bare `randomUUID()` at calculate-line.ts:266, not from createRequestId, and is never written to a log line -- so it correlates a calculation_results row to an audit_events row and to nothing else. Every other event type is 100% NULL. (4) There is no security_events table in the schema, and no logging of authentication failures, capability denials, RLS 42501 refusals, or rate-limit rejections -- a rate-limited search simply does `return []` (app/(importer)/shipments/[id]/actions.ts:383) with no record that throttling occurred. app/error.tsx:52 does call console.error, but it is a client component, so that lands in the visitor's browser console, not in any server log.

src/infrastructure/observability/ contains exactly two files: logger.ts and logger.test.ts.
findings.why_controls_fail: The pieces exist and are individually well built -- logger.ts has a considered field-name deny-list for secrets, reserved keys that cannot be spoofed, and a UUID request-id generator -- but almost nothing is wired to them. The logger's own comment describes app/api/health/route.ts as "the only production call site today", which is accurate and is the problem rather than a caveat. The one place a failure signal does exist and is honoured is the cross-org consumption path (crossOrgConsumptionRecorded, read at app/(importer)/shipments/[id]/actions.ts:1009), which shows the pattern is achievable; it just was not applied anywhere else. record-audit-event.ts's decision not to import the logger is defensible on layering grounds in isolation, but it was taken without the compensating step -- threading the outcome to the Server Actions, which the same comment identifies as both able to reach the logger and the natural home for a request id -- being done, and the comment records that as deferred.
findings.impact: On a production incident an operator has Next.js's own request log and audit_events, and nothing else. There is no request id to correlate a user's report to a server-side event, no record of authentication or authorization failures, no record of rate limiting, and no record of any application error. Worse, the one datastore that would carry incident evidence is the same one the first blocker lets an ordinary user silently suppress and the third lets them forge -- so the fallback is itself untrustworthy. Detecting either of those two attacks from telemetry is not merely hard, it is impossible with what is shipped.
findings.recommendation: Do not treat this as a post-release nicety, because it is the reason the audit-suppression blocker is silent. Minimum for release: generate a request id at the entry of every Server Action with createRequestId(), pass it as correlationId into every recordAuditEvent call (which already accepts the field and writes the column), and log one structured line per action outcome including that id. Then log, at minimum, every non-OK recordAuditEvent result, every rate-limit rejection, and every unexpected error caught in a Server Action. That is a mechanical change across the action files and it makes the correlation_id column -- which exists, is indexed by the audit list query, and is 98.6% NULL -- actually mean something.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: No gate anywhere detects a skipped test: 177 integration tests including every cross-org isolation suite vanish silently and vitest exits 0
findings.boundary: CI quality gate -> RLS / cross-tenant isolation regression coverage
findings.precondition: A single HTTP probe to http://127.0.0.1:54321/auth/v1/health taking longer than 1500 ms, or returning non-2xx, at vitest module-load time. On a shared GitHub-hosted runner that has just started ~10 Docker containers and is running a 61-migration replay, that is an ordinary transient — not an exotic condition.
findings.affected_actor: Cross-tenant: every tenant relying on the RLS isolation these suites are the standing regression coverage for, plus the own-tenant write-hardening boundary (emission_data ACTIVE+VERIFIED, shipment-line determination forgery).
findings.exploit: No attacker needed. The probe at tests/integration/organizations-isolation.test.ts:134-150 catches every error and returns false; `describe.skipIf(!localSupabaseReachable)` then skips the entire file. Repeat for 12 files. `vitest run` reports the tests as skipped and exits 0. .github/workflows/ci.yml contains no step that inspects the skip count, so the job is green with zero isolation coverage. An attacker who wants this deterministically only needs a change that makes the probe slow (or a reviewer who never notices it happened once).
findings.why_controls_fail: The workflow believes it has closed this. ci.yml:166-172 states the explicit health probe "closes the second half of this finding's suggested fix: if the stack ever fails to actually become reachable for any reason, this step fails LOUDLY, rather than the isolation suites silently skipping again." That reasoning does not hold: the preflight at ci.yml:291 and ci.yml:324 uses `curl --max-time 5` at stack-startup time, while each suite re-probes independently with a 1500 ms abort minutes later, inside the `Test` step. The two checks have different timeouts, different clients and different moments. Proving the stack was up at T0 proves nothing about 12 independent probes at T1. Nothing bridges the gap, and `vitest run`'s exit code cannot: a skipped test is not a failure to vitest, which I confirmed empirically.
findings.impact: The suites written specifically to lock in every previously-found cross-org bug (per the workflow's own comment at ci.yml:143-156) can silently not run, on the exact release the candidate is being certified for, with a green check mark. This is the same 'green by omission' failure mode the workflow's comments describe four separate times for other steps — and it is still live for the largest block of security coverage in the repository.
findings.recommendation: Make the skip count a hard gate. Run vitest with `--reporter=json --outputFile=` and fail the step if `numPendingTests`/`numTodoTests` for tests/integration/** is non-zero, or assert an exact expected passing-test count for that directory. Second, remove the self-skip from CI entirely: gate on an env var the workflow sets (e.g. `REQUIRE_LOCAL_SUPABASE=1`) that turns the probe failure into a thrown error rather than a skip — the same pattern already applied correctly to the Storage-gated E2E specs at tests/e2e/producer-journey.spec.ts:117-124 (`if (process.env.CI && !storageAvailable) throw new Error(...)`). That pattern exists in this repo and simply was not applied to the vitest side.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: CI re-applies seed.sql after every migration, provably reversing 20+ deliberate REVOKEs; only 3 are hand-re-asserted, so the security suites certify an ACL posture no deployed environment has
findings.boundary: CI environment fidelity -> function/table privilege posture (the layer below RLS)
findings.precondition: None. ci.yml:315 executes seed.sql unconditionally after `supabase migration up --local`, on every build-and-test run.
findings.affected_actor: Own-tenant and cross-tenant: the privilege layer that RLS does not constrain (EXECUTE on SECURITY DEFINER RPCs, TRUNCATE) is the layer being mis-modelled.
findings.exploit: Not an attack on the app — an attack on the gate. 1) Add a migration with `revoke all on function public.<new_rpc>(...) from public; grant execute ... to authenticated;`. 2) Push. 3) ci.yml:315 runs supabase/seed.sql, whose line 23 `grant all on all functions in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role;` re-grants EXECUTE on that function to anon. 4) Every security test in the job now runs against a posture where anon holds EXECUTE. seed.sql's hand-maintained re-assert list (lines 84-105) covers only calculation_results and record_calculation_result, so the new revoke is untested forever and nothing reports it.
findings.evidence:
Sandbox (disposable p14_review_sandbox only; read-only query):

The anon grant provably does not come from the migrations:
$ grep -rn "grant execute on function public.record_declaration_filed|...create_organization_with_owner|...accept_organization_invitation" supabase/migrations/*.sql
20260828080000_organization_onboarding_rpc.sql:108:grant execute on function public.create_organization_with_owner(text, text, text[]) to authenticated;
20260828130000_organization_invitations.sql:303:grant execute on function public.accept_organization_invitation(uuid) to authenticated;
20260829330000_p9_declarations_schema.sql:1031:grant execute on function public.record_declaration_filed(uuid, text) to authenticated;
20260829380000_p11_review_...sql:349:grant execute on function public.accept_organization_invitation(uuid) to authenticated;

Each is immediately preceded in its own migration by `revoke all on function public.<name>(...) from public;` (24 such REVOKEs enumerated by `grep -rniE "^\s*revoke " supabase/migrations/*.sql`). Only `record_calculation_result` survives with the narrow posture — the single function seed.sql hand-re-asserts.

file:line — .github/workflows/ci.yml:315 (the deliberate re-apply); supabase/seed.sql:23 (`grant all on all functions in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role;`); supabase/seed.sql:68-70 (the file's own admission: "These statements mirror the migrations named above and must be updated with them... the alternative -- teaching this file which tables are special -- is a list that rots silently").
findings.why_controls_fail: seed.sql's own header argues the blanket grant "only restore[s] the base table-level ACL both environments are supposed to share" and that "RLS policies are the real access control in every environment." Both premises fail for this candidate: 20260903170000 and 20260903190000 exist precisely because RLS is *not* the whole control — TRUNCATE and EXECUTE are outside RLS. The mitigation chosen (a hand-maintained re-assert list) is acknowledged in the file as rot-prone, and no gate verifies it stays in step. The one test cited as the guard (tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts, "the calculation-result write boundary") covers exactly the three entries already on the list — it cannot detect the 21 revokes that are already being reversed, nor the next one added.
findings.impact: Every security assertion made by the CI-run integration suites is made against a privilege posture that is strictly more permissive than the migrations define, differing on 20+ functions. The job therefore cannot certify the function-level ACLs of any deployed environment, and cannot detect the recurrence of the exact class of defect that produced 20260903190000 (a member calling the trusted write channel directly). A gate whose environment does not match what it certifies is not a gate.
findings.recommendation: Stop re-applying seed.sql after migrations. Either (a) replace ci.yml:315 with a targeted grant of only the base-table privileges the hosted platform bootstraps, applied BEFORE the second migration pass so migration revokes land last; or (b) after seed.sql, replay the privilege-relevant statements by extracting every `revoke`/`grant` from supabase/migrations/*.sql in order, rather than maintaining a hand-written list. Then add a posture assertion to the job: dump `proacl` for every public-schema function and every table's relacl, and diff it against a committed expected-posture fixture — a gate that fails on drift instead of a comment that asks humans to remember. scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs already exists and appears to do this kind of comparison; it is not invoked anywhere in ci.yml.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The invitation UPDATE policy checks only the new status, so an ADMIN can rewrite every other column of any invitation record — including an already-ACCEPTED one — reattributing it to an outsider, or relocating it into another organization, with no audit event
findings.boundary: Intra-tenant integrity / non-repudiation of the membership record, and (in the org_id variant) the tenant boundary itself. This is the record that answers "how did this person become an administrator of this organization" — the exact question P14/F5 added membership.invitation_created and .invitation_revoked audit events to answer.
findings.precondition: ADMIN or OWNER of the organization, and nothing else. The write is plain PostgREST — PATCH /rest/v1/organization_invitations?id=eq.<id> with the public anon key and the admin's own JWT. It never goes near revokeInvitation() and needs no service-role key. The org_id-relocation variant additionally needs the attacker to be ADMIN/OWNER of a second organization, which anyone can create for themselves through onboarding.
findings.affected_actor: Own-tenant: the organization whose invitation history is falsified, the innocent colleague the invitation is reattributed to, and any auditor or regulator relying on the platform's account of who granted whom access. Cross-tenant in the org_id variant, which moves one organization's record into another's.
findings.exploit:
Setup (isolated ids in the sandbox): org VictimCo b0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001 with OWNER a0000000-...-001, ADMIN a0000000-...-002, MEMBER a0000000-...-003; outsider a0000000-...-004 who is a member of nothing.

Step 1 — an invitation exists and has been ACCEPTED, the honest record: id d0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003, email invitee@partner.test, role ADMIN, status ACCEPTED, invited_by a0000000-...-002 (the admin), accepted_by a0000000-...-005.

Step 2 — the same ADMIN, acting only as `authenticated`, issues ONE update whose only concession is that the final status reads REVOKED:

  set local role authenticated;
  set local request.jwt.claims = '{"sub":"a0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002","role":"authenticated","email":"admin@victimco.test"}';
  update public.organization_invitations
     set status='REVOKED',
         email='nobody@nowhere.test',
         role='MEMBER',
         invited_by='a0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000004',   -- an outsider, member of no org
         accepted_by=null,
         accepted_at=null,
         created_at='2020-01-01',
         expires_at='2020-01-08'
   where id='d0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003';

Step 3 — variant: instead of rewriting fields, move the record out of the organization entirely. As an admin of both VictimCo and OtherCo (b0000000-...-002):

  update public.organization_invitations
     set status='REVOKED', org_id='b0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002'
   where id='d0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001';

Both succeed. The record now says a different person, at a different role, was invited on a different date by someone who has never been a member — or it is no longer in this organization at all.
findings.evidence:
Live SQL in postgresql://127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox, inside a real `begin; ... rollback;` psql transaction.

The policy, read from the running database (not from the migration file):
  select policyname||' | '||cmd||' | USING='||coalesce(qual,'-')||' | CHECK='||coalesce(with_check,'-') from pg_policies where tablename='organization_invitations';
  organization_invitations_insert_admin_or_owner | INSERT | CHECK=(app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of(org_id) AND (invited_by = auth.uid()) AND (status = 'PENDING'::text))
  organization_invitations_update_admin_or_owner | UPDATE | USING=app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of(org_id) | CHECK=(app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of(org_id) AND (status = 'REVOKED'::text))

Note the asymmetry: INSERT carries `invited_by = auth.uid()`; UPDATE does not.

The rewrite, before and after:
  BEFORE: | d0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003 | invitee@partner.test | ADMIN  | ACCEPTED | invited_by a0000000-...-002 | accepted_by a0000000-...-005
  UPDATE 1
  AFTER : | d0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003 | nobody@nowhere.test  | MEMBER | REVOKED  | invited_by a0000000-...-004 | accepted_by (null) | created_at 2020-01-01 00:00:00+00

  select 'audit rows for this invitation:', count(*) from public.audit_events where aggregate_id='d0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003';
  audit rows for this invitation: | 0

The org_id relocation:
  UPDATE 1
  id d0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001 | org_id b0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002 | status REVOKED

No trigger intercepts any of this:
  select pg_get_triggerdef(t.oid) from pg_trigger t join pg_class c on c.oid=t.tgrelid where c.relname='organization_invitations' and not tgisinternal;
  (0 rows)

Source: supabase/migrations/20260828130000_organization_invitations.sql:156-166 (the policy) and :142-150 (the INSERT policy that DOES carry the invited_by clause). The contradicted comment is at :152-155: "this policy only needs to guard against an ADMIN/OWNER using a bare update to do anything other than revoke (e.g. it cannot be used to forge an ACCEPTED row)."
findings.why_controls_fail: Three controls should have stopped this and none does. (a) The RLS WITH CHECK is column-blind: it asserts one predicate about the NEW row's `status` and one about `app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of(new.org_id)`, and Postgres row-level WITH CHECK says nothing at all about the other nine columns. The migration author reasoned about the state machine ("can it forge ACCEPTED?" — no) and never about the payload. (b) The `invited_by = auth.uid()` anti-forgery clause exists on INSERT and was simply not carried to UPDATE, so the identical forgery blocked at creation is permitted at modification. (c) The audit trail cannot compensate, because recordAuditEvent lives in src/application/organizations/invitations.ts:307-324 and only runs when the write goes through revokeInvitation(); a direct PostgREST PATCH with the same JWT produces zero audit rows, as measured above. The one residual defence is that the historical `membership.invitation_accepted` event written by the RPC (20260828130000:265-285) retains {email, role} in its payload — so a reader who knows to cross-check the append-only audit stream can detect the divergence. Nothing in the product does that, and the org_id-relocation variant leaves the audit event pointing at an aggregate_id that is no longer in the organization.
findings.impact: The platform's record of who was granted administrative access to a CBAM declarant organization, at what role, by whom, and when, is editable by any administrator with no trace. An administrator who granted an accomplice ADMIN access can, after the fact, restate that invitation as a MEMBER invitation issued by a colleague who was never involved, backdate it, and erase who accepted it. The relocation variant removes the record from the organization's own view entirely. For a regulated compliance product this is a non-repudiation failure in exactly the artefact the P14 audit-catalog work (20260903130000_p14_audit_catalog_invitation_events.sql) was added to make trustworthy.
findings.recommendation: Tighten organization_invitations_update_admin_or_owner's WITH CHECK to pin every column the transition must not touch, in the same shape the INSERT policy already uses. Concretely, a new migration redefining the policy so the only permitted change is PENDING -> REVOKED: add `and org_id = <old>` semantics via a BEFORE UPDATE trigger (RLS WITH CHECK cannot see OLD), or — simpler and matching this schema's existing precedent (app.prevent_org_id_change, app.prevent_membership_user_id_change on public.memberships) — add a BEFORE UPDATE trigger on organization_invitations that raises unless `new.status='REVOKED' and old.status='PENDING'` and every one of org_id, email, role, invited_by, created_at, expires_at, accepted_at, accepted_by is unchanged. Do it as a trigger, not a policy, so it also covers the service-role path. Add an integration test that asserts the rewrite above is rejected — this class of defect is invisible to every test that only checks the status latch.

findings.title: expires_at is client-controllable on INSERT, so an admin can mint an invitation that never expires — the seven-day window the P11 review's own read-time hardening depends on is not enforced anywhere
findings.boundary: Tenant admission. The expiry is the control that bounds how long a grant of organizational access remains claimable by whoever comes to control an email address.
findings.precondition: ADMIN or OWNER of the organization. The write is plain PostgREST with the public anon key and the admin's own JWT; the application's inviteMember() never sets expires_at, so this is reachable only by calling the REST API directly — which any admin can do, since the anon key is public and their JWT is in their own browser.
findings.affected_actor: Own-tenant: the organization, whose admission window is silently unbounded. Also whoever later controls the invited mailbox — the "mailbox reassignment" scenario the schema's own comments name as the reason a seven-day expiry exists at all.
findings.evidence:
Live SQL in p14_review_sandbox, COMMITTED deliberately to prove persistence past the transaction:

  --- and now with literal infinity ---
                    id                  |       email        | role  | status  | expires_at 
   d0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002 | other@partner.test | ADMIN | PENDING | infinity
  INSERT 0 1

  --- and backdated created_at, arbitrary accepted_at/accepted_by ---
   d0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003 | created_at 1999-01-01 00:00:00+00 | accepted_at 1999-01-01 00:00:00+00 | accepted_by a0000000-...-001 | status PENDING
  INSERT 0 1

  COMMIT
  ### state after commit
   d0000000-...-001 | invitee@partner.test | ADMIN | PENDING | created_at 2026-09-03 15:13:52 | expires_at 2126-09-03 15:13:52
   d0000000-...-002 | other@partner.test   | ADMIN | PENDING | created_at 2026-09-03 15:13:52 | expires_at infinity
   d0000000-...-003 | third@partner.test   | ADMIN | PENDING | created_at 1999-01-01 00:00:00+00 | expires_at 2026-09-10 15:13:52

And the infinity row remains RLS-visible to its addressee indefinitely — as that addressee:
   d0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002 | b0000000-...-001 | ADMIN | PENDING | infinity

Source: supabase/migrations/20260828130000_organization_invitations.sql:79-80 (`expires_at timestamptz not null default (now() + interval '7 days')` — a DEFAULT, not a constraint) and :142-150 (the INSERT policy, which constrains org_id, invited_by and status and says nothing about expires_at). src/application/organizations/invitations.ts:83-101 shows the application insert omits the column, which is why the default has been mistaken for an invariant.
findings.why_controls_fail: The seven-day window is a column DEFAULT. A default is advice to a caller who omits the column; it is not a constraint and does nothing to a caller who supplies one. The RLS INSERT policy — the only other gate — enumerates three predicates and expires_at is not among them. The P11 hardening (20260829380000) then built two policies ON TOP of this value (`expires_at > now()` in organization_invitations_select_own_email and organizations_select_via_pending_invitation), and the accept RPC checks `v_invite.expires_at < now()`, so all three read-time and accept-time expiry checks are enforcing a bound the writer chooses. There is no CHECK constraint bounding expires_at relative to created_at or now(), and no trigger on the table at all (`select pg_get_triggerdef(...) where c.relname='organization_invitations'` → 0 rows).
findings.impact: On its own: a permanent, standing claim on ADMIN access to a CBAM declarant organization, held by whoever controls one email address, for as long as the row exists. Chained with finding 3 (nothing revokes an issuer's invitations when the issuer is removed), it is a durable backdoor that survives the offboarding of the administrator who planted it — I demonstrate that chain end to end in finding 3. Backdating created_at additionally sinks the row to the bottom of the Team screen's `order by created_at desc` list (src/application/organizations/invitations.ts:454-457), so it is not the first thing a reviewing admin sees.
findings.recommendation: Add a CHECK constraint bounding the window in the schema — e.g. `check (expires_at > created_at and expires_at <= created_at + interval '7 days')` — in a new migration, so the bound holds for every writer including service-role. Add `and expires_at <= now() + interval '7 days'` to organization_invitations_insert_admin_or_owner's WITH CHECK as the RLS-layer counterpart. Consider also making created_at non-writable (revoke the column privilege, or pin it in the same BEFORE-INSERT trigger), since a forged creation date defeats the chronological review the Team screen offers. This finding is already recorded in docs/plans/P14_ADVERSARIAL_REVIEW_FINDINGS.json and is unremediated at cad99adb — I re-derived it independently against the running database before reading that file.

findings.title: Removing an administrator does not revoke the invitations they issued: a fully removed ex-admin's pending ADMIN invitation still mints a fresh ADMIN membership
findings.boundary: Tenant admission and offboarding. The organization believes it has removed an administrator's authority; it has removed only their membership row, not the standing grants they left behind.
findings.precondition: An administrator who has (or had) ADMIN/OWNER, issues an invitation to an address they control, and is subsequently offboarded — by hard DELETE (removeMember) or, per the codebase's preferred path, by deactivation. No access is retained at the moment of removal; the capability is entirely in the row left behind.
findings.affected_actor: Own-tenant: the organization that believes it offboarded an administrator. Because an ADMIN of a declarant organization can read every producer's shared verified emissions data flowing into it and can act on declarations, the blast radius reaches the counterparties whose data that organization holds.
findings.evidence:
Live SQL in p14_review_sandbox, real `begin; ... rollback;`:

  DELETE 1
   admin memberships left: | 0
   invitation status after removal: | PENDING | infinity

   issuer still a member of victimco? | f

   result_status | result_org_id                        
   OK            | b0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001

   resulting membership: | ADMIN | deactivated_at (null)

That is: the issuer holds zero memberships in the organization, and their invitation still mints a fresh, active ADMIN membership.

No revocation machinery exists. `grep -rln "organization_invitations" supabase/migrations/` lists eight files, none of which is a removal/deactivation hook; `grep -n 'invitation' src/application/organizations/manage-membership.ts` returns one unrelated comment at line 339 and nothing else. There is no trigger on public.memberships that touches organization_invitations (`select pg_get_triggerdef(...)` on memberships returns exactly three: memberships_enforce_last_active_owner_trg, memberships_prevent_org_id_change_trg, memberships_prevent_membership_user_id_change_trg).
findings.why_controls_fail: accept_organization_invitation (verified against the live body via pg_get_functiondef, not the migration file) validates the ACCEPTOR — authenticated, confirmed email matching, PENDING, unexpired, not already a member — and never revalidates the ISSUER. It reads v_invite.role and inserts a membership at that role without asking whether invited_by still holds any authority in v_invite.org_id, or ever did at accept time. The deactivation work (20260829360000) was careful and correct about the issuer's own live access — I confirmed a deactivated admin cannot mint a NEW invitation (`ERROR: new row violates row-level security policy`) — but it treats an already-created invitation as a settled fact rather than a delegation that should lapse with its delegator. Nothing in removeMember, deactivateMembership or changeMembershipRole touches the invitations table, and the expiry that would otherwise bound the exposure is itself attacker-chosen (finding 2).
findings.impact: Offboarding is incomplete in a way the Team screen does not show. A departing or dismissed administrator retains a standing, self-service route back to ADMIN of the organization — with finding 2, one that never lapses. Re-entry is via the ordinary accept flow, so it produces a normal membership.invitation_accepted audit event that looks like any other onboarding; the anomaly is only visible to someone who notices the invitation was issued by a person who is no longer there, which is precisely the field finding 1 lets an admin rewrite.
findings.recommendation: On membership removal, deactivation, and demotion below ADMIN, revoke that user's PENDING invitations for that organization in the same transaction. The natural place is a trigger on public.memberships (AFTER DELETE OR UPDATE), mirroring how 20260829360000 chose a single change point over patching each call site; setting status='REVOKED' inside a SECURITY DEFINER trigger sidesteps the RLS UPDATE policy correctly. Independently, harden the accept path: have accept_organization_invitation re-check that invited_by still holds an active ADMIN/OWNER membership in v_invite.org_id and return a distinct status (e.g. ISSUER_NO_LONGER_AUTHORISED) otherwise — that closes the window even for invitations already in flight. This finding is recorded in docs/plans/P14_ADVERSARIAL_REVIEW_FINDINGS.json and is unremediated at cad99adb; I re-derived it live before reading that file.

findings.title: /auth/callback establishes an attacker-supplied session from the URL fragment on page load, with no consent step and no identity-switch warning — the exact guard that was added to /auth/confirm was never applied to the callback that is still live
findings.boundary: Session identity. Which account the browser is acting as, on the product's own trusted, branded origin.
findings.precondition: The victim opens a link. Nothing else — no credentials, no prior access, no membership anywhere. The attacker needs only their own ordinary Snowkap account (to obtain a real access_token/refresh_token pair) and a way to put a URL in front of the victim.
findings.affected_actor: Any user, signed in or not. Cross-tenant in effect: the victim ends up operating inside the ATTACKER's organization while believing they are in their own.
findings.exploit:
1. Attacker signs up normally and reads their own session tokens from their browser.
2. Attacker sends the victim, on the real product origin:
     https://<app>/auth/callback#access_token=<attacker_at>&refresh_token=<attacker_rt>&type=invite
3. The page mounts and the effect runs unconditionally. parseAuthLinkError finds no error params, so it proceeds; searchParams has no `code`, so it reads access_token and refresh_token from window.location.hash and calls establishSessionAction(accessToken, refreshToken) — a Server Action, deliberately built (per its own doc comment) so that its cookie writes become real Set-Cookie headers the browser CANNOT refuse, specifically so that it OVERWRITES an existing httpOnly session. The victim's own session is replaced.
4. On success the page calls router.replace(next), defaulting to /accept-invitation. The only text the victim ever sees is "Signing you in…". No identity is named, no confirmation is requested.
5. The victim, believing they are themselves, works: creates shipments, enters emissions, uploads evidence — into the attacker's organization, readable by the attacker at leisure.
findings.why_controls_fail: isSafeRedirectPath was the fix applied to this page (page.tsx:145-155), and it addresses the wrong half of the chain its own header comment describes. That comment names "open redirect + session injection" and "session fixation" — the redirect was fixed and the injection was not. The mitigation the codebase already invented for exactly this (show who you are about to become; require a click) was applied only to /auth/confirm, in the same commit series, because that page was rewritten for the unrelated token-burning incident of 2026-09-02. /auth/callback was left on its original auto-establish design. Next.js Server Action origin checking does not help: the action is invoked by the real origin's own JavaScript after the victim loads the URL, so it is same-origin by construction. The CSP in next.config.ts:122-149 does not help either — no script is injected; the attack is entirely within the page's intended behaviour.
findings.impact: Silent, unauthenticated forced login on the trusted origin. A CBAM declarant's staff member can be moved into an attacker-controlled organization without any visible identity change, and any shipment, emissions figure, or evidence document they subsequently enter lands where the attacker can read it — including commercially sensitive supplier emissions data. In the reverse direction it is a phishing primitive: the attacker controls the org name and content the victim then sees, rendered under Snowkap branding on Snowkap's own domain.
findings.recommendation: Give /auth/callback the same shape /auth/confirm already has: do not establish anything on mount. Read the tokens, call getUser() read-only to learn who is currently signed in and who the token belongs to, render both identities, and establish the session only on an explicit user action. At minimum, refuse silently to replace a DIFFERENT existing identity — if a session already exists and the incoming token's sub differs, show the switch and require confirmation. Longer term, retire the implicit hash-fragment path entirely: all four templates in supabase/templates/ already route through /auth/confirm with a token_hash, so the fragment shape exists only for links already in flight and can be given a hard deprecation date. This finding is recorded in docs/plans/P14_ADVERSARIAL_REVIEW_FINDINGS.json and is unremediated at cad99adb; I derived it from source before reading that file.

findings.title: The verifier's evidence can be swapped for different documents at DRAFT+VERIFIED and the record then ACTIVATEd -- the exact window upload-evidence.ts's own comment claims is closed
findings.boundary: Intra-tenant privilege boundary: MEMBER vs the ADMIN/OWNER verification decision.
findings.precondition: A MEMBER of the producer org, and a record sitting at DRAFT + VERIFIED -- the normal resting state after an ADMIN verifies and before anyone activates.
findings.affected_actor: The ADMIN/OWNER whose verification signature (verifier_user_id) stays attached to a document set they never saw, plus every downstream importer and the regulator relying on it.
findings.exploit: Three statements as a MEMBER against a DRAFT+VERIFIED record: upload (or directly INSERT) a second evidence_files row against the same emission_data -- permitted, since evidence_files_insert_own_org has no verification clause and evidence GROWTH is deliberately allowed; then `update public.emission_data set evidence_file_ids = array['<new id>']`, which detaches the verifier's actual basis and substitutes the new file; then `update public.emission_data set status='ACTIVE'`. The activation gate passes because it tests only `coalesce(array_length(new.evidence_file_ids,1),0) = 0`. verifier_user_id is untouched, so the record presents as ADMIN-verified. The original evidence_files row survives (its delete is still blocked) but is no longer referenced by anything, so it never appears in the record's evidence list.
findings.why_controls_fail: src/application/evidence/upload-evidence.ts:462-464 states the delete lock was deliberately keyed on verification_status rather than status precisely so it would cover 'a DRAFT+VERIFIED record sitting unactivated, which is exactly the moment a producer could otherwise strip evidence the verifier already signed off on and then ACTIVATE anyway.' That reasoning protects the evidence_files ROWS and stops there. The evidence_file_ids ARRAY -- which is what the record, the activation gate and the determination validator actually read -- is protected only by 20260903150000's shrink rule, and that rule requires old.status='ACTIVE'. At DRAFT it does not run. app.prevent_emission_data_fact_change deliberately whitelists evidence_file_ids (20260829240000 Part 1). So the named window is closed for one artefact and open for the one that matters.
findings.impact: A verification decision can be silently re-pointed at documents the verifier never reviewed, and the record then goes live carrying that verifier's identity. This is the substantive integrity claim of the whole evidence subsystem -- that a VERIFIED figure is backed by what the verifier approved -- and it does not hold.
findings.recommendation: Freeze the evidence set at the moment of verification, not at activation: capture an immutable `verified_evidence_file_ids` snapshot in the same trigger branch that sets verifier_user_id := auth.uid(), and have the activation gate require that new.evidence_file_ids CONTAINS that snapshot (growth allowed, substitution and removal not). Equivalently, extend the shrink rule to fire on `old.verification_status = 'VERIFIED'` regardless of old.status. Add a test asserting a DRAFT+VERIFIED record cannot activate with an evidence set that does not contain the verified snapshot.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: sha256, size_bytes and original_filename on evidence_files are freely client-chosen through a direct API insert, contradicting the schema's own written guarantee and destroying the only tamper-detection the evidence subsystem has
findings.boundary: Application-layer trust boundary: the schema treats these columns as server-measured facts; the RLS-only path lets the client author them.
findings.precondition: A MEMBER of the owning org and the public anon key. No admin, and no PRODUCER_OPERATOR capability check applies -- that gate lives only in upload-evidence.ts, not in RLS.
findings.affected_actor: Any auditor, verifier, regulator or importer who would otherwise use the digest to detect that the stored evidence is not the evidence that was verified.
findings.exploit: `insert into public.evidence_files (id, org_id, emission_data_id, storage_path, original_filename, mime_type, size_bytes, sha256, uploaded_by_user_id) values (..., 'Independent Verifier Report 2025.pdf', 'application/pdf', 4096, '0000...0000', <self>);` -- accepted. The row can then be appended to an ACTIVE+VERIFIED record, since evidence GROWTH is deliberately permitted. There is no UPDATE policy on evidence_files, so the fabricated digest is thereafter immutable and indistinguishable from a genuine one.
findings.why_controls_fail: The server-side computation is real but lives entirely in the application (createHash in src/application/evidence/upload-evidence.ts). evidence_files_insert_own_org checks only org membership and parent ownership; the CHECK constraints check only FORM (`sha256 ~ '^[0-9a-f]{64}$'`, `size_bytes > 0 and <= 20971520`), never correspondence to any stored object. There is no FK and no trigger from evidence_files to storage.objects -- `select count(*) from pg_constraint where confrelid='storage.objects'::regclass` -> 0, and `pg_trigger` on evidence_files -> 0. So the 'two walls, always both' posture the repository states everywhere has exactly one wall here, and it is the bypassable one: PostgREST reaches the table directly with the anon key.
findings.impact: The digest is the mechanism by which evidence substitution would be caught. Since it is authored by the same party who could substitute the evidence, it detects nothing. Combined with finding 3, a swapped document arrives with a plausible filename, a plausible size and a digest that will never be checked against anything. The row can also name a storage_path with no object behind it, so the record shows attached evidence that cannot be downloaded -- and satisfies the activation gate and the determination validator regardless.
findings.recommendation: Either revoke INSERT on public.evidence_files from anon/authenticated and route all creation through a SECURITY DEFINER RPC that computes sha256/size_bytes itself (matching how organization onboarding is already handled in 20260828080000), or add a trigger that verifies storage_path resolves to a storage.objects row and derives size_bytes/sha256 from its metadata rather than accepting the client's. At minimum, stop asserting the guarantee in the migration comment while the RLS path does not enforce it -- that comment was read as evidence by at least one prior audit.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The P14 TRUNCATE revoke is scoped to `schema public` only; anon and authenticated still hold TRUNCATE on storage.objects, the table that indexes every tenant's evidence
findings.boundary: Role-privilege boundary. TRUNCATE is not subject to row-level security, so it crosses every tenant boundary in the system at once.
findings.precondition: Any path that executes SQL as anon or authenticated. As 20260903170000's own header argues for the public-schema case, PostgREST exposes no HTTP verb that issues TRUNCATE, so this is a privilege-escalation amplifier rather than a one-request exploit: a SECURITY INVOKER function, a raw-query injection, or a mis-scoped RPC.
findings.affected_actor: Every tenant simultaneously, and the regulator -- a single statement makes all evidence in all orgs unreachable.
findings.exploit: `set local role authenticated; truncate table storage.objects;` -- every object row for every bucket and every tenant is removed. RLS is not consulted. The evidence_files metadata rows survive, so the application keeps displaying evidence that can no longer be downloaded and whose sha256 digests can never be checked again.
findings.evidence:
psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox":

select has_table_privilege('authenticated','storage.objects','TRUNCATE'), has_table_privilege('anon','storage.objects','TRUNCATE'), has_table_privilege('authenticated','public.emission_data','TRUNCATE');
-> t|t|f

select table_schema,table_name,grantee from information_schema.role_table_grants where privilege_type='TRUNCATE' and grantee in ('anon','authenticated') order by 1,2;
-> storage|buckets|anon
   storage|buckets|authenticated
   storage|objects|anon
   storage|objects|authenticated
   (nothing in schema public)

Destruction demonstrated, with the count taken as postgres inside the same transaction so RLS cannot mask it:
begin;
  select 'postgres sees before', count(*) from storage.objects;   -> 2
  set local role authenticated; set local request.jwt.claims='{"sub":"aaaa0000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002","role":"authenticated"}';
  truncate table storage.objects;                                  -> TRUNCATE TABLE
  reset role;
  select 'postgres sees after authenticated TRUNCATE', count(*) from storage.objects;  -> 0
rollback;   post-rollback -> 2

For contrast, in the same session `delete from storage.objects;` as authenticated returned `DELETE 0` -- RLS governs DELETE and not TRUNCATE, exactly as the migration's header argues.

file:line -- supabase/migrations/20260903170000_p14_revoke_truncate_from_api_roles.sql: `revoke truncate on all tables in schema public from anon, authenticated;` and `alter default privileges in schema public revoke truncate on tables from anon, authenticated;`. No statement in that migration, or in any other migration in the repository, mentions the storage schema.

PARTIAL: the sandbox's storage schema is a shim, so the grant itself may not reflect the hosted project. The file:line scoping of the remediation is not in doubt; the live grant needs a read-only has_table_privilege check against production.
findings.why_controls_fail: The remediation correctly diagnosed the vulnerability class -- its own words: 'the single privilege in this schema that RLS does not constrain at all' -- and correctly identified the source as Supabase's `grant all on all tables in schema <X>` bootstrap, which Supabase applies to the storage schema as well as to public. It then scoped the fix to one schema. The migration also states 'Deliberately NOT revoking anything else', reasoning only about DELETE; the storage schema is not considered anywhere in it. Nothing else compensates: storage.objects RLS is irrelevant to TRUNCATE by definition.
findings.impact: Total, cross-tenant, unrecoverable-from-RLS destruction of the evidence object index for an append-only regulatory compliance record -- the precise outcome 20260903170000 was written to prevent, on the one table it did not cover. anon holds it too, so the reachable surface is wider than for a member-only defect.
findings.recommendation: Extend the revoke: `revoke truncate on all tables in schema storage from anon, authenticated;` plus the matching `alter default privileges`. Audit every non-public schema the API roles can reach (storage, graphql_public, any extension schema) with `select table_schema, table_name, grantee from information_schema.role_table_grants where privilege_type='TRUNCATE' and grantee in ('anon','authenticated')` and assert the result is empty in a test. Confirm against the real project first with the read-only has_table_privilege call above.

findings.title: The same shipment and the same calculation_results row can be frozen into two different filed declarations for two different reporting periods
findings.boundary: Declaration filing integrity -- the one-shipment-one-declaration assumption the LOCK-on-filing mechanism appears to enforce.
findings.precondition: ADMIN or OWNER of an IMPORTER_DECLARANT org writing member_shipment_ids directly (same precondition as finding 2).
findings.affected_actor: The regulator, and any reconciliation of a declarant's filings across periods. Own-tenant.
findings.exploit: File declaration D1 for ANNUAL 2026 containing shipment A. record_declaration_filed LOCKs A. Then create declaration D2 for ANNUAL 2025 whose member set also contains A. record_declaration_filed's lockability check accepts LOCKED alongside READY (deliberately, so amendments can re-cover already-locked shipments), so D2 files successfully. Both filed_snapshots claim the same shipment and cite the same calculation_result_id.
findings.why_controls_fail: The LOCK-on-filing mechanism looks like it prevents reuse, and record_declaration_filed's comment presents accepting LOCKED as safe because "an amendment covers shipments the superseded version already locked". But the acceptance is unconditional -- it is not restricted to declarations that actually supersede the one that did the locking, nor to the same reporting period. There is no uniqueness constraint or index anywhere binding a shipment id to at most one non-VOID filed declaration; declarations_period_original_uq and declarations_supersedes_uq constrain declarations per period, never shipments per declaration. And since the member shipments' own periods are never compared to the declaration's (finding 2), nothing else catches it either.
findings.impact: One import counted in two reporting periods, or attributed to the wrong one. Depending on direction this is double-counting or period-shifting; combined with finding 2 it lets a declarant move emissions between periods at will while every individual filing looks internally consistent and re-provable. The provenance block -- the artifact designed to make a filing re-provable years later -- actively corroborates both claims.
findings.recommendation: Restrict the LOCKED branch of the lockability check to the amendment case it was written for: accept a LOCKED member only when the declaration has supersedes_declaration_id set and that predecessor's own member_shipment_ids contains the shipment. Independently, add a uniqueness invariant that a shipment appears in at most one non-VOID FILED_RECORDED declaration outside an amendment chain, and reject at filing time with a named status.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Filing accepts calculation rows produced by superseded engine versions the current build cannot reproduce, including 1.1.0 — the version with the documented 1000x kgCO2e/t defect
findings.boundary: Time / release boundary: rows produced by a known-defective engine version cross into a freshly filed, immutable declaration snapshot without ever being recalculated.
findings.precondition: Any line whose latest calculation_results row carries an engine_version older than the running ENGINE_VERSION, and whose emission_determination and quantity have not changed since. No attacker required — this is the default outcome of calculating before a release and filing after it.
findings.affected_actor: Own tenant and the regulator. The filed figure is one the current engine disowns.
findings.exploit: 1. A line is calculated under engine 1.1.0 (or 1.2.0) and the row is persisted. 2. The engine is upgraded to 1.3.0. 3. Nothing recalculates. checkCalculationCurrency defines staleness as determination inequality only, so the line reads CURRENT. record_declaration_filed's INCOMPLETE gate compares determination, quantity and quantity_unit — never engine_version. 4. The declaration files, and filed_snapshot.totals.embedded_emissions_tco2e is summed from those rows. 5. An auditor later runs the reproduction proof and gets ENGINE_VERSION_CHANGED — an honest 'cannot check', reported as a named non-failure state that no gate acts on. The filed number is, by the platform's own contract, unprovable from the day it was filed.
findings.evidence:
psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox":
select engine_version, count(*) from public.calculation_results group by 1 order by 1;
 1.1.0 |  4
 1.2.0 | 14
 1.3.0 |  9

select id, filed_snapshot->'provenance'->'engine_versions', filed_snapshot->'totals'->>'embedded_emissions_tco2e' from public.declarations where status='FILED_RECORDED';
 d3d91df0-694e-4f0a-9ca0-f08fc26e4486 | ["1.1.0"] | 139
 aff726e5-9102-4743-b119-5dae6bac3b07 | ["1.1.0"] | 139
 5aaac096-1355-4dd2-933a-515d55fb5c11 | ["1.1.0"] | 139
 43038a5b-e29a-43b6-a917-033ccf7f58f0 | ["1.2.0"] | 139
 ... (10 further declarations at 1.2.0)

Code: src/domain/emissions/check-calculation-currency.ts — checkCalculationCurrency() takes only (calculatedAgainst, currentDetermination); engine_version is not a parameter. record_declaration_filed's member_line_counts filter (dumped from the sandbox with pg_get_functiondef) filters on `c.line_id is null or c.determination is distinct from ml.emission_determination or c.quantity is distinct from ... or c.quantity_unit is distinct from ...` — no engine_version clause. src/application/calculations/reproduce-calculation-result.ts:323 returns ENGINE_VERSION_CHANGED. grep for engine_version across app/ and components/ finds it only in the on-demand why-this-number panel and the CSV/XLSX exports — no blocking surface.
findings.why_controls_fail: The ENGINE_VERSION column exists precisely so that 'same inputs + version => byte-identical output' can be checked, and src/domain/calculations/types.ts states the consequence of the 1.2.0 -> 1.3.0 bump plainly: 'every calculation_results row already carrying "1.2.0" now reproduces as ENGINE_VERSION_CHANGED rather than REPRODUCIBLE.' The correct inference from that is that such rows must be recalculated before they can be filed. Instead the system treats ENGINE_VERSION_CHANGED as an informational outcome and files them anyway. The P13 report's 'we cannot retroactively fix historical rows' reasoning is about not rewriting engine_version on append-only rows — a correct decision that says nothing about whether filing should ACCEPT them. 1.1.0 specifically predates the numerator fix that stopped 'kgCO2e/t' being computed 1000x over, per the same file's own history.
findings.impact: A filed CBAM declaration can carry, today, a total assembled from calculations the current engine will not reproduce and in the 1.1.0 case is known to have produced 1000x-overstated values for a class of unit strings. The reproduction proof — the platform's headline audit guarantee — degrades to 'cannot check' on exactly the rows where checking matters most, and nothing in the filing flow tells the declarant that.
findings.recommendation: Add engine_version currency to the same gate that already enforces determination and quantity currency: fold `c.engine_version is distinct from <current>` into record_declaration_filed's uncalculated_count filter and into checkCalculationCurrency, so a stale-engine line surfaces as INCOMPLETE and the existing 'recalculate' workflow clears it. Since the current engine version is TypeScript, pass it into the RPC as a parameter (bound the same way p_engine_version already is) rather than hardcoding it in SQL. Surface stale-engine lines on the shipment detail screen with the same badge pattern already used for a stale determination.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Hydrogen (CN 2804 10 00) is omitted from the Annex II gate, adding indirect emissions the dataset never publishes — an over-report in the direction the release note says is impossible
findings.boundary: Regulatory correctness of the ACTUAL-path figure; also the accuracy of the candidate's own recorded risk statement.
findings.precondition: An importer determines a CN 2804 10 00 line from a verified ACTUAL record carrying a non-zero indirect_specific. Ordinary workflow.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant (surrenders more certificates than owed) and the regulator (receives an overstated figure that does not reconcile with the published defaults).
findings.exploit:
1. cbam_goods.sector for CN 2804 10 00 is 'HYDROGEN', which is not in ANNEX_II_SECTORS (calculate-line-emissions.ts:46-52).
2. The gate does not fire, so calculateFromActualDetermination sums direct + indirect (:326-332).
3. The ACTIVE dataset publishes NO indirect value for hydrogen for any of 122 countries — indirect_status is UNAVAILABLE on all 96 rows, and total = direct exactly. That is the identical signature the dataset gives every good the proxy DOES gate.
4. Real engine, 1000 t, direct 17.740 (the Other-Countries published default) plus a producer-reported indirect of 5.000: 22,740 tCO2e instead of 17,740 — 28% over.

findings.why_controls_fail: The D1 decision note (calculate-line-emissions.ts:54-101) is explicit that the proxy's imprecision now 'points the other way' and produces UNDER-reporting, and records that as the single accepted cost. It never considers the omission case, so the over-reporting direction is recorded nowhere — not in the comment, not in the rule register, not in the release report. The proxy was reasoned about as an over-inclusive set; nobody checked whether it was also under-inclusive. No test covers a HYDROGEN sector value.
findings.impact: Overstatement of embedded emissions on every ACTUAL-determined hydrogen line whose producer reports non-zero indirect emissions — the declarant surrenders and pays for certificates they do not owe, and the filed figure cannot be reconciled against the published defaults for the same good. Compounding this, the candidate's own recorded risk register asserts a single error direction that is demonstrably wrong, which will misdirect the next person who reviews this gate.
findings.recommendation: Same fix as the previous finding — this is the second half of the same defect and should be closed by the same change. Separately, correct the recorded risk statement: the D1 note asserts a single error direction and that assertion is false. A risk register that names the wrong direction is worse than one that names none, because it stops the next reviewer looking.

findings.title: An EU member state as origin country resolves through the Other-Countries fallback and produces a full CBAM figure for a good outside CBAM's scope
findings.boundary: CBAM scope boundary: third-country origin (in scope) vs. EU / Annex III-exempt origin (out of scope). The platform has no representation of this boundary at all.
findings.precondition: A shipment line declares origin_country 'DE' (or FR, IT, NL, ...; or NO, CH, IS, LI). shipment_lines_origin_country_check is `origin_country ~ '^[A-Z]{2}$'` and parseCountryCode (src/domain/shared/country.ts) validates only the same shape — any two uppercase letters are accepted.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant and the regulator: a CBAM liability is computed, presented and filable for goods that carry none.
findings.exploit:
1. mapCountry('DE') (supabase-regulatory-repository.ts:986-1030) queries countries by iso2 with country_type='COUNTRY' and active=true, finds nothing, and returns `{ status: "UNLISTED" }`.
2. The adapter's candidate-country list still includes the OTHER_TERRITORIES row (:299-310), so the resolver is handed the Other-Countries records.
3. resolveDefaultValue finds no records for the requested country (hasExactMatch false) and takes the R7 clause 1 fallback (:770-810), returning RESOLVED / OTHER_COUNTRIES_FALLBACK.
4. The DB validator's UNLISTED branch checks only that the iso2 is genuinely absent from `countries`, that the matched record is the Other-Countries row, and that the reason is OTHER_COUNTRIES_FALLBACK. 'DE' satisfies all three, because the regulatory dataset legitimately does not list EU member states.
5. A full embedded-emissions figure is produced (17.740 tCO2e/t for hydrogen), calculated, and eligible for a declaration.
The design turns the absence of EU states from the dataset — which is a signal that they are OUT OF SCOPE — into a trigger for the third-country fallback.

No EU or EFTA state is in the regulatory geography — so every one of them takes this path:
$ psql ... -tAc "select iso2, name from countries where iso2 in ('DE','FR','IT','ES','NL','PL','BE','AT','SE','NO','CH','IS','LI','GB','TR','UA','RS','BA','ME','MK','AL');"

(121 COUNTRY rows total, all third countries; DE/FR/IT/ES/NL/PL/BE/AT/SE and NO/CH/IS/LI all absent.)

Nothing downstream flags it — the declaration completeness report has no country or scope blocker at all:
$ grep -n -i "country|scope" src/domain/declarations/completeness.ts  ->  no matches
findings.why_controls_fail: This is documented, at src/domain/emissions/types.ts:41-56 and MASTER_PLAN §41, as a 'KNOWN OPEN GAP ... a deliberate, documented escalation -- not an oversight', pending an owner decision on how in-scope/out-of-scope should enter as a versioned dataset. I agree with that framing of the FIX. I do not accept it as a reason to ship: documenting a gap is not mitigating it. There is no warning in the UI, no blocker in buildCompletenessReport, no flag on the filed_snapshot, and no marker on the determination distinguishing 'genuine third country absent from the dataset' from 'EU member state, out of scope' — the type comment says so itself: 'Both currently resolve through the same R7 fallback.' A declarant cannot tell the two apart from anything the product shows them.
findings.impact: The product fabricates a CBAM liability where none exists, for any origin outside the dataset's 121 third countries — which includes every EU member state and every Annex III-exempt EFTA country. A declarant following the product's output files and pays for emissions on goods CBAM does not cover, and the platform gives them no signal that anything is unusual. The failure is silent and looks exactly like a normal Other-Countries fallback.
findings.recommendation: The proper fix is the versioned in-scope/out-of-scope dataset the escalation already describes, and it should not be short-circuited with a hardcoded country list. But shipping without ANY mitigation is the wrong call. A minimum acceptable interim, requiring no new regulatory fact: since country_type already distinguishes COUNTRY from OTHER_TERRITORIES, treat an UNLISTED origin as a hard blocker on the DECLARATION (a new CompletenessBlocker reason) rather than a silent fallback, and surface it on the line. That refuses to file a figure the platform cannot justify, and it fails in the safe direction, which is the posture the rest of this subsystem takes.

findings.title: shipments.release_date and reporting_period are member-mutable after creation, falsifying the domain's 'fixed by the release date alone' claim and reproduce-calculation-result.ts's explicit immutability premise
findings.boundary: Derived-fact integrity: reporting_period is documented as a pure function of release_date, and release_date is documented as immutable. Both are writable by any member through the ordinary RLS policy.
findings.precondition: Any authenticated member (not admin, not owner) of the owning org, on a shipment not in LOCKED or VOID status, writing directly via PostgREST. `shipments_update_own_org_not_terminal` grants UPDATE on `org_id IN (select app.user_org_ids()) AND status <> ALL (ARRAY['LOCKED','VOID'])` with no column restriction, and there is no trigger protecting these columns — `shipments_prevent_org_id_change_trg` guards org_id only.
findings.affected_actor: The regulator and the filing. A shipment can be moved out of its true reporting period, disappearing from that period's declaration with no completeness blocker raised; or its release date can be moved to silently change how its lines are classified and calculated.
findings.exploit:
Two consequences, both reachable:
1. PERIOD REALLOCATION. Rewrite reporting_period_kind/year/quarter. compute-declaration-draft-facts.ts selects members by matching reporting_period columns, so the shipment vanishes from its true period's declaration. buildCompletenessReport reports NO blocker — it only inspects shipments it was handed. record_declaration_filed re-verifies org, status, line counts, calculation currency and quantity, but never that a member shipment's reporting period matches the declaration's. The period under-reports by that shipment's entire embedded emissions.
2. SILENT RECLASSIFICATION AND GATE FLIP. release_date is the as-of date for findCbamGoodsByCode (`.or("active_from.is.null,active_from.lte.<asOf>")`), and every cbam_goods row has active_from = 2026-01-01 with none NULL. Setting release_date before 2026-01-01 makes the lookup return zero rows, so resolveGoodSectorForActualLine returns null, so the Annex II gate stops firing (calculate-line-emissions.ts:298-300 requires goodSector !== null). A recalculation of an untouched ACTUAL line then produces a different regulated number. The determination-validator trigger cannot intervene: it fires on shipment_lines, not shipments, and short-circuits when emission_determination is unchanged.
findings.evidence:
The policy, unrestricted by column:
$ psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "select policyname, cmd, qual, with_check from pg_policies where tablename='shipments';"

No protecting trigger (only org_id is guarded):
$ psql ... -tAc "select event_object_table, trigger_name, event_manipulation from information_schema.triggers where trigger_schema='public' and event_object_table='shipments';"
shipments|shipments_prevent_org_id_change_trg|UPDATE

UPDATE 1

Every good is dated from 2026-01-01, so a pre-2026 release date empties the classification lookup:
$ psql ... -tAc "select min(active_from), max(active_from), count(*) filter (where active_from is null) from cbam_goods;"
2026-01-01|2026-01-01|0
findings.why_controls_fail: Two explicit written claims in the candidate are false, and both are load-bearing. (a) src/domain/shared/reporting-period.ts:100-104: 'This is a pure classification, not a policy choice -- which regime applies is fixed by the release date alone.' It is derived once, in createShipment (src/application/shipments/create-shipment.ts:92), stored, and thereafter unprotected. (b) src/application/calculations/reproduce-calculation-result.ts:261-266 justifies re-deriving good_sector rather than freezing it precisely on this basis: 'shipment_id.release_date is a stable, immutable historical fact (no update path exists for it -- only create-shipment.ts ever writes it)'. That sentence is the stated reason a regulated input is not frozen into calculation_results, and it is untrue at the database layer. Notably, that same comment was already corrected once (P8 finding #1) for making the identical wrong assumption about cn_code; the release_date half of the assumption was left standing. The application has no update path — but RLS is the boundary that matters, and it grants one.
findings.impact: A period's filed total can be silently reduced by moving shipments out of it, with the completeness gate reporting no blocker because the shipment is simply no longer a member — an under-report that leaves no trace in the declaration. Independently, a regulated figure the platform treats as frozen and reproducible can be changed after the fact by editing a field on a different table, and the reproducibility check will then report MISMATCH on a calculation nobody touched, destroying the audit story for that line.
findings.recommendation: Protect both columns at the database, where the boundary actually is: a BEFORE UPDATE trigger on shipments rejecting any change to release_date and to the three reporting_period columns (the same shape as declarations_prevent_fact_change_trg, which already does exactly this for declarations). Then either freeze good_sector into calculation_results, or keep re-deriving it and let the now-true immutability claim stand. Independently, record_declaration_filed should verify each member shipment's reporting period against the declaration's — it already re-verifies org, status and calculation currency, and this is the one membership fact it takes on trust.

findings.title: compare-database-posture.mjs ignores the storage schema entirely: it certifies POSTURE MATCHES on a database with storage.objects RLS disabled and the evidence bucket's size/MIME limits gone
findings.boundary: Recovery verification boundary: the tool BACKUP_RESTORE.md:520-534 names as the acceptance test for a restore, applied to the evidence-file access-control surface.
findings.precondition: A restore or rebuild in which the storage-side objects do not come back exactly — the logical dump is `--schema=public --schema=app` (BACKUP_RESTORE.md:145-146) and carries none of them, and a Storage service that recreates storage.objects afresh may not carry the project's policies or the bucket's limits. The operator then runs the documented acceptance test and gets POSTURE MATCHES.
findings.affected_actor: Every producer/operator and importer organisation whose evidence files are in the evidence bucket. Cross-tenant: any authenticated member of any organisation can list and read every other organisation's evidence objects.
findings.exploit:
1. Restore/rebuild. storage.objects comes back with RLS off (or its three policies absent), and storage.buckets.evidence comes back with file_size_limit and allowed_mime_types NULL.
2. Run the documented acceptance test. It reports POSTURE MATCHES and the restore is accepted.
3. Any authenticated user now selects every organisation's evidence objects, and can upload an unbounded-size object of any MIME type through the direct Storage API — reopening P13 release blocker S7, whose fix is migration 20260829510000.
findings.evidence:
(a) The two databases differ by the entire storage control set and the tool cannot see it.

psql "...p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "select coalesce(string_agg(policyname,','),'<NONE>') from pg_policies where schemaname='storage'"
  <NONE>
psql "...p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "select count(*)::text||' bucket rows' from storage.buckets"
  0 bucket rows

psql "...p14rev_a10" -tAc "select string_agg(policyname,',') from pg_policies where schemaname='storage'"
  evidence_storage_delete_own_org,evidence_storage_insert_own_org,evidence_storage_select_own_org
psql "...p14rev_a10" -tAc "select id||' size='||coalesce(file_size_limit::text,'NULL')||' mimes='||coalesce(array_length(allowed_mime_types,1)::text,'NULL') from storage.buckets"
  evidence size=20971520 mimes=5

node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs <sandbox> <p14rev_a10>  ->  RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES

(b) The exposure is fail-OPEN, not fail-closed. In p14rev_a10_stor (p14rev_a10 + the sandbox's auth.users/organizations/memberships), with two evidence objects in two different organisations:

-- as shipped (RLS on, three policies present), user a5776b5a-52dc-447a-8950-da5d39741b96 of org d8c44bb5-00da-4d54-bd96-d38f2b6ea158:
  visible: d8c44bb5-00da-4d54-bd96-d38f2b6ea158/aaaa/orgA-secret.pdf

psql -c "alter table storage.objects disable row level security"
-- same user, same query:
  visible: d8c44bb5-00da-4d54-bd96-d38f2b6ea158/aaaa/orgA-secret.pdf
  visible: 1b635dfb-fb68-43f6-9001-2b9cacfc2a21/bbbb/orgB-secret.pdf

psql -tAc "select id||' size='||coalesce(file_size_limit::text,'NULL')||' mimes='||coalesce(array_length(allowed_mime_types,1)::text,'NULL') from storage.buckets"

node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs <sandbox> <p14rev_a10_stor>  ->  RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES

file:line — every one of the 14 comparison checks filters to public/app: scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:72, 87, 102, 118, 131, 146, 164, 178, 193, 207, 219. The self-checks filter to public only: :296, :321, :334, :351, :420. The only occurrence of the word 'storage' in the file is the `why:` string at :56, attached to the `schemas` check, which compares schema NAMES only — so 'storage' matches on both sides no matter what is inside it.
findings.why_controls_fail: The script's stated purpose (:14-18) is 'the text of every policy, the exact grant set, and whether the references those policies make actually resolve'. It delivers that for public and app and silently excludes storage, where three of the project's RLS policies and the entire platform-enforced upload-safety control set live. BACKUP_RESTORE.md:620 does disclose that storage OBJECTS are not in the dump, and the P14 review logged the dump-scope half — but graded it INFO/LOW on the reasoning that a missing policy is 'denial-only, self-announcing on first use'. That reasoning is wrong in both directions I measured: storage.objects RLS returning as DISABLED is fail-open cross-tenant read, not denial; and a bucket row restored without file_size_limit/allowed_mime_types is a working bucket with no limits, which is S7 reopened, not denial. Neither state is self-announcing — both look healthy and both are certified POSTURE MATCHES.
findings.impact: The declared acceptance criterion for production recovery cannot see the evidence-file access control at all. A restore that quietly loses it is signed off as proven, after which any authenticated member of any tenant can enumerate and download every other tenant's regulatory evidence, and the 20 MiB / 5-MIME platform-layer upload guard that closed a P13 release blocker is silently absent.
findings.recommendation: Add storage to the tool before this ships: (1) a comparison check for pg_policies where schemaname='storage' with full USING/WITH CHECK text; (2) a comparison check for storage.buckets rows including public, file_size_limit and allowed_mime_types; (3) a self-check that hard-fails when storage.objects exists with relrowsecurity=false, when the evidence bucket is missing, or when its file_size_limit/allowed_mime_types are NULL. Until then, BACKUP_RESTORE.md must not present POSTURE MATCHES as the acceptance criterion, because the sandbox this whole review was conducted against is itself missing all three storage policies and the bucket.

findings.title: View definitions and reloptions are never compared: losing security_invoker=true on latest_calculation_results leaks every tenant's emissions figures, and the tool still says POSTURE MATCHES
findings.boundary: Recovery verification boundary, and the RLS tenancy boundary on calculation_results reached through public.latest_calculation_results.
findings.precondition: A restore, rebuild or manual repair in which public.latest_calculation_results is recreated without `security_invoker=true`. The view is owned by postgres (which holds rolbypassrls=true on this cluster) and anon/authenticated hold SELECT on it, so without the reloption it reads the base table as its owner.
findings.affected_actor: Every importer/declarant organisation. Cross-tenant: an authenticated member of one organisation reads every other organisation's embedded emissions, certificates due and liability amounts.
findings.exploit:
1. Restore/rebuild loses the reloption (a plain `create view` without the option is enough).
2. Run the documented acceptance test -> POSTURE MATCHES; the restore is accepted.
3. Any authenticated user selects from public.latest_calculation_results and gets every organisation's rows.
findings.evidence:
On p14rev_a10_leak (template clone of the review sandbox, 26 calculation_results rows across 25 orgs), as user 4ad99e1a-3a55-48b2-be08-a08125568abd, a member of exactly one organisation:

-- as shipped
psql -tAc "select coalesce(array_to_string(reloptions,','),'NULL') from pg_class where relname='latest_calculation_results'"
  security_invoker=true
begin; set local role authenticated;
set local request.jwt.claims = '{"sub":"4ad99e1a-3a55-48b2-be08-a08125568abd","role":"authenticated"}';
  VIEW rows visible: 1
rollback;

-- restore loses the reloption
psql -c "alter view public.latest_calculation_results reset (security_invoker)"
psql -tAc "select coalesce(array_to_string(reloptions,','),'NULL') from pg_class where relname='latest_calculation_results'"
  NULL
begin; set local role authenticated;
set local request.jwt.claims = '{"sub":"4ad99e1a-3a55-48b2-be08-a08125568abd","role":"authenticated"}';
  auth.uid() = 4ad99e1a-3a55-48b2-be08-a08125568abd
  own orgs: 1
  base table rows visible: 1
  VIEW rows visible: 26
  VIEW distinct orgs leaked: 25
rollback;

And the verdict on that database (isolated mutation on p14rev_a10_mut, reloption reset and nothing else):

  [MATCH] schemas / tables / columns / rls_enabled / policy_definitions / effective_grants /
          schema_usage_grants / functions / function_grants / triggers / constraints / indexes /
          sequences / extensions  (all 14)
  [OK] all 9 self-checks
