And for authenticated the same delete-and-reinsert route is closed: DELETE -> 'DELETE 0' (no DELETE policy on declarations), forged INSERT -> 'ERROR: new row violates row-level security policy for table "declarations"'.

Source: app.prevent_declaration_fact_change is attached only as `CREATE TRIGGER declarations_prevent_fact_change_trg BEFORE UPDATE ON public.declarations FOR EACH ROW` (pg_get_triggerdef). pg_roles: service_role rolbypassrls = t.
findings.why_controls_fail: app.prevent_declaration_fact_change() is a genuinely well-built control and its own comment states the intent precisely — 'a filed row's own snapshot/reference/timestamp can never be rewritten later by any statement at all, not even another SECURITY DEFINER one that forgot to check the current status first'. It achieves that for UPDATE. It is not attached to INSERT or DELETE, so delete-then-reinsert is not a rewrite as far as the trigger is concerned and it never runs. 20260903190000's scope note ('service_role retains its direct table grant... the trusted boundary by definition') covers the calculation_results decision honestly, but it does not make the stated immutability claim for filed_snapshot true, and nothing else does either: the snapshot carries no hash, no signature, and no chain to an append-only log, so a substituted snapshot is indistinguishable from the original. The declaration.filed audit_events row does carry the original embedded_emissions_tco2e, which is a partial mitigation — but audit_events is likewise writable by service_role.
findings.impact: The one artifact the whole subsystem exists to protect is not tamper-evident against a compromised service-role key or a mistaken server-side code path. Given the design intent stated in the trigger's own comment, this is a gap between claim and behaviour rather than an accepted risk, and the review question was asked precisely because the claim is load-bearing.
findings.recommendation: Two cheap steps. (1) Attach a BEFORE INSERT branch to app.prevent_declaration_fact_change() (or a sibling trigger) rejecting any INSERT with status='FILED_RECORDED' or a non-null filed_snapshot/filed_reference/filed_at — nothing legitimate inserts a pre-filed declaration, since the only sanctioned creation is a DRAFT. (2) Add a BEFORE DELETE trigger refusing deletion of a FILED_RECORDED row outright. Both close the loop without touching service_role's grants. If tamper-EVIDENCE (as opposed to prevention) is wanted, store a digest of filed_snapshot in the declaration.filed audit event and check it when the snapshot is rendered — that also covers the case where the whole row is legitimately restored from a backup.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Self-dealing: a plain MEMBER of a dual-capability organisation issues itself OPERATOR_PROVIDED verified actual data, and capabilities are self-asserted and append-only
findings.boundary: Owner decision D2's provenance boundary — the distinction between OPERATOR_PROVIDED (attested by the operator running the installation) and IMPORTER_ENTERED (transcribed by the importer from an external operator).
findings.precondition: For the MEMBER path: membership of an organisation holding both IMPORTER_DECLARANT and PRODUCER_OPERATOR. For reaching that state from an importer-only organisation: one OWNER, once — capabilities are self-service.
findings.affected_actor: The regulator, and any downstream reader of a declaration. The provenance field is the mechanism by which a declarant's claim about where its numbers came from is recorded; here an organisation asserts the stronger claim about itself with nothing external attesting to it.
findings.exploit:
C2, as importer OWNER 1111...0004: `update organizations set capabilities = array['IMPORTER_DECLARANT','PRODUCER_OPERATOR'] where id='2222...0002';`
C3, as plain MEMBER 1111...0003 of the dual-capability org 2222...0003, all in one transaction: insert an ACTIVE+VERIFIED emission_data row on the org's own OPERATOR_PROVIDED installation with fabricated evidence and self-named verifier; insert a shipment; insert a shipment line carrying an ACTUAL determination with `record_provenance:'OPERATOR_PROVIDED'` and `sharing_grant_id: null`.
findings.evidence:
C2: `before | {IMPORTER_DECLARANT}` -> `UPDATE 1` -> `after | {IMPORTER_DECLARANT,PRODUCER_OPERATOR}`. The only trigger on organizations is `organizations_capabilities_append_only`, which permits addition.
C3: `actor role in RevBoth | MEMBER`, then `INSERT 0 1` three times, then `C3 SELF-DEALT operator-attested determination | 8888...0009 | OPERATOR_PROVIDED | (sharing_grant_id null) | {"direct_specific": "0.0000001", "indirect_specific": "0.0000001"}`.
findings.why_controls_fail:
`app.enforce_record_provenance_capability` is the control, and it enforces exactly one thing: that the installation's provenance matches a capability its own organisation holds. Capabilities are asserted by the organisation about itself (`organizations_update_owner` permits an OWNER to set them, and the append-only trigger only stops removal), so the check is circular — an organisation that wants OPERATOR_PROVIDED grants itself PRODUCER_OPERATOR and now legitimately holds it.
The validator's D2 check (`v_snapshot->>'record_provenance' is distinct from v_installation_provenance -> return false`) then faithfully confirms the snapshot matches the installation, which is a real and useful anti-tampering check but says nothing about whether the installation's provenance claim is true.
The part that is unambiguously a defect rather than a design limit is that no ADMIN is involved. The comment in the D2 migration argues the widening is safe because 'the verification lifecycle, the evidence-completeness gate, and every condition on using a record as an ACTUAL determination' are unchanged — and that is exactly what finding 1 removes. With the INSERT hole open, a plain MEMBER performs the operator attestation, the verification, and the importer-side consumption in a single transaction, and no ADMIN or OWNER of any organisation is consulted at any point.
findings.impact: The provenance distinction that owner decision D2 introduced, and that migration 20260903120000 and the v10 validator both work to protect, can be produced to order by a single organisation acting alone — and, given finding 1, by a single non-admin user of it. A filed declaration's claim to rest on operator-attested emissions is therefore self-certified. I am reporting this MEDIUM rather than HIGH because the self-assertion of capabilities may well be an accepted product decision (an organisation genuinely can be both), and because the sharp edge — no admin in the loop — is finding 1's. It is here because it changes what closing finding 1 buys you: it does not, by itself, make OPERATOR_PROVIDED mean anything externally.
findings.recommendation: Decide and document explicitly whether `record_provenance: OPERATOR_PROVIDED` is intended as an externally meaningful claim or merely a description of which screen the data was entered on; the D2 migration's comment currently reads as the former ('materially different claims about the same numbers'). If the former, the honest minimum is that an OPERATOR_PROVIDED record consumed by the same organisation that entered it — `sharing_grant_id is null` and the installation is own-org — should be surfaced and filed as self-attested rather than as operator-attested, since no counterparty relationship exists. Separately, and independent of that decision, `verifyEmissionData`'s ADMIN+ requirement should hold at the database on every path (see finding 1's recommendation): the MEMBER-only self-dealing chain in C3 is the part that is clearly wrong under the project's own roles matrix.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Two unauthenticated server actions on the public /auth/callback page have no rate limiter, while every sibling auth action has one
findings.boundary: Unauthenticated internet -> Supabase Auth, through Server Actions that accept fully attacker-supplied tokens and codes.
findings.precondition: None. /auth/callback is a public "use client" page and both actions are registered dispatchable server actions (server-reference-manifest.json lists 49 actions and includes auth/callback). No session or account needed.
findings.affected_actor: Every tenant, via the same shared GoTrue quota as finding #1; and the refresh-token grant is exercised with attacker-chosen values on an endpoint with no attempt ceiling.
findings.exploit:
1. POST the establishSessionAction server action with an attacker-minted access_token and arbitrary refresh_token. No credential is required to mint the JWT — it is never signature-checked before the network call, only decoded.
2. app/auth/callback/actions.ts's establishSessionAction calls supabase.auth.setSession({access_token, refresh_token}) with no preceding limiter check.
3. auth-js _setSession decodes the JWT; if exp is past it calls _callRefreshToken(refresh_token) -> POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=refresh_token. If exp is future it calls _getUser -> GET /auth/v1/user. Either way exactly one GoTrue request per invocation, unbounded.
4. Repeat at will. There is no counter, so no retry-after is ever returned.
findings.evidence:
app/auth/callback/actions.ts — `grep -n '\.check(\|createInMemoryRateLimiter' ` returns NO matches, while the file exports two actions (establishSessionAction, exchangeCodeForSessionAction). Per-file sweep: `app/auth/callback/actions.ts  actions=2  checks=0`, against `app/auth/confirm/actions.ts  actions=1  checks=1` (limiter at :63, limit 30 / 10 min, checked at :72), `app/(auth)/actions.ts 3/2`, `app/(auth)/forgot-password/actions.ts 1/1`, `app/(auth)/reset-password/actions.ts 1/1`, `app/accept-invitation/actions.ts 2/2`.
app/auth/callback/page.tsx:1 `"use client";` and imports both actions — a public page.
server-reference-manifest.json in the shipped artifact: 49 registered actions; substring 'auth/callback' present -> true.

LIVE PROBE (isolated stub listener, no Supabase touched), <scratchpad>/probe-callback2.mjs. An unsigned, attacker-minted JWT — no secret needed:
```
setSession(EXPIRED jwt) -> outbound: ["POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=refresh_token"]
setSession(FUTURE-dated jwt) -> outbound: ["GET /auth/v1/user"]
exchangeCodeForSession(with verifier cookie) -> outbound: []
```
PARTIAL, stated plainly: the establishSessionAction half is proven. I could NOT reproduce an outbound call for exchangeCodeForSessionAction — my guessed code_verifier cookie name did not take, so its network behaviour is unverified and I am not claiming it. An earlier probe with a non-JWT string ('attacker') produced no calls at all, which is why the well-formed-JWT retest matters and why the first result should not be generalised from.
findings.why_controls_fail: This is a coverage gap, not a broken control: 45 limiters are correctly placed across 20 files, and the file's own sibling app/auth/confirm/actions.ts is limited at 30/10min, which shows the pattern was applied deliberately elsewhere on this exact surface. app/auth/callback/actions.ts was added/reworked on 2026-09-03 (its own doc comment dates the error-code change to P14) and did not receive one. The per-file audit that would have caught it — exported actions vs. check sites — does not appear to have been run; nothing in the test suite or CI asserts that every exported server action is preceded by a limiter check.
findings.impact: An unmetered unauthenticated path to the shared GoTrue quota, compounding finding #1 from a second direction, plus an uncapped oracle against the refresh-token grant. Lower severity than #1 only because it requires a specific action POST rather than any URL, and because refresh-token entropy makes guessing impractical — the availability cost, not the guessing, is the real exposure.
findings.recommendation: Add a getClientIp()-keyed limiter to both actions in app/auth/callback/actions.ts, mirroring app/auth/confirm/actions.ts:58-63 (30 per 10 minutes) and checked as the first statement of each. Separately, add a test that enumerates every exported server action and every app/api route handler and asserts a limiter check precedes the first external call, so the next action added to a public surface cannot ship without one — the sweep that found this took seconds and would have caught it in CI.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: All 45 rate limiters key on client IP alone, so unrelated tenants sharing an egress address share every bucket, including declaration and export limits
findings.boundary: Cross-tenant. Two customer organizations with no relationship to each other occupy one rate-limit bucket on every limited operation in the product.
findings.precondition: Two organizations whose users reach the app from the same public address — one corporate NAT, one VPN exit node, one cloud egress, one conference or co-working network. No compromise, no privilege. For deliberate abuse, an attacker need only arrange to share an egress with the victim, which is trivially purchasable on any consumer VPN.
findings.affected_actor: Any tenant sharing an egress with a heavier or hostile user. The operations affected are the ones with regulatory deadlines attached.
findings.exploit:
1. Every limiter's key is `await getClientIp()` and nothing else — no user id, no org id, no operation subject. Verified across all 45 call sites.
2. Org A's user exhausts a bucket. Report export is 10 per 5 minutes; declaration lifecycle limiters (startDeclaration, refreshDeclarationDraft, markDeclarationReady, recordDeclarationFiled, createDeclarationAmendment) are 30/10/15 per 10 minutes.
3. Org B, behind the same address, is refused with 'Too many requests. Try again in N seconds.' having performed no operations at all.
4. Deliberately: an attacker on the same egress as a target org, holding only their own free account, burns the export and declaration budgets on a filing day. The get-client-ip hardening guarantees they cannot pick a victim's bucket by header — but it equally guarantees they cannot avoid sharing one.
findings.why_controls_fail: The IP-only key is a considered choice for the two UNAUTHENTICATED limiters and correctly justified there — app/(auth)/actions.ts:79-97 explains that sign-in has no authenticated identity yet and that keying on the submitted email would leak account existence. That reasoning is sound, and it was then applied uniformly to 43 limiters that DO have an authenticated identity in hand: every one of these actions resolves an org context and role before doing its work, so org_id and user_id are available and simply are not used. get-client-ip.ts's own caveat covers proxy topology and the dev no-header case, but not the many-users-behind-one-address case, which is the normal condition for the corporate customers this product targets. Nothing tests the cross-tenant interaction.
findings.impact: Availability coupling between tenants that should be isolated, on exactly the operations with statutory deadlines — declaration preparation, marking ready, recording filed, amendments, and report export. A CBAM quarterly deadline concentrates all tenants' usage into the same hours, which is when collisions are both most likely and most costly. It is also a cheap targeted denial: one attacker account on a shared VPN exit can hold a competitor's export budget at zero for as long as they care to.
findings.recommendation: For the authenticated limiters, key on the identity that is already resolved — `${org_id}:${ip}` at minimum, or `${org_id}:${user_id}` for per-operation budgets, keeping IP-only for the pre-authentication limiters (sign-in, sign-up, forgot-password, confirm, accept-invitation) where the existing enumeration argument genuinely applies. Note this increases the distinct-key count per limiter, which interacts with finding #7's ceiling arithmetic, so size maxKeys deliberately rather than leaving the 50,000 default.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Any ADMIN can rewrite an invitation's email, role, invited_by and status — including an already-ACCEPTED row — through the Data API, with no audit event
findings.boundary: Record integrity within the tenant: the invitation row is the product's stated record of how a person came to be a member, and at what role.
findings.precondition: ADMIN or OWNER of the organization, issuing a raw PostgREST UPDATE. No other privilege.
findings.affected_actor: The organization's own owners and auditors, and any regulator or reviewer relying on the Team screen or the invitations table to reconstruct who admitted whom.
findings.exploit: Issue `update organization_invitations set status='REVOKED', role='MEMBER', email='rewritten@evil.test', invited_by='<the OWNER''s user id>' where id=<any row in my org>`. organization_invitations_update_admin_or_owner's USING clause has no status filter and its WITH CHECK pins only `status = 'REVOKED'`; every other column is column-level UPDATE-granted to `authenticated`. An ACCEPTED invitation can be flipped to REVOKED after the fact while accepted_at/accepted_by stay populated — a self-contradictory row — and authorship can be reassigned to an innocent user.
findings.evidence:
Sandbox, scratchpad/a7_p5.sql, as ADMIN a7-admin@victim.test under `set local role authenticated`.

Before: a7222222-...-00000000000a | a7-invitee@victim.test | ACCEPTED | accepted_at 2026-09-03 12:41:46.680098+00 | accepted_by a7000000-...-000000000007
P12: `update ... set status='REVOKED' where id='a7222222-...-00000000000A'`
  -> accepted->revoked | a7222222-...-00000000000a | REVOKED | accepted_at 2026-09-03 12:41:46.680098+00 | accepted_by a7000000-...-000000000007   (UPDATE 1)
P13: `update ... set status='REVOKED', role='MEMBER', email='rewritten@evil.test', invited_by='a7000000-...-000000000001'`
  -> field-rewrite | a7222222-...-00000000000a | rewritten@evil.test | MEMBER | REVOKED | a7000000-...-000000000001   (UPDATE 1)
P14 control (a PENDING row's role bumped while staying PENDING) correctly fails: `ERROR: new row violates row-level security policy for table "organization_invitations"`.

Policy: supabase/migrations/20260828130000_organization_invitations.sql:156-166.
findings.why_controls_fail: The policy comment (same file, lines 152-155) states its intent as "this policy only needs to guard against an ADMIN/OWNER using a bare update to do anything other than revoke (e.g. it cannot be used to forge an ACCEPTED row)" — it does prevent forging ACCEPTED, and prevents nothing else. There is no immutability trigger on organization_invitations (pg_trigger returns zero non-internal triggers for the table), unlike memberships, which has three. The application-layer revokeInvitation (src/application/organizations/invitations.ts) filters `.eq("status","PENDING")` and writes a membership.invitation_revoked audit event, but a direct Data-API call reaches neither. audit_events retains membership.invitation_created / .invitation_accepted, so the tampering is detectable by cross-reference — but only by someone who already suspects it.
findings.impact: The Team screen and the invitations table can be made to disagree with what actually happened, and the disagreement is attributable to the wrong person. In a regulated filing context, an admin who admitted a confederate can, after the fact, point the row's invited_by at the OWNER and change the role it records.
findings.recommendation: Add a BEFORE UPDATE trigger on organization_invitations that rejects any change other than status PENDING -> REVOKED (org_id, email, role, invited_by, created_at, expires_at, accepted_at, accepted_by all immutable), mirroring app.prevent_membership_user_id_change / app.prevent_org_id_change on memberships. Tighten the policy's USING to `... and status = 'PENDING'` so a terminal row is untouchable at all.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: An ADMIN can demote or hard-delete an OWNER; the product enforces "only an OWNER may grant OWNER" but nothing stops a lower role taking ownership away
findings.boundary: The role hierarchy inside one tenant — ADMIN acting on a strictly higher role.
findings.precondition: ADMIN of an organization that has at least two active OWNERs. Reachable through the product's own Team screen (changeRoleAction / removeMemberAction), not only through the Data API.
findings.affected_actor: The demoted or deleted OWNER, and the organization, whose owner-only controls (organizations_update_owner) they lose access to.
findings.exploit: As ADMIN, submit the Team screen's role-change form for a co-OWNER with role=MEMBER, or its remove form for that co-OWNER. Both succeed. The demoted owner cannot restore themselves — only a remaining OWNER can — and a hard delete additionally destroys the row that resolves their historical audit_events back to a person (the stated reason deactivation exists).
findings.evidence:
Sandbox, scratchpad/a7_p4.sql, as ADMIN a7-admin@victim.test against OWNER a7-owner2@victim.test while two active OWNERs exist:
  P8a deactivate an OWNER -> ERROR: new row violates row-level security policy for table "memberships"   (correctly refused)
  P8b `update memberships set role='MEMBER' where user_id=<owner2>` -> admin-demoted-owner | c8a3544e-1baf-4ba9-b3e2-c5ea0137a05a | MEMBER   (UPDATE 1); read-back confirms role MEMBER
  P8c `delete from memberships where user_id=<owner2>` -> admin-deleted-owner | c8a3544e-1baf-4ba9-b3e2-c5ea0137a05a | OWNER   (DELETE 1)
  P8d ADMIN self-promotes to OWNER -> ERROR: new row violates row-level security policy   (correctly refused)
  P8e/P8f both OWNERs -> ERROR: memberships: organization a7111111-... would be left with no active OWNER   (trigger holds)
Policies: memberships_update_admin_or_owner WITH CHECK `(app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of(org_id) AND ((role <> 'OWNER') OR app.user_is_owner_of(org_id)))`; memberships_delete_admin_or_owner USING `app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of(org_id)` with no role term (supabase/migrations/20260828110000_membership_management_policies.sql:105-111). Domain: src/domain/organizations/invariants.ts:95-146 checks callerRole only for `newRole === "OWNER"`; removeMembership (line 158) takes no callerRole at all.
findings.why_controls_fail: The P13 fix documented at src/domain/organizations/invariants.ts:78-94 closed exactly one direction — an ADMIN promoting a confederate to OWNER — and its own comment describes the remaining half of the attack it names ("the org's real founding OWNER can then be demoted (now legal, since another OWNER exists)") without closing it. RLS mirrors the asymmetry precisely: the UPDATE policy's WITH CHECK evaluates the NEW row, so setting deactivated_at on an OWNER is refused (new role still OWNER) while demoting one to MEMBER passes (new role is MEMBER), and the DELETE policy has no role predicate at all. app.enforce_last_active_owner_per_org only guarantees that one active OWNER survives; it says nothing about who may remove the others.
findings.impact: An organization that deliberately keeps two owners for continuity can be reduced to one by an administrator, unilaterally, and the removed owner has no self-service path back. Hard-deleting an owner also breaks audit-actor resolution for every event they ever wrote.
findings.recommendation: Make the two directions symmetric. Add `and (old.role <> 'OWNER' or app.user_is_owner_of(org_id))` semantics to the DELETE path (a policy predicate on the row being deleted) and to the UPDATE path's USING clause, so only an OWNER may modify or remove an OWNER — and mirror it in changeMembershipRole/removeMembership by passing and checking callerRole for an OWNER target, not only for an OWNER newRole.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: A password change needs no re-authentication, so any live session converts into permanent account takeover with the real user locked out
findings.boundary: Session compromise -> account compromise. A stolen or injected session should not become ownership of the account.
findings.precondition: Any live session in the victim's browser — obtained by a stolen cookie, a shared/unlocked machine, or the /auth/callback fragment injection in finding 2. No knowledge of the current password.
findings.affected_actor: The account holder, and through them their organization.
findings.exploit: Navigate to /reset-password (no session-origin check, no guard in app/(auth)/layout.tsx) and submit a new password. updatePasswordAction requires only that getUser() returns a user (app/(auth)/reset-password/actions.ts:157) and then calls updateUser({password}) (line 168) — the form collects password and confirmPassword only, never the current password. It then calls signOut({scope:"others"}) (line 214), which terminates every other session the legitimate owner holds. The attacker keeps the session they are standing in.
findings.evidence: app/(auth)/reset-password/actions.ts:157 `const { data: { user } } = await supabase.auth.getUser();` — the only authorization check; line 168 `await supabase.auth.updateUser({ password: parsed.data.password })`; line 214 `await supabase.auth.signOut({ scope: "others" })`. app/(auth)/reset-password/reset-password-form.tsx / the zod schema at lines 82-100 take password + confirmPassword only. supabase/config.toml:321 `secure_password_change = false`. app/(auth)/layout.tsx renders children with no session or recovery-AAL check. No live reproduction (no GoTrue in the sandbox).
findings.why_controls_fail: The only mechanism that would require proof of the current password is GoTrue's own `secure_password_change` ("require reauthentication"), and the one Auth configuration this repository carries sets it to false (supabase/config.toml:321). The action's own doc comment reasons about not blocking the invited-user flow and about signing other sessions out, but never about whether the caller proved they are the account holder. The `scope: "others"` sign-out — added in P14 as a hardening — is what converts the takeover from temporary to permanent, because it evicts the legitimate owner from every other device while preserving the attacker's session.
findings.impact: Any session-level compromise becomes irreversible account takeover: password changed, all other sessions terminated, the real user locked out and forced through email recovery. That materially raises the cost of every other session-handling weakness in the product, including finding 2.
findings.recommendation: Require the current password (or a fresh recovery/AAL2 assertion) for a password change made from an ordinary session, and enable `secure_password_change` on the hosted project. Keep the no-current-password path only for a session that genuinely originated from a recovery or invite token — GoTrue exposes the AMR/AAL needed to tell those apart. Confirm which way the hosted project is configured before shipping; supabase/config.toml governs local dev only.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The P11 "confirmed email" control does not hold "regardless of what enable_confirmations is set to", contrary to the claim in its own migration header
findings.boundary: The mailbox-control boundary that every email-claim authorization in this schema rests on — invitation acceptance, invitation visibility, organization visibility, and the sharing-grant equivalents.
findings.precondition: The Auth project has email confirmations disabled (GOTRUE_MAILER_AUTOCONFIRM=true). That is the setting this repository's only Auth configuration ships (supabase/config.toml:319 `enable_confirmations = false`). Then: an attacker who learns a victim organization has invited an address signs up with that address and accepts.
findings.affected_actor: Any organization with a PENDING invitation, and any producer sharing data into it.
findings.exploit: Under autoconfirm, GoTrue confirms the account at sign-up — it sets email_confirmed_at and returns a session without ever mailing the address (which is exactly why signUpAction's `if (!data.session)` branch at app/(auth)/actions.ts:296 exists). app.user_confirmed_email() then returns that address, organization_invitations_select_own_email admits the row, and accept_organization_invitation's `email_confirmed_at is not null` gate passes — granting the invited role, up to ADMIN, on nothing but a typed string. This is the identical org-takeover 20260829380000 was written to close.
findings.evidence: Partial — mechanism, not live reproduction. supabase/migrations/20260829380000_...sql:32-38 claims the fix "holds regardless of what `enable_confirmations` is set to on any environment: an unconfirmed user's email claim is now worthless for this class of authorization no matter how Auth is configured, closing the silent-dependency problem at its root rather than only asserting it should be set correctly elsewhere." The control it installs is `where id = auth.uid() and email_confirmed_at is not null` — a column GoTrue itself populates at sign-up when autoconfirm is on, so the control is exactly as strong as the setting it claims independence from. Repository configuration: supabase/config.toml:319 `enable_confirmations = false`. Sandbox confirms only the negative half — a row with email_confirmed_at IS NULL is refused (scratchpad/a7_p3.sql P6: `unconfirmed-can-see | 0` and `unconfirmed-accept | EMAIL_MISMATCH |`) and the same user with email_confirmed_at set is admitted (P7: `confirmed-can-see | 1`, `confirmed-accept | OK | a7111111-...`). I could not exercise GoTrue to show that autoconfirm sets that column, because the sandbox's auth.users is a shim with no GoTrue attached.
findings.why_controls_fail: The control was designed to remove a dependency on hosted Auth configuration and instead relocated it: from `auth.jwt() ->> 'email'` to `auth.users.email_confirmed_at`, both of which GoTrue writes according to the same setting. Independent evidence in this repository points the same way — docs/plans/P13_RELEASE_READINESS_REPORT.md:724 records `enable_confirmations = false` (finding S3) as "Documented, not code-fixed" with a pre-go-live checkbox in docs/runbooks/DEPLOYMENT.md, which is only coherent if the setting still matters. Mitigating, and stated plainly: the same report records the hosted project as `mailer_autoconfirm: false` (lines 2686-2687, 2984, 3390), so on production today the gate is real. This is therefore a false claim about a security control, and a single-setting dependency that the claim tells a future reader not to check.
findings.impact: Today: a security control whose documented guarantee is untrue, which will be relied on by the next reviewer or the next environment. If autoconfirm is ever enabled on any environment — a dashboard toggle, a new staging project, a restored project — organization takeover via any known invited address reopens instantly, and the migration header says explicitly that it cannot.
findings.recommendation: Correct the claim in 20260829380000's header and in app.user_confirmed_email()'s COMMENT: the guarantee holds only where Auth actually requires confirmation. Then make it verifiable rather than asserted — extend /api/health (which already has checkAppUrl) with a GoTrue settings probe that degrades when mailer_autoconfirm is true, and add the same check to the pre-go-live runbook so it is measured, not remembered.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The unit guard accepts magnitude-prefixed and non-mass denominators: tCO2e/kilotonne computes as if per tonne (1000x)
findings.boundary: Producer- or importer-entered free text (emission_data.emission_unit) -> the engine's mass-basis guard -> a COMPUTED authoritative figure.
findings.precondition: An ACTUAL determination whose emission_unit uses a spelled-out magnitude-prefixed denominator. emission_data.emission_unit has no CHECK constraint, no enum and no application-layer allow-list; recordEmissionData passes it through unvalidated, and the producer form only suggests a placeholder.
findings.affected_actor: Own tenant and the filing -- the embedded-emissions figure is wrong by three or six orders of magnitude while reporting COMPUTED.
findings.exploit: Enter emission_unit as 'tCO2e/kilotonne' (or 'tCO2e/megatonne', 'TCO2E_PER_KILOTONNE', 'tCO2e/1000 tonnes', 'tCO2e/tonne of clinker'). unitMatchesQuantityBasis's mass branch is `normalized.includes("TONNE") || /\/T(?![A-Z0-9])/.test(normalized)` (src/domain/calculations/calculate-line-emissions.ts:185). "KILOTONNE" contains "TONNE", so the substring test passes and the value is multiplied by a quantity in tonnes as though the factor were per tonne.
findings.why_controls_fail: The guard was hardened twice -- once for the numerator (kgCO2e/t, P13) and once for the abbreviated denominator trap (/TJ, /TWh, /Th) -- and both fixes hold. Neither addressed the plain-language denominator: `includes("TONNE")` is an unanchored substring test over the whole normalized string, so any word containing TONNE satisfies it regardless of prefix or position. The function's own doc comment names the correct fix ("an allow-list on EmissionData.emission_unit at entry (a DB CHECK or a small enum, mirroring default_emission_values' own constraint) so the engine stops string-sniffing free text at all -- this function remains a stop-gap") and that allow-list has not landed. The DEFAULT path is protected only because 20260826133116 constrains the dataset's own emission_unit to two literals; the ACTUAL path has no such constraint and is the one this reaches.
findings.impact: A single mis-entered but entirely plausible unit string yields a COMPUTED result overstated 1000x or 1,000,000x, or computed against a different functional basis, with no warning. It is the same failure class as the kgCO2e/t finding that justified the 1.1.0 -> 1.2.0 engine bump, in the other half of the string.
findings.recommendation: Land the allow-list the function's own comment calls for: a CHECK constraint (or enum) on emission_data.emission_unit restricted to the accepted spellings, applied at entry. Until then, anchor the denominator test the same way the numerator was anchored -- match the segment after the separator against an explicit set ('T','TONNE','TONNES','MWH') rather than testing for a substring anywhere in the string -- and add the kilotonne/megatonne/'1000 tonnes'/'tonne of clinker' cases to the engine test suite. Any behavioural change here needs an ENGINE_VERSION bump.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The database validator accepts a regulated numeric the engine cannot parse: a whitespace-padded value passes ::numeric comparison and throws an unhandled DecimalError out of the pure engine
findings.boundary: Member-written shipment_lines.emission_determination jsonb -> the SQL determination validator -> the pure calculation engine's decimal parser.
findings.precondition: A member of the owning org writing a DEFAULT determination directly (PostgREST UPDATE on shipment_lines, which RLS permits on a non-terminal shipment).
findings.affected_actor: Own tenant: an unhandled exception where the design contract promises a named outcome. The engine crashes before persisting, so no wrong number is stored.
findings.exploit: Take the line's own valid determination and pad resolution.values.total.value with spaces (' 1.390 '). app.emission_determination_matches_regulatory_record compares it with app.try_cast_numeric(...) against default_emission_values.total_value, and PostgreSQL's numeric input accepts surrounding whitespace, so the comparison succeeds and the trigger stores it. calculateLineEmissions then calls toDecimal(' 1.390 '), which does not re-validate by contract, and decimal.js throws.
findings.evidence:
Validator verdicts, run as `authenticated` (uid 4b1e0a75, OWNER of org 976297bf) against real line 1c913da8-f60b-4b15-b735-f2f9746972fb (total.value = 1.390), script scratchpad/area4_decimal.sql:

  PG numeric casts:  ' 100 '=100   '0x64'=100   '1_0'=10   '1e2'=100
  --- validator verdicts on the SAME determination with a mangled total.value ---
  unchanged (control) -> true
  total.value = " 100 "-style whitespace pad -> true
  total.value = underscore form -> false
  total.value = exponent form 1e-9 padded -> false

Engine behaviour on the values the validator accepts, running the real engine under tsx (quantity 100), script scratchpad/pad.ts:

  " 1.390 "    -> THREW: Error | [DecimalError] Invalid argument:  1.390 
  "1.390"      -> COMPUTED 139
  "0x64"       -> COMPUTED 10000
  "1_0"        -> COMPUTED 1000
  "1e2"        -> COMPUTED 10000

Comparison sites: supabase/migrations/20260902140000_..._validator_v10.sql:523-527 (`app.try_cast_numeric(...)` for direct/indirect/total). Parser: src/domain/shared/decimal.ts toDecimal, which states "this function does not re-validate".
findings.why_controls_fail: src/domain/shared/decimal.ts's header describes exactly this class as closed -- P11 finding #9, "a value can be accepted by this function, stored verbatim in a regulated numeric column, and disagree with what the calculation engine actually computed from it" -- and CANONICAL_DECIMAL_PATTERN does close it at parseDecimalString. But the determination JSON never goes through parseDecimalString. Its only gate is the SQL validator, which compares by casting to numeric, and PostgreSQL's numeric input grammar is looser than the canonical pattern in one direction (whitespace) and than decimal.js in others. The engine then trusts the DecimalString brand, which for this path is a cast, not a validation. CLAUDE.md's own rule -- expected outcomes are discriminated {status, reason} unions, throw is for infrastructure failures and integrity violations only -- is violated by a data path a member controls.
findings.impact: An uncaught DecimalError escapes a pure domain function into the Server Action, producing a 500 instead of a named rejection, and the planted determination keeps crashing every calculate attempt on that line until someone rewrites it. It is a self-inflicted denial of service on the org's own workflow, but it is also the same accept-here/reject-there divergence in regulated numerics that the codebase treats as a first-order integrity concern, sitting in the one place a regulated number arrives as untrusted JSON.
findings.recommendation: Make the SQL validator compare regulated numerics as canonical text, not via ::numeric -- require the value to match '^-?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?$' and equal the dataset value's own canonical rendering -- the same byte-equality posture record_declaration_filed already chose deliberately for quantity ("Text comparison on purpose ... A ::numeric cast would accept '1000.0' for '1000' -- true of the number, false of the frozen fact"). Independently, have the mapper that reads emission_determination out of jsonb run parseDecimalString over the snapshot/resolution values and surface INPUT_UNRESOLVED rather than letting toDecimal throw.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: An ACTUAL emissions record from any reporting period can be applied to any shipment, and the frozen snapshot does not record which period it came from
findings.boundary: Temporal boundary between an actual-emissions dataset's reporting period and the shipment's own period. There is no check at any layer.
findings.precondition: An importer with access (own-org or via an ACTIVE sharing grant) to more than one period's emission_data for an installation.
findings.affected_actor: The regulator and the filing; and any later auditor of a frozen calculation, who cannot tell from the snapshot which period the figures describe.
findings.exploit: 1. Have (or create) emission_data rows for several reporting periods. 2. listAvailableActualEmissionData filters on org visibility, status='ACTIVE', verification_status='VERIFIED' and cn_scope coverage — never on period. 3. determineFromActualData's line fetch selects org_id, cn_code, emission_determination only; it never reads the shipment's period or release_date. 4. The database validator's ACTUAL branch checks installation, provenance, version, evidence, unit, both values and the verifier — never the period. Pick whichever period gives the lowest figure.
findings.evidence:
Live (sandbox, rolled back): a record with reporting_period_year 2031 was inserted ACTIVE+VERIFIED and then accepted as the determination for a line whose shipment's reporting_period_year is 2026:
  select 'shipment period', s.reporting_period_year from shipments s join shipment_lines l on l.shipment_id=s.id where l.id='3e76b531-...';  ->  2026
  update public.shipment_lines set emission_determination = ... 'emission_data_id':'cccccccc-...-0002' ... ;  ->  UPDATE 1
  select 'accepted: 2031-period ... on a 2026 line';  ->  accepted

Code: `grep -n "period" src/application/emissions/determine-from-actual-data.ts` returns exactly one hit, a type-only import at line 29. `grep -n` over list-available-actual-data.ts shows reporting_period only as an output field (lines 74, 504), never as a filter. src/domain/emissions/types.ts:106-158 — ActualEmissionSnapshot has no period field at all.
findings.why_controls_fail: Every other property of the source record is frozen and re-validated: id, version, installation, unit, both values, verifier, evidence file list, provenance. The period is the one property that is neither frozen nor checked, and it is the one that says which year's operations the figures describe. cnScopeCoversCnCode was added specifically to stop the picker offering a dataset for goods it was not scoped to; the identical argument applies to periods and was not made.
findings.impact: Emissions from one year applied to imports of another — plausibly by accident, and selectable for the lowest number if not. Because the snapshot omits the period, a filed declaration cannot be audited for this: the frozen record is silent about the very fact that would reveal the mismatch.
findings.recommendation: Add `period` to ActualEmissionSnapshot and freeze it. Filter listAvailableActualEmissionData by the shipment's reporting period, and have determineFromActualData reject a period mismatch with its own rejection reason rather than silently accepting. Add the same check to the ACTUAL branch of app.emission_determination_matches_regulatory_record so it holds against a raw write.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: emission_data.cn_scope is entirely unvalidated, and a one-character scope entry prefix-covers whole CBAM sectors
findings.boundary: Scope boundary for actual emissions data — which goods a producer's figures are declared to cover.
findings.precondition: Any member of the org that owns the installation (or an importer entering data for an off-platform operator).
findings.affected_actor: Any importer offered that record — including cross-org grantees — and through them the filing.
findings.exploit: Record emission data with cn_scope = ['7']. cnScopeCoversCnCode treats any strictly shorter string that is a prefix as covering, so '7' covers every iron & steel and aluminium CN code; '2' covers every cement, fertiliser and hydrogen code. The record is then offered by the picker, and accepted by the validator, for every line in those sectors.
findings.evidence:
Domain function run under tsx (src/domain/emissions/cn-scope-covers-code.ts):
  ["7"] 72061000 => true
  ["7"] 76041000 => true
  ["72"] 72061000 => true
  ["2"] 28041000 => true

Live acceptance (sandbox, rolled back):
  insert into public.emission_data (... cn_scope, reporting_period_year, emission_unit ...) values (..., array['7'], 1998, 'tCO2e/kilotonne', ...) returning cn_scope, reporting_period_year, emission_unit;
  -> {7} | 1998 | tCO2e/kilotonne   (INSERT 0 1)

SQL: `select conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) from pg_constraint where conrelid='public.emission_data'::regclass` — constraints exist for direct_specific, indirect_specific, methodology, period kind/quarter, status, verification_status, verifier presence and version. None for cn_scope. None for emission_unit.

file:line — app/(producer)/emission-data/actions.ts:251 (`cnScope: z.string().min(1, ...)`) and :355-359 (split on comma, trim, drop empties — no format check); src/application/emissions/manage-emission-data.ts:314 (passed straight through).
findings.why_controls_fail: cnScopeCoversCnCode's doc comment is careful and correct about the direction that matters ('a cn_scope entry that is LONGER/more specific than the line's own declared code is never treated as covering it') and reasons explicitly about CN8-covers-TARIC10. But the function accepts ANY shorter prefix, and the entries it consumes are unvalidated free text, so the CN8/TARIC10 relationship it was designed around is only one of many things a scope entry can be. The one control that exists on this path, `.min(1)`, is satisfied by a single digit. The database enforces nothing, so a raw write bypasses even that.
findings.impact: A single emissions figure applied across an entire sector's goods — e.g. an aluminium-scrap intensity used for primary steel. Combined with finding 3 (fabricated ACTIVE+VERIFIED records) and finding 7 (no period check), the picker's narrowing job is defeated on all three axes at once. The importer still chooses, so the primary harm is bad data rather than a forced wrong number — but the picker exists precisely to make that choice safe.
findings.recommendation: Validate cn_scope at entry and in the database: each entry must be 4, 6, 8 or 10 digits, and should exist in cbam_goods at the corresponding level. Consider requiring TRADE_GOOD-level entries outright, since that is what a line ever declares. Add a DB CHECK so the constraint holds against any write path, matching how shipment_lines.cn_code is already constrained.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Hydrogen is excluded from the Annex II proxy although the ACTIVE dataset publishes no indirect value for it, so ACTUAL adds indirect emissions the dataset itself declines to count
findings.boundary: Same boundary as finding 1, opposite direction: a good the sector proxy leaves outside Annex II that the dataset's own structure treats as direct-only.
findings.precondition: An ACTUAL determination on a line for CN 28041000 (Hydrogen), the dataset's only HYDROGEN good, with non-zero indirect emissions on the producer's record.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant, who over-reports and over-buys certificates; and the consistency of the filing, since the DEFAULT path for the same good yields a different treatment.
findings.exploit: Determine a hydrogen line from ACTUAL data. goodSector = 'HYDROGEN' is not in ANNEX_II_SECTORS, so no ANNEX_II_DIRECT_ONLY step is emitted and RULE-EE-009 sums direct + indirect. The DEFAULT path for the same good uses total_value, which equals direct_value because the dataset publishes no indirect at all.
findings.evidence:
SQL (sandbox):
  select d.source_sheet, d.source_trade_code, d.direct_value, d.indirect_value, d.indirect_raw_source_value, d.total_value from default_emission_values d join cbam_goods g on g.id=d.good_id where g.sector='HYDROGEN' order by 1 limit 6;
Output (96 country rows, all the same shape):
  _Other Countries and Territorie | 2804 10 00 | 17.740 | (null) | (null) | 17.740
  Albania | 2804 10 00 | 14.030 | (null) | (null) | 14.030
  Algeria | 2804 10 00 | 10.820 | (null) | (null) | 10.820
indirect_status is UNAVAILABLE for all 96; total_value = direct_value throughout.

Real engine (tsx, 1000 t, direct 10.820, indirect 4.000):
  CN 28041000 Hydrogen ACTUAL sector=HYDROGEN     | COMPUTED | 14820 | LINE_EMBEDDED_EMISSIONS
  CN 28041000 Hydrogen ACTUAL sector=ALUMINIUM(cf)| COMPUTED | 10820 | ANNEX_II_DIRECT_ONLY,LINE_EMBEDDED_EMISSIONS

file:line — src/domain/calculations/calculate-line-emissions.ts:46-52.
findings.why_controls_fail: The proxy was chosen from the sector column alone, without consulting the emission values the same dataset publishes for those sectors. Had that been done, the partition would have been visible: 15/15 aluminium goods, 118/119 iron & steel goods and the 1 hydrogen good publish no indirect value, while all 8 cement and all 27 fertiliser goods do. ANNEX_II_APPLICABILITY_DATASET_REQUIREMENTS.md's table lists HYDROGEN as 'not treated as Annex II by the proxy' without asking whether that is right.
findings.impact: Over-reported embedded emissions for hydrogen imports (+37% in the illustration above), and a DEFAULT/ACTUAL divergence on the same good in the opposite direction to finding 1. Over-reporting is the safer direction, which is why this is MEDIUM and not a blocker — but it is the same defect and should be fixed with the same change.
findings.recommendation: Fix with finding 1. Whichever remediation is chosen there — reverting D1 or building the applicability dataset — must resolve hydrogen explicitly rather than by omission from a set.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: A superseded regulatory dataset produces no staleness signal: determinations frozen against an old dataset version are filed without warning
findings.boundary: Dataset-version boundary. Snapshots are deliberately frozen (correct for audit), but nothing tells anyone that a frozen snapshot predates a corrected dataset.
findings.precondition: A new DEFAULT_EMISSION_VALUES dataset is activated after lines were determined — which is precisely what the currently ACTIVE version, named '2026-definitive-corrected', shows happens.
findings.affected_actor: The regulator and the filing, in whichever direction the correction moved the value.
findings.exploit: Determine lines against dataset version A. Activate the corrected dataset B. Nothing flags the existing determinations. checkCalculationCurrency compares the calculation's frozen determination against the line's current determination — both still reference A, so the line reads CURRENT. buildCompletenessReport has no blocker for it. The declaration is filed on superseded values.
findings.evidence:
SQL (sandbox):
  select id, dataset_type, version, status, effective_from from regulatory_datasets;
  -> efcd5c92-... | DEFAULT_EMISSION_VALUES | 2026-definitive-corrected | ACTIVE | 2026-01-01

Code: `grep -rn dataset_version --include=*.ts src/ app/ | grep -v '\.test\.'` shows dataset_version only being written into snapshots, summarised for audit, exported, and surfaced on the health endpoint — never compared against the ACTIVE dataset. src/domain/declarations/types.ts:86-114, CompletenessBlockerReason: NO_SHIPMENTS_IN_PERIOD, SHIPMENT_NOT_LOCKABLE, SHIPMENT_HAS_NO_LINES, LINE_NOT_DETERMINED, LINE_NOT_CALCULATED, LINE_CALCULATION_STALE — no dataset-supersession blocker. src/application/emissions/check-actual-determination-staleness.ts:46 states outright that 'a DEFAULT-determined or not-yet-determined line is' out of its scope.
findings.why_controls_fail: Staleness detection was built for the ACTUAL path only — a superseded emission_data row produces a real, surfaced signal. The DEFAULT path got the freezing (right) without the corresponding 'the world moved' detection. The health endpoint reports the ACTIVE dataset version but nothing joins it against the versions frozen in live determinations.
findings.impact: Declarations filed on values the Commission has since corrected, with no prompt to redetermine and no blocker at the completeness gate. The direction and size depend on the correction; the platform cannot say, because it never asks.
findings.recommendation: Add a completeness blocker (e.g. DETERMINATION_DATASET_SUPERSEDED) for any DEFAULT determination whose dataset_version differs from the ACTIVE DEFAULT_EMISSION_VALUES version, mirroring LINE_CALCULATION_STALE. Do not rewrite frozen snapshots — surface the divergence and let the declarant redetermine deliberately, exactly as the ACTUAL path already does.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The P14 grantee-capability control is absent from the direct-grant acceptance path, and self-serve on the path where it exists
findings.boundary: Cross-tenant data sharing: which organizations a producer's verified emissions data may be bound to. The control exists in exactly one of two acceptance paths.
findings.precondition: For the bypass: MEMBER role in an organization named as grantee_org_id on an INVITED direct grant. For the self-serve defeat: OWNER of any organization.
findings.affected_actor: Producer/operator organizations, whose verified emissions figures and installation details become readable by organizations that do not hold IMPORTER_DECLARANT — the exact condition the P14 migration added this gate to prevent.
findings.exploit:
Two independent defeats.
(a) DIRECT-GRANT PATH. accept_sharing_grant_invitation() carries the P14 check, but it refuses any grant whose invited_email is null — so it only ever handles bootstrap (email) grants. Direct grants are accepted through the raw RLS policy sharing_grants_update_grantee_accept, whose WITH CHECK is `grantee_org_id IN user_org_ids() AND status='ACTIVE' AND invited_email IS NULL` — no capability test, no admin test. The application's own acceptSharingGrant() (src/application/sharing/manage-sharing-grants.ts:420-528) likewise has no capability check; it is the only accept function in that file without one. issueSharingGrant() (same file, 197-300) checks the GRANTOR's PRODUCER_OPERATOR capability but never the grantee's, and sharing_grants_insert_own_org only calls app.organization_exists(grantee_org_id).
(b) THE GATE ITSELF. organizations.capabilities is append-only, not fixed — app.enforce_organization_capabilities_append_only only refuses REMOVAL. Any OWNER can add IMPORTER_DECLARANT to their own org in one UPDATE and then satisfy the check on the bootstrap path too.
findings.evidence:
(a) Producer-only org d0000000-… (capabilities = {PRODUCER_OPERATOR}), plain MEMBER dddd…0001. Victim rev-vic issues a DIRECT grant of installation b2000000-… to it.
  set local request.jwt.claims='{"sub":"dddd0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001","role":"authenticated","email":"po@prod2.test"}';
  E1a RPC path (capability gate):
    select * from accept_sharing_grant_invitation('b7000000-…','d0000000-…');
    result_status = EMAIL_MISMATCH      <- the gated path never even reaches its own check
  E1b RAW RLS path (plain MEMBER, no capability, no admin):
    update sharing_grants set status='ACTIVE' where id='b7000000-…';
    UPDATE 1
    grant now ACTIVE grantee=d0000000-0000-4000-8000-00000000000d
  E1c can this producer-only org now read the victim installation + emission data?
    installations visible | 1
    emission rows visible | 1
    direct_specific leaked = 2.500 / indirect 0.300

(b) As the OWNER of a PRODUCER_OPERATOR-only org:
  before=PRODUCER_OPERATOR
  update organizations set capabilities=array['PRODUCER_OPERATOR','IMPORTER_DECLARANT'] where id='b0000000-…';
  UPDATE 1
  after=PRODUCER_OPERATOR,IMPORTER_DECLARANT

The control being bypassed, from the live accept_sharing_grant_invitation body:
  -- 2026-09-03 (P14): the new check. Membership alone was never enough
  -- -- it establishes that the caller may act for this organization,
  -- not that this organization is one a producer's data may be bound to.
  if not exists (select 1 from public.organizations o where o.id = p_org_id and 'IMPORTER_DECLARANT' = any(o.capabilities)) then
      return query select 'CAPABILITY_NOT_HELD'::text, null::uuid;
findings.why_controls_fail: The P14 change was applied to accept_sharing_grant_invitation() and to acceptSharingGrantInvitation() — the bootstrap pair — and to nothing else. Because that RPC self-selects to bootstrap grants (`if v_grant.invited_email is null … EMAIL_MISMATCH`), it is structurally incapable of covering direct grants, and no equivalent conjunct was added to sharing_grants_update_grantee_accept's WITH CHECK, which is the only thing standing on that path. The database was therefore never the enforcement point the migration's header claims it is. Separately, the gate reads a mutable, self-asserted attribute: app.enforce_organization_capabilities_append_only guards only against removal (its error text is about stranding grants), so capabilities can always be widened by the org's own OWNER, and there is no privileged process that grants IMPORTER_DECLARANT. A capability that a subject can grant itself is not an authorization control.
findings.impact: The stated P14 invariant — that a producer's data may only be bound to an organization vetted as an importer/declarant — does not hold. On the direct-grant path it is absent entirely, so any org named as grantee, whatever its capabilities, is accepted by any of its plain members and immediately reads the grantor's installation details and verified emissions figures. On the bootstrap path it is defeated by one self-service UPDATE. The grantor did name the counterparty, which is why this is MEDIUM rather than a cross-tenant breach — but the release is carrying a documented security control that does not do what its own migration header says.
findings.recommendation: Add the capability conjunct to sharing_grants_update_grantee_accept's WITH CHECK so it holds at the database on both paths — `AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM organizations o WHERE o.id = grantee_org_id AND 'IMPORTER_DECLARANT' = ANY(o.capabilities))` — and add the matching guard to acceptSharingGrant() for symmetry with acceptSharingGrantInvitation(). Also enforce it at issue time in sharing_grants_insert_own_org, which today validates only that the grantee org exists. Then decide, and document, whether capabilities are a self-service attribute or an authorization fact; if any SECURITY DEFINER function gates on them (record_calculation_result and accept_sharing_grant_invitation both do), they must not be writable by the subject they authorize.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: A plain MEMBER can attribute an evidence file to any user, including a user in another organization
findings.boundary: Provenance integrity of the evidence chain, inside a tenant, with a cross-tenant identity as the forged value.
findings.precondition: MEMBER role in the organization owning the emission_data row. Colleague user ids are trivially available via public.list_org_members(), which any member may call for their own org; cross-org ids are available to anyone who has consumed shared data or seen a verifier stamp.
findings.affected_actor: The organization's own ADMIN/OWNER, and any third-party user named as an uploader. The record shows someone else as having supplied the evidence backing an emissions figure.
findings.exploit: INSERT into evidence_files with uploaded_by_user_id set to any auth.users id. evidence_files_insert_own_org's WITH CHECK validates org_id and that the parent emission_data belongs to that org — it never requires uploaded_by_user_id = auth.uid(), unlike the sibling policies on import_batches (`created_by = auth.uid()`), declarations (`created_by_user_id = auth.uid()`) and organization_invitations (`invited_by = auth.uid()`). evidence_files has no UPDATE policy, so the forged attribution is then permanent.
findings.evidence:
As plain MEMBER aaaa…0003 of rev-atk:
  insert into evidence_files(org_id,emission_data_id,storage_path,original_filename,mime_type,size_bytes,sha256,uploaded_by_user_id)
   values('a0000000-…','a7000000-…','a0000000-…/x.pdf','x.pdf','application/pdf',5,repeat('c',64),'aaaa0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001');
  INSERT 0 1
  as own-org OWNER: ok, uploaded_by=aaaa0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001

  insert into evidence_files(... ,'bbbb0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001');
  INSERT 0 1
  as CROSS-ORG user: ok, uploaded_by=bbbb0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001
(bbbb…0001 is the OWNER of rev-vic, an unrelated organization.)

The policy, in full:
  evidence_files_insert_own_org :: INSERT :: roles=authenticated
    CHECK: ((org_id IN (SELECT app.user_org_ids())) AND (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emission_data ed WHERE ed.id = evidence_files.emission_data_id AND ed.entered_by_org_id = evidence_files.org_id)))
findings.why_controls_fail: The policy enforces tenancy but not actor identity, and the FK on uploaded_by_user_id references auth.users globally — it is checked as the table owner, outside RLS, so any real user id passes regardless of tenant. Every comparable table in this schema pins its actor column to auth.uid() in the WITH CHECK; evidence_files is the outlier. There is no trigger on evidence_files at all to compensate, and no UPDATE policy means nothing can correct a forged row afterwards.
findings.impact: The uploader recorded against each piece of evidence — the audit answer to 'who supplied this document?' — is attacker-controlled. A junior member can make evidence appear to have come from an ADMIN, an OWNER, or a named individual at a counterparty organization. Combined with Blocker 1 (where verifier_user_id is likewise forgeable) the entire human-attribution layer of the emissions record is writable by any member.
findings.recommendation: Add `AND uploaded_by_user_id = auth.uid()` to evidence_files_insert_own_org's WITH CHECK, matching import_batches_insert_own_org and declarations_insert_own_org. Consider also requiring the uploader to hold an active membership of org_id, so a since-removed user cannot be named.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: A plain MEMBER can write forged events into their organization's append-only audit trail
findings.boundary: Integrity of the audit trail, inside a tenant. Append-only by design, with no retraction path.
findings.precondition: MEMBER role in the organization. Nothing else.
findings.affected_actor: The organization's ADMINs and OWNERs, and any regulator or auditor who reads the audit trail as a record of what occurred.
findings.exploit: INSERT directly into audit_events. audit_events_insert_own_org_as_self permits any authenticated member to write an event for their own org, as themselves, with any of 38 whitelisted event_types and an arbitrary 8 KB JSONB payload. There is no correspondence check between the claimed event and any actual state change. Because the table has no UPDATE and no DELETE policy, the forged row is permanent — as the record_shared_data_consumption body itself notes about a related case, the stream 'by design has no UPDATE or DELETE policy and therefore no way to retract'.
findings.evidence:
As plain MEMBER aaaa…0003:
  insert into audit_events(org_id,actor_type,actor_user_id,event_type,aggregate_type,aggregate_id,payload)
  values('a0000000-…','USER','aaaa0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003','emission_data.verified','EMISSION_DATA',
         'a3000000-…','{"forged":true,"verifier":"someone else"}');
  INSERT 0 1
  forged rows=1
  delete from audit_events where payload->>'forged'='true';
  DELETE 0        <- permanent

The whitelist includes, among others: emission_data.verified, emission_data.activated, declaration.marked_ready, shipment.locked, membership.role_changed, sharing_grant.issued, sharing_grant.accepted, sharing_grant.revoked.

Correctly pinned and NOT forgeable, which is why this is MEDIUM: actor_user_id is bound to auth.uid() by the policy; org_id is bound to user_org_ids(); occurred_at is overwritten by app.pin_audit_event_occurred_at() (`new.occurred_at := now()`), so events cannot be backdated; event_type is whitelisted, and notably sharing_grant.data_consumed is absent from the whitelist so the cross-tenant event written by record_shared_data_consumption cannot be forged directly.
findings.why_controls_fail: The audit trail is written by the application through the user's own session, so the INSERT policy must admit member writes; the design then relies on the application being the only writer. It is not — the table is a live authenticated endpoint. The policy constrains WHO and WHEN precisely and correctly, but says nothing about WHETHER the described event happened, and there is no mechanism (no trigger, no correspondence check, no signing) that could. Immutability, which is the trail's other guarantee, works against remediation here: a forged entry cannot be retracted by anyone short of service_role.
findings.impact: Any member can permanently insert plausible, correctly-attributed, correctly-timestamped events that never occurred — 'emission_data.verified', 'declaration.marked_ready', 'membership.role_changed' — into the record their own organization and any auditor would rely on to reconstruct what happened. Conversely, a genuine trail can be flooded to obscure a real event. For a compliance product whose audit trail is part of the evidence, that materially reduces its value.
findings.recommendation: Decide whether audit_events is an application-written record or a user-written one; it cannot be both. The clean fix is to move audit writes to a SECURITY DEFINER RPC (or the service role, as record_calculation_result already does) and drop audit_events_insert_own_org_as_self entirely, so the only writers are code paths that have just performed the action they are recording. If member INSERT must stay, add a `source` column distinguishing trigger-written from client-written events so a reader can tell an asserted event from an observed one, and narrow the whitelist so that security-relevant types (emission_data.verified, membership.role_changed, shipment.locked, declaration.*) are writable only by definer functions.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: An ADMIN can demote or remove an OWNER whenever more than one OWNER exists
findings.boundary: Intra-tenant privilege hierarchy: whether ADMIN is subordinate to OWNER.
findings.precondition: ADMIN role in an organization that has at least two active OWNERs. (With exactly one OWNER the last-active-owner trigger correctly refuses.)
findings.affected_actor: The organization's OWNERs, who can be stripped of ownership by a subordinate role.
findings.exploit: memberships_update_admin_or_owner's USING is `app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of(org_id)` — it does not exclude rows whose current role is OWNER. Its WITH CHECK stops an ADMIN from creating an OWNER (`role <> 'OWNER' OR app.user_is_owner_of(org_id)`) but places no constraint on the OLD row. So an ADMIN can UPDATE any OWNER's row to role='MEMBER', or set deactivated_at, or DELETE it via memberships_delete_admin_or_owner (also USING admin-or-owner). Repeated, this reduces the org to exactly one OWNER of the ADMIN's choosing.
findings.evidence:
Org rev-atk given a second OWNER (aaaa…0004), then acting as the ADMIN aaaa…0002:
  set local request.jwt.claims='{"sub":"aaaa0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002","role":"authenticated"}';
  update memberships set role='MEMBER' where org_id='a0000000-…' and user_id='aaaa0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001';
  UPDATE 1
  aaaa0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001 -> MEMBER      <- was OWNER
  aaaa0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002 -> ADMIN
  aaaa0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003 -> MEMBER
  aaaa0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000004 -> OWNER
The subsequent DELETE of the remaining OWNER is correctly refused:
  ERROR:  memberships: organization a0000000-… would be left with no active OWNER
And escalation is correctly refused (see held_under_attack):
  update memberships set role='OWNER' where ... user_id=<self>;
  ERROR:  new row violates row-level security policy for table "memberships"
findings.why_controls_fail: The WITH CHECK guards the NEW role only — it is written to stop an ADMIN minting an OWNER, and it does that. Nothing guards the OLD role, so acting ON an OWNER is unrestricted for an ADMIN. app.enforce_last_active_owner_per_org is a floor, not a hierarchy: it only ensures at least one active OWNER survives, which is why the attack works on every OWNER but the last. The policy name, memberships_update_admin_or_owner, describes who may act and is silent on whom they may act upon — the gap this finding is about.
findings.impact: ADMIN is not actually subordinate to OWNER for membership management. An ADMIN can strip ownership from every OWNER except one, permanently changing who controls the organization, without being able to claim ownership themselves. In an organization that follows the sensible practice of keeping multiple OWNERs for continuity, that practice is precisely what makes the attack available. Not a full takeover, which is why it is MEDIUM rather than HIGH.
findings.recommendation: Add `AND (role <> 'OWNER' OR app.user_is_owner_of(org_id))` to memberships_update_admin_or_owner's USING clause and to memberships_delete_admin_or_owner's USING clause, so that acting on an OWNER row requires OWNER — mirroring the constraint the WITH CHECK already applies to creating one. Verify the corresponding application gates in the organizations/membership services match.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The importer emissions screen prints a green "Current" badge on the same row where it says "Access since revoked"
findings.boundary: UI assertion vs. what the data can support (own-tenant reader, cross-org data)
findings.precondition: A producer revokes or lets expire a sharing grant that backs an importer's ACTUAL determination. This is an ordinary, fully supported product action — no attack, no raw API, no misconfiguration.
findings.affected_actor: The importer declarant relying on the screen to know whether its figures are current.
findings.exploit: 1. Importer determines a line from a producer's shared actual data; the snapshot is frozen. 2. The producer revokes the grant (or it expires). 3. app.user_shared_installation_ids() stops returning that installation, so the emission_data row is no longer visible to the importer. 4. checkActualDeterminationStalenessByShipment gets no row back, checkActualSnapshotStaleness returns CURRENT, and the emissions page renders a green success badge reading "Current" — in a column adjacent to its own correct "Access since revoked" note. The producer may have activated three newer versions in the meantime; the importer is told the figure is current.
findings.evidence: app/(importer)/emissions/page.tsx:251-292 renders both, in the same row: {line.sharing_grant_status === "REVOKED" ? (Access since revoked) : null} {line.sharing_grant_status === "EXPIRED" ? (Access since expired) : null} ... {line.staleness === "STALE" ? (Stale — newer data available) : (Current)} The else-branch is unconditional: anything that is not STALE is asserted as "Current". Visibility is lost on revoke/expiry — app.user_shared_installation_ids(): select installation_id from public.sharing_grants where status = 'ACTIVE' and grantee_org_id in (select app.user_org_ids()) and (expires_at is null or expires_at > now()); And the grantee branch of emission_data_select_own_org requires status='ACTIVE' AND verification_status='VERIFIED'. Staleness then degrades to CURRENT twice over: src/domain/emissions/check-actual-snapshot-staleness.ts:53-55 — `if (currentEmissionData === null) { return "CURRENT"; }` src/application/emissions/list-actual-determined-lines.ts:455 — `staleness: stalenessByLineId[line.id] ?? "CURRENT"` The application layer also fails closed on its own grant lookup (check-actual-determination-staleness.ts, activeGrantedInstallationIds returns an empty Set on error), producing the same CURRENT. Separately: the shipment detail screen — where determinations are actually made and where the user is standing when they choose to file — has no revocation indicator at all. `grep -rn "revok\|Revok" --include=*.tsx "app/(importer)/"` returns exactly one hit, in emissions/page.tsx.
findings.why_controls_fail: Someone thought carefully about the revoked case and added the right label — the comment above it says "Names the past accurately above, the present accurately here." But the staleness column beside it was written as a binary, and a binary has no way to express "cannot tell". So the screen simultaneously discloses that access ended and asserts that the figure is current, which are contradictory claims about the same row. The domain function's doc comment reasons that it "fails toward the quieter result rather than raising a false alarm when the evidence is merely absent" — sound reasoning for a hint, but the UI does not render it as a hint; it renders it as a green success badge.
findings.impact: An importer reviewing its emissions before filing is affirmatively told that figures are current when the system has no basis for that claim and the underlying data may have been superseded several times. It is the same false-assertion class as the filing blocker's silent audit gap and the audit screen's "no events recorded", and it arises with no adversary at all.
findings.recommendation: Introduce the third staleness state (UNKNOWN) proposed in the previous finding and render it as a neutral or warning badge — "Cannot confirm (access ended)" — never as success. Suppress the green "Current" badge entirely whenever sharing_grant_status is REVOKED or EXPIRED. Carry the revocation indicator onto the shipment line screen too, since that is where determination and filing decisions are made.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Any org member can permanently inject fabricated audit events; the helper's own comment claims this is impossible
findings.boundary: Authenticated member -> own-tenant audit trail (evidentiary integrity)
findings.precondition: Any active member of any organization, of any role, using the Supabase anon key and their own JWT — both already present in the browser.
findings.affected_actor: Anyone who reads the organization's audit trail as evidence: internal reviewers, external auditors, a regulator.
findings.exploit: Issue a direct PostgREST INSERT into audit_events with your own org_id, actor_type='USER', actor_user_id=your own uid, any of the 38 catalog event types, any aggregate_type, any aggregate_id (free text, no foreign key, only a 200-char cap), and any payload up to 8KB. The row is accepted, is unremovable (no UPDATE or DELETE policy exists), and its payload renders verbatim on the audit screen. Repeat to flood: occurred_at is pinned to now(), so a burst lands at the same instant as a real event and cannot be separated from it by the screen's date filters, while the list is hard-capped at 200 rows with no pagination.
findings.evidence:
Live, as a plain MEMBER, in p14_review_sandbox:
  set local role authenticated;
  set local request.jwt.claims = '{"sub":"88888888-8888-8888-8888-888888888888","role":"authenticated"}';
  insert into audit_events (org_id, actor_type, actor_user_id, event_type, aggregate_type, aggregate_id, payload)
  values ('22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222','USER','88888888-...','emission_data.verified','EMISSION_DATA','totally-made-up-id',
          jsonb_build_object('verifier_name','EU Accredited Verifier GmbH','to_verification_status','VERIFIED','note','never happened'))
  returning id, event_type, aggregate_id;
  ->  df4cc2e7-0b3b-4e11-ba73-469e41145127|emission_data.verified|totally-made-up-id
     INSERT 0 1

The policy permits it by design:
  audit_events_insert_own_org_as_self | a | WITH CHECK ((actor_type = 'USER') AND (actor_user_id = auth.uid()) AND (org_id IN (SELECT app.user_org_ids())) AND (event_type = ANY (ARRAY[... 38 types ...])))
There is no constraint on aggregate_id beyond `length(aggregate_id) <= 200`, no foreign key from aggregate_id to anything, and no constraint on payload content.

Grants make it HTTP-reachable: `authenticated` holds INSERT on audit_events (information_schema.role_table_grants).

The payload is rendered verbatim to the reader — components/audit/audit-event-view.ts (payloadSummary/payload) and components/audit/audit-event-table.tsx's per-row <details>.

No pagination to escape a flood: src/application/audit/list-audit-events.ts, DEFAULT_LIST_LIMIT = 200, ordered `occurred_at desc, id desc`, `.limit(limit)`, with no offset or cursor; the UI's only affordance is "Narrow the filters above to see further back" (components/audit/audit-event-table.tsx:156-161).

The false claim: src/application/audit/record-audit-event.ts:27-31 — "that policy's WITH CHECK (actor_user_id = auth.uid(), org_id in the caller's own orgs) makes a plain client-side insert safe from forgery".

This insert COMMITTED in p14_review_sandbox. Removal: delete from audit_events where id='df4cc2e7-0b3b-4e11-ba73-469e41145127';
findings.why_controls_fail: The policy defends the property it names — you cannot impersonate another actor or another tenant, and I confirmed both hold. What it does not defend, and what the comment overclaims, is the truthfulness of the event: that it describes something that happened, to an object that exists, that the actor was entitled to act on. Because recordAuditEvent deliberately writes through the user-scoped client rather than a per-mutation SECURITY DEFINER RPC, the client necessarily holds the same INSERT capability the server uses, and the database has no way to distinguish the two. Append-only then works against integrity rather than for it: injected rows cannot be removed by anyone short of service_role. The 200-row unpaginated cap turns volume into a practical suppression vector, since same-instant pinning defeats the date filter that is the screen's only escape hatch.
findings.impact: The audit trail cannot be relied on as evidence of what occurred, only as evidence of what someone in the org asserted occurred. A member can permanently insert plausible, catalog-valid events — a verification that never happened, a shipment lock, a grant revocation — with attacker-chosen payload text shown verbatim to auditors, and can bury a genuine event under a same-timestamp flood. For a compliance product this is a material weakening of the trail's standing, even though it is not a cross-tenant breach.
findings.recommendation: Move audit writes behind SECURITY DEFINER RPCs that write the event in the same transaction as the mutation they describe and derive event_type, aggregate_type and aggregate_id from the mutation rather than from the caller — then revoke INSERT on audit_events from `authenticated` entirely, as migration 20260903190000 already did for calculation_results (the precedent exists in this codebase).
