If that is too large for this release, at minimum: correct record-audit-event.ts's comment so it stops asserting forgery-safety, add a foreign-key-ish existence check on aggregate_id where the aggregate type allows it, and add cursor pagination to the audit list so a flood cannot hide older rows.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: `auth_user_foreign_keys_present` reports OK with 9 of its 10 foreign keys missing, and no self-check exists for a missing UPDATE or DELETE policy
findings.boundary: Disaster recovery self-consistency checks (the `--check` mode BACKUP_RESTORE.md tells operators to run against a target before restoring).
findings.precondition: A restore that drops some but not all references to `auth.users`, or one that loses a table's UPDATE policy while keeping its INSERT policy — the exact shape of the 2026-09-03 loss, where 5 of 56 policies vanished and the rest survived.
findings.affected_actor: The operator running the recovery, who is handed a false all-clear; then every tenant.
findings.exploit: Drop nine of the ten product foreign keys to `auth.users`, drop `shipment_lines_update_parent_not_terminal`, and run `--check`.
findings.evidence:
select count(*) from pg_constraint con ... where con.contype='f' and cn.nspname='auth' and c.relname='users' and rn.nspname in ('public','app');
  -> 1   (after dropping 9 of 10)
select cmd from pg_policies where tablename='shipment_lines';
  -> DELETE / INSERT / SELECT      (UPDATE policy absent)
node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs --check <that database>
  -> [OK] auth_schema_and_helpers_present
     [OK] auth_user_foreign_keys_present
     [OK] policy_functions_resolve
     [OK] tables_without_rls
     [OK] rls_without_policies
     [OK] tables_without_insert_policy
     [OK] api_roles_hold_their_grants
     [OK] truncate_granted_to_api_roles
     [OK] security_definer_without_search_path
     RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES

The check's own message string reads 'NO product foreign key references auth.users -- expected 10' while its predicate is `... ) = 0` (scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:285-300). It fires only when ALL ten are gone.
findings.why_controls_fail: The check was deliberately rewritten to avoid a different vacuous pass (its comment explains it used to count auth's own internal FKs) and landed on a zero-versus-nonzero test while its message promises a count of ten. `tables_without_insert_policy` exists because INSERT policies were the 2026-09-03 casualty, but there is no `tables_without_update_policy` and no `tables_without_delete_policy` — and a missing UPDATE policy is just as silent, since RLS reports it as `UPDATE 0` rather than an error.
findings.impact: Two of the nine self-consistency checks can pass on a database that has lost most of what they name. The `--check` mode is what operators are told to run when no source is available to compare against, i.e. precisely when nothing else will catch it.
findings.recommendation: Change the predicate to `< 10` and print the actual count, or better, compare the named constraint list rather than a count. Add `tables_without_update_policy` and `tables_without_delete_policy` mirroring the INSERT one, with the same explicit exemption list.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The comparator never compares object ownership or default privileges, so the P14 TRUNCATE forward-proofing can be silently undone and a SECURITY DEFINER function can come back owned by a different role
findings.boundary: Disaster recovery acceptance. Object owner is the effective privilege for a SECURITY DEFINER function; `pg_default_acl` is what makes migration 20260903170000's revoke survive the next table creation.
findings.precondition: A restore or rebuild in which default privileges are re-granted (the hosted Supabase bootstrap and `seed.sql` both issue `alter default privileges ... grant all on tables`) or in which functions come back owned by a different superuser-ish role than they had.
findings.affected_actor: Every tenant, latently — the next migration that creates a table re-grants TRUNCATE to `anon` and `authenticated`, which is the decay mode 20260903170000 was written to prevent.
findings.exploit: Run `alter default privileges in schema public grant truncate on tables to anon, authenticated;` on the restored target and run the comparator.
findings.evidence:
Before:
  select defaclacl from pg_default_acl d join pg_namespace n on n.oid=d.defaclnamespace where n.nspname='public' and defaclobjtype='r';
  -> {anon=arwdxtm/postgres,authenticated=arwdxtm/postgres,service_role=arwdDxtm/postgres}
Sabotage:
  alter default privileges in schema public grant truncate on tables to anon, authenticated;
  -> ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES
After:
  -> {anon=arwdDxtm/postgres,authenticated=arwdDxtm/postgres,service_role=arwdDxtm/postgres}   ** D restored for both API roles **
Comparator verdict: [MATCH] effective_grants, [MATCH] function_grants, [OK] truncate_granted_to_api_roles.
No query in the file reads pg_default_acl (grep: zero hits), and none reads proowner or relowner (grep: zero hits). The `functions` check at :160-175 selects prosecdef, proconfig, provolatile and md5(prosrc) — everything about a SECURITY DEFINER function except whose privileges it defines to.
The owner half is reported on file evidence only: I could not demonstrate it, because `alter function ... owner to service_role` returned `ERROR: permission denied for schema public` and `owner to supabase_admin` returned `ERROR: must be able to SET ROLE "supabase_admin"` in this cluster.
findings.why_controls_fail: `truncate_granted_to_api_roles` inspects only tables that exist now. The default ACL governs tables that do not exist yet, which is exactly the decay path 20260903170000's own header calls out ('without this, the next migration that creates a table re-grants TRUNCATE through the default privileges and this fix quietly decays'). The migration guarded against it; the verification tool does not check that the guard survived.
findings.impact: The TRUNCATE revoke can silently expire at the next migration after a restore, with the acceptance test reporting a match. For ownership, a SECURITY DEFINER RPC restored under a different owner executes with different privileges while its prosecdef, proconfig, body hash and ACL all compare identical.
findings.recommendation: Add a `default_privileges` check over `pg_default_acl` (role, schema, objtype, acl) and a self-check asserting no `D` for anon/authenticated in the table default ACL. Add `|| ' | owner=' || pg_get_userbyid(p.proowner)` to the functions check and `|| ' | owner=' || pg_get_userbyid(c.relowner)` to rls_enabled.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: seed.sql's blanket function grant hands `anon` EXECUTE on seven of eight SECURITY DEFINER RPCs, overriding a pending migration's deliberately narrower grant — the hand-maintained revoke list the P14.3 fix chose has already rotted
findings.boundary: Local/CI environment fidelity vs. migration intent. `seed.sql` is the file that reconstructs base-table privileges in every locally rebuilt or CI-built database, i.e. the database every security test and every adversarial reproduction in this review cycle runs against.
findings.precondition: Any `supabase db reset`, `supabase start`, or the DEPLOYMENT.md fresh-rebuild recipe — seed.sql runs LAST, after every migration.
findings.affected_actor: Not end users directly (no leak demonstrated); the affected party is the release process, which is drawing conclusions from an environment whose function-privilege posture is not the one the migrations declare.
findings.exploit: Rebuild from migrations + seed and compare declared grants against effective grants.
findings.evidence:
Migration 20260902150000 (one of the 11 pending) declares, at lines 194-196:
  revoke all on function public.sharing_counterparty_org_names() from public;
  grant execute on function public.sharing_counterparty_org_names() to authenticated;
  grant execute on function public.sharing_counterparty_org_names() to service_role;
  -- anon deliberately not granted
After seed.sql, in BOTH the fresh rebuild and the sandbox:
  select proacl from pg_proc where proname='sharing_counterparty_org_names';
  -> {postgres=X/postgres,authenticated=X/postgres,service_role=X/postgres,anon=X/postgres}   ** anon=X added by seed **
Across all SECURITY DEFINER functions, identical in both databases:
  accept_organization_invitation      anon_exec=true
  accept_sharing_grant_invitation     anon_exec=true
  create_organization_with_owner      anon_exec=true
  list_org_members                    anon_exec=true
  record_calculation_result           anon_exec=false   <- the one seed.sql names explicitly
  record_declaration_filed            anon_exec=true
  record_shared_data_consumption      anon_exec=true
  sharing_counterparty_org_names      anon_exec=true
Reachability probed, not assumed:
  begin; set local role anon; select count(*) from public.sharing_counterparty_org_names(); rollback;
  -> 0    (the function filters on auth.uid(); no data leaked)
findings.why_controls_fail: seed.sql's own header argues against maintaining a list of special objects: 'the alternative -- teaching this file which tables are special -- is a list that rots silently, whereas this one is covered by tests that already caught it once.' It then does exactly that, for three named objects, and the list has already rotted: 20260902150000 landed a fourth narrow grant that the blanket `grant all on all functions in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role` overrides. The comparator cannot catch it either, because it compares two databases that are equally wrong.
findings.impact: Every locally rebuilt and CI-built database — the ones the isolation suites, the E2E journeys and this review cycle's adversarial probes all run against — has a broader function-privilege surface than the migrations describe. Whether production matches is untestable from here (seed.sql is local-only, but the hosted bootstrap sets comparable default privileges), so the divergence's direction on production is unknown rather than benign.
findings.recommendation: Replace the blanket `grant all on all functions` with a targeted revoke-then-grant that reads the intent from the migrations, or add a self-check to compare-database-posture.mjs asserting absolutely that `anon` holds EXECUTE on no SECURITY DEFINER function in `public` unless explicitly allowlisted. Add `sharing_counterparty_org_names` to seed.sql's revoke block now, as an interim fix.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The migration set is not self-contained: a fresh apply aborts at the third file, and the activation migration is not re-runnable
findings.boundary: Fresh reconstruction / disaster rebuild. The protected regulatory migration 20260827110000 asserts a precondition only an offline Python pipeline can satisfy.
findings.precondition: Rebuilding from the repository alone — a new developer environment, a provider migration, or the 'platform-level, logical dump is the only path' arm of BACKUP_RESTORE.md's recovery decision tree.
findings.affected_actor: Whoever is rebuilding, during an incident.
findings.exploit: Create an empty database with the standard Supabase preconditions and apply `supabase/migrations/*.sql` in order.
findings.evidence:
psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f supabase/migrations/20260827110000_activate_definitive_regulatory_dataset.sql
  -> ok   20260826133116_create_regulatory_foundation.sql
     ok   20260827093000_support_regulatory_geography.sql
     FAIL 20260827110000_activate_definitive_regulatory_dataset.sql
     ERROR:  Validated regulatory dataset 2026-definitive-corrected was not found
     CONTEXT:  PL/pgSQL function inline_code_block line 18 at RAISE
(migration source lines 24-27; the same block also requires exactly 12540 rows at lines 34-42)

And once applied, it cannot be applied again — the dataset is now ACTIVE, not DRAFT:
  -> ERROR: Expected dataset status DRAFT, found ACTIVE   (source lines 29-33)
So the file is a one-shot that fails both from empty and from applied.

My workaround, stated plainly: I loaded regulatory_sources, regulatory_datasets, countries, cbam_goods, production_routes and default_emission_values from the sandbox between migration 2 and 3 and reset the dataset to DRAFT so the guard would run for real. I did NOT re-derive the 12,540 rows from data/raw/*.xlsx via scripts/regulatory/*.py, so I have not verified the pipeline arm of the rebuild.
findings.why_controls_fail: This is documented — DEPLOYMENT.md 'Rebuilding on a fresh database' states 'The migration set is not self-sufficient' and gives a six-step recipe, added 2026-09-03 because 'a recipe that exists only in CI is a recipe nobody can follow during an incident'. I am reporting it because the recipe's step 1 ('CI does this by deferring 61 migrations out of the directory') is a manual file-shuffling procedure with a count that is already stale — there are 74 migrations now, not 63 — and because the reconstruction it produces depends on a Python toolchain, a committed workbook and a `supabase/.temp/pooler-url` file, none of which are verified by any gate. The rebuild path is documented but not tested by anything except the CI job that inspired it.
findings.impact: A disaster rebuild from the repository requires an undocumented-in-count, manually-sequenced, Python-dependent procedure. If the pipeline cannot run (no Python, no workbook, changed dependencies) there is no path from the repository to a working database.
findings.recommendation: Either commit the DRAFT dataset as a data-loading migration positioned before 20260827110000 (a new versioned dataset file, not an edit to a protected one), or add a CI job that performs the DEPLOYMENT.md recipe verbatim from the document rather than from the workflow file, so the recipe itself is the thing under test. Update the '61 migrations' count.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The limiter's memory cap was sized for five limiters; the app now constructs 45, so the aggregate ceiling is 662 MiB - 2.2 GiB and every one of them is fillable before authentication
findings.boundary: Unauthenticated internet -> the Node server process's heap. The per-limiter cap is enforced; the aggregate across limiters is not bounded anywhere.
findings.precondition: Ability to send HTTP requests from ~50,000 distinct source addresses. On IPv6 this is a routine /64 allocation, which is the same premise the original P11 finding accepted when it introduced maxKeys. No account and no session are needed, because the limiter runs before the auth check in every action.
findings.affected_actor: All tenants. The process is shared; an OOM or restart takes down the service for everyone and simultaneously resets all 45 rate limiters to empty, which is itself the precondition for defeating every other limit in the app.
findings.exploit:
1. Read the 45 action IDs out of the public client bundle (same grep as finding 1 -- no auth needed).
2. For each action, POST once from each of 50,000 distinct source addresses. Next.js executes a Server Action BEFORE rendering the route, and every action's first statement is `limiter.check(await getClientIp(), Date.now())` -- so the limiter records the key and the request never needs to pass an auth check to have its cost. proxy.ts adds no gate.
3. Each limiter's Map fills to DEFAULT_MAX_KEYS = 50,000 and stays there; LRU eviction caps each map but nothing caps the sum across 45 maps.
4. Total 2,250,000 requests -- about 37 minutes at 1000 rps -- retains ~662 MiB. Sustaining traffic so keys reach their configured limit instead of one hit each pushes it to ~2.2 GiB.
5. Node OOMs. railway.json sets restartPolicyType ON_FAILURE with maxRetries 3, so the process restarts with all 45 counters at zero -- the memory attack and the rate-limit-reset attack are the same attack.
findings.evidence:
The sizing assumption, stated in the module's own header, src/infrastructure/rate-limit/rate-limiter.ts:66:
  * across five module-scope singleton limiters, a real unauthenticated

The actual count today -- 45:
  $ grep -rc 'createInMemoryRateLimiter($' app --include=*.ts | grep -v ':0' | grep -v test
  app/(auth)/actions.ts:2                     app/(importer)/declarations/actions.ts:5
  app/(auth)/forgot-password/actions.ts:1     app/(importer)/shipments/actions.ts:1
  app/(auth)/reset-password/actions.ts:1      app/(importer)/shipments/[id]/actions.ts:8
  app/(importer)/suppliers/actions.ts:2       app/(producer)/emission-data/actions.ts:5
  app/(producer)/installations/actions.ts:4   app/(producer)/sharing/actions.ts:2
  app/accept-invitation/actions.ts:2          app/api/evidence/upload/route.ts:1
  app/api/evidence/[id]/download/route.ts:1   app/api/reports/export/route.ts:1
  app/auth/confirm/actions.ts:1               app/onboarding/actions.ts:1
  app/organization/actions.ts:1               app/team/actions.ts:6      => 45

Measured against the REAL module (node --expose-gc --import tsx, importing src/infrastructure/rate-limit/rate-limiter.ts directly, not a re-implementation):

  ONE request per key, 50000 keys:
    retained: 14.7 MiB   per key: 309 bytes
    first key still present (not evicted): {"allowed":true,"retryAfterMs":0}
    x45 module-scope limiters: 662.5 MiB from 2250000 total requests

  50000 keys x 60 hits (limit=60, the largest configured in the app):
    heapUsed 6.6 -> 57.0 MiB  delta 50.4 MiB
    rss      61.7 -> 145.6 MiB  delta 83.9 MiB
    per key: 1058 bytes
    first key still rate-limited (proves not evicted): {"allowed":false,"retryAfterMs":599940}
    x45 limiters: 2.22 GiB heap

Pre-auth reachability, src/infrastructure/rate-limit call ordering -- e.g. app/team/actions.ts:255-270, the limiter is the first statement and getServerSupabaseClient()/getCurrentOrgSummary come ~20 lines later; app/api/evidence/upload/route.ts:60-64 documents this ordering explicitly ('Keyed on IP alone (not IP+user) ... the caller's identity isn't known yet at the point this check has to run'). proxy.ts has no redirect: its body ends `await supabase.auth.getUser(); return response;`.
findings.why_controls_fail: The maxKeys LRU cap works exactly as designed and I confirmed it live -- the 50,001st key evicts nothing the attacker cares about and the first key is still retained at the cap. The defect is that the cap is per-limiter and the constant was chosen when five limiters existed. Nothing recomputes it, no test asserts an aggregate ceiling, and the count has grown 9x with no one re-deriving the number. The module comment still describes the five-limiter world, so anyone reading it for reassurance gets a figure that is off by an order of magnitude.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated remote memory exhaustion leading to OOM-kill, and on restart every rate limit in the application resets to zero -- so this both denies service and unlocks brute-force headroom against sign-in, invitation acceptance and every mutation limiter.
findings.recommendation: Re-derive DEFAULT_MAX_KEYS against the real limiter count and the deployment's memory budget (45 x 50,000 x ~1 KB is not a budget anyone chose), or better, replace the 45 independent Maps with one shared store so the ceiling is a single number that cannot drift as call sites are added. Add a test that asserts the number of createInMemoryRateLimiter call sites times maxKeys times the measured per-key cost stays under an explicit budget, so the next call site added fails loudly instead of silently raising the ceiling. Update the module header, which still says five.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The Storage availability gate cannot detect an unreachable Storage endpoint: the '000' branch is unreachable because curl's failure path produces '000000'
findings.boundary: CI quality gate -> evidence-storage RLS and bucket-limit coverage
findings.precondition: The Storage endpoint is unreachable at the TCP/connection level (container not listening, Kong route absent, connection refused/reset) rather than returning HTTP 503.
findings.affected_actor: Own-tenant: the evidence-upload/verification path that 20260829510000's bucket limits and storage.objects policies protect.
findings.exploit: If http://127.0.0.1:54321/storage/v1/bucket refuses the connection, `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}'` writes the literal `000` to stdout AND exits non-zero, so `|| echo "000"` appends a second `000`. STORAGE_CODE becomes `000000`, which equals neither "503" nor "000", so the guard at ci.yml:334 does not fire and the step continues as though Storage were healthy.
findings.evidence:
$ STORAGE_CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1:59999/storage/v1/bucket || echo "000")
$ echo "STORAGE_CODE=[${STORAGE_CODE}]"
STORAGE_CODE=[000000]
$ if [ "${STORAGE_CODE}" = "503" ] || [ "${STORAGE_CODE}" = "000" ]; then echo "GATE FIRES (correct)"; else echo "GATE PASSES -- storage unreachable but job continues"; fi
GATE PASSES -- storage unreachable but job continues

file:line — .github/workflows/ci.yml:332 (`STORAGE_CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 5 ... || echo "000")`) and ci.yml:334 (the two-branch guard).

The guard is additionally narrow beyond this bug: it enumerates only 503 and 000, so 404 (Kong route absent), 502 and 504 all pass.
findings.why_controls_fail: The `|| echo "000"` was written to normalise curl's failure into the sentinel the guard checks, but `-w '%{http_code}'` already emits `000` on connection failure, so the two mechanisms concatenate rather than substitute. The author appears to have reasoned about the two paths independently rather than composing them. Partial backstops do exist and I credit them: the subsequent `BUCKETS` check (ci.yml:341) fails if storage.buckets has no 'evidence' row, and tests/e2e/producer-journey.spec.ts:117-124 and tests/e2e/actual-data-determination.spec.ts throw under `process.env.CI` when their live Storage probe fails. So the most likely real-world outcome is a later loud failure rather than a silent green — but it is not the failure this step promises, and the BUCKETS check tests DB schema, not whether the Storage HTTP service is answering.
findings.impact: A guard whose stated purpose is 'Storage must be genuinely up, or the evidence-storage RLS and bucket-limit tests silently do not run' is provably unable to detect the connection-refused case it explicitly enumerates. Partial evidence: I proved the branch is unreachable; I could not run the full job to prove no downstream step catches the same condition.
findings.recommendation: Use `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 5 <url>` without the `|| echo` and let `set -e` handle a curl failure, or capture status separately: `STORAGE_CODE=$(curl ... ) || STORAGE_CODE=000` (note `||` on the assignment, not inside the substitution). Then invert the guard to an allowlist — fail unless the code is 200 or 400 — rather than a denylist of two codes.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The Playwright gate does not fail on a flaky test: retries:2 plus exit 0 means an intermittently-failing security journey ships green
findings.boundary: CI quality gate -> end-to-end cross-org sharing / evidence / determination journeys
findings.precondition: A journey spec that fails on some runs and passes on others — exactly the profile of a concurrency-dependent RLS or determination-validator defect, which is the class this suite exists to catch.
findings.affected_actor: Cross-tenant: cross-org-sharing-journey.spec.ts, actual-data-determination.spec.ts and producer-journey.spec.ts are the only end-to-end coverage of the sharing and evidence boundaries.
findings.exploit: A defect that manifests under concurrent load fails attempt 1, passes attempt 2 or 3, is reported as `1 flaky`, and `playwright test` exits 0. The step at ci.yml:454-455 is `run: pnpm exec playwright test` with no `--max-failures`, no flaky-to-failure conversion, and no post-processing of the report. The job goes green.
findings.evidence:
Reproduced with the repo's own @playwright/test and the same retries value, in a throwaway project under the scratchpad (repo untouched):
$ cat playwright.config.ts   # retries: 2, same as playwright.config.ts:118
$ cat tests/flaky.spec.ts    # fails on first attempt via a marker file, passes thereafter
$ pnpm exec playwright test -c <scratch>/playwright.config.ts
  ...
  1 flaky
    .../flaky.spec.ts:4:5 > intermittently failing security journey
PLAYWRIGHT_EXIT=0

file:line — playwright.config.ts:118 (`retries: 2`) and .github/workflows/ci.yml:455 (`run: pnpm exec playwright test`).
findings.why_controls_fail: playwright.config.ts:110-117 argues two retries "absorbs a genuine transient concurrency blip without masking a test that is actually, persistently broken -- that would still fail all three attempts." That is true only for deterministic breakage. The defect classes this repository has actually shipped and then found — a determination-validator bypass, cross-org row visibility — are precisely the ones that surface under concurrency and disappear when re-run serially, which the config's own comment describes happening repeatedly during P13. The retry policy is therefore tuned to suppress the signal shape most likely to indicate a real security regression. There is no compensating control: nothing reads playwright-report/ (uploaded at ci.yml:465-471 as an artifact only, never asserted on).
findings.impact: An intermittently-reproducing cross-tenant leak in the E2E journeys cannot fail the release gate. It is recorded as 'flaky' in a log line and an artifact nobody's automation reads.
findings.recommendation: Keep retries for infrastructure flakiness but make flakiness visible as a failure signal on the release branch: run with `--reporter=json` alongside `list` and fail the step if any test has `status: 'flaky'` (or set `retries: 0` for the security journey specs via a dedicated project). At minimum, add an explicit step that parses the report and fails when the flaky count is non-zero, so 'passed on retry' is a decision a human makes rather than a default.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The regulatory verification gate is never run in CI although the job now has every prerequisite; the only regulatory check is a row count that cannot detect wrong values
findings.boundary: CI quality gate -> protected regulatory dataset integrity
findings.precondition: None. The build-and-test job regenerates the canonical regulatory JSON and loads 12,540 rows on every run and never verifies them.
findings.affected_actor: The regulator/filing: every CBAM declaration derived from default emission values whose provenance CI regenerates but never checks.
findings.exploit: Corrupt the parse in a way that preserves cardinality — e.g. a change in scripts/regulatory/parse-definitive-default-values.py that shifts a column, transposes a route mapping, or rounds a value — and the pipeline still produces 12,540 rows. ci.yml:317-322 asserts only `count(*) = 12540` and passes. The regulatory suites then run against corrupted data and, because they assert against the same loaded dataset, largely agree with it.
findings.evidence:
file:line — .github/workflows/ci.yml:11-14: "pnpm regulatory:verify is NOT run here — it requires a Python environment plus live database credentials (SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD) and remains a locally-run / manually-dispatched gate."

That justification is stale as of the P14.x edits to this same file. The job now has all three prerequisites:
  ci.yml:222-225  actions/setup-python@v5, python-version 3.12
  ci.yml:227-228  pip install -r scripts/regulatory/requirements.txt  (provides psycopg)
  ci.yml:233      SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD: postgres
  ci.yml:300      printf 'postgresql://postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/postgres' > supabase/.temp/pooler-url

And those are exactly and only what the verifier needs:
  scripts/regulatory/verify-definitive-regulatory-data.py:126-154 connect():
    if not POOLER_URL.exists(): raise FileNotFoundError(...)
    password = os.environ.get("SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD")
    if not password: raise RuntimeError("SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD is not set.")
    return psycopg.connect(connection_url, password=password, ...)

What is being left unchecked (verify script lines 44-53):
  EXPECTED_RECORDS = 12540; EXPECTED_COUNTRIES = 122; EXPECTED_GOODS = 283; EXPECTED_ROUTES = 10
  EXPECTED_SOURCE_CHECKSUM = "900583811c7e1194799eb9bdbad2d6d7e1100f5a7d80a664c1584a8fce6f9f35"

The workbook checksum, the country/goods/route cardinalities and the full reconciliation report are all computed by a script the job already has installed and could run in seconds. It is simply not invoked — `grep -n "regulatory:verify\|verify-definitive" .github/workflows/ci.yml` returns only the prose at lines 11-14.

Sandbox cross-check that the count assertion is satisfiable independently of correctness:
$ psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "select count(*) from public.default_emission_values dev join public.regulatory_datasets rd on rd.id=dev.dataset_id where rd.status='ACTIVE'"
12540
findings.why_controls_fail: The count assertion at ci.yml:317-322 does propagate correctly — I verified psql exits 1 on error and that `set -e`+pipefail abort the step — so it is a working gate. It is just the wrong assertion: cardinality is invariant under every value-level corruption. The header comment that excuses the real gate's absence describes an environment that no longer exists in this workflow, and nothing re-examined it when Python and the database were added to the job in the 2026-09-02/09-03 edits.
findings.impact: The protected regulatory dataset is regenerated from the workbook inside CI on every run, loaded as the ACTIVE dataset that every regulatory suite and every E2E determination resolves against, and never verified. The project's own strongest integrity control exists, is runnable in that job at near-zero cost, and does not run.
findings.recommendation: Add a step after ci.yml:322: `SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD=postgres pnpm regulatory:verify` and require `RESULT: VALID`. Everything it needs is already present. Also correct the stale claim at ci.yml:11-14 rather than leaving a comment that tells future readers the gate cannot run here.

findings.title: No CI result gates a deployment: Railway deploys on push independently of every gate in this workflow
findings.boundary: CI quality gate -> production release
findings.precondition: None.
findings.affected_actor: Every tenant and the regulator/filing: the deployed artifact is not required to have passed any gate.
findings.exploit: Push a commit to the Railway-watched branch. Railway builds from the Dockerfile and deploys on the push event. A red fast-gates or build-and-test run does not prevent, delay or roll back that deploy; a cancelled run (concurrency.cancel-in-progress at ci.yml:39-41) does not either.
findings.why_controls_fail: The 2026-09-02 change made CI *observe* the deploy branch (`branches: ['**']`), which is a genuine improvement, but observation is not gating. The comment's own framing — "strictly safer, not weaker" — is accurate and also concedes the point: CI now reports on the deployed commit, and nothing consumes that report. Branch protection with required status checks is a GitHub-side setting I cannot read from the repository, so I state this as: nothing in the repository establishes gating, and the deploy platform's own config explicitly does not.
findings.impact: Every finding above about a gate that cannot fail is compounded by the fact that even a gate that does fail blocks nothing. The release-readiness posture rests on a human noticing a red check before or after an automatic deploy has already happened.
findings.recommendation: Either move deployment behind a workflow that `needs: [fast-gates, build-and-test]` (deploy from CI on success, with Railway's auto-deploy disabled), or enable branch protection with both jobs as required status checks and record that requirement in docs/runbooks/DEPLOYMENT.md so it is auditable from the repository. Verify by pushing a deliberately failing commit to a scratch branch and confirming no deploy occurs.

findings.title: The confirmed-email gate that the P11 review installed as a BLOCKING fix is vacuous under the Auth configuration this repository ships, and the migration's own comment asserts a config-independence guarantee it does not have
findings.boundary: Proof of mailbox control — the sole thing standing between knowing an invited email address and holding the organizational access that invitation carries.
findings.precondition: Knowledge of an address that has a pending invitation, an account creatable through the product's own /sign-up with the public anon key, and an environment where GoTrue's mailer autoconfirm is on. supabase/config.toml:319 ships `enable_confirmations = false`, so every environment this repository builds — local, CI, E2E — is such an environment. Production is a hosted dashboard setting this repository cannot express, enforce, or observe.
findings.affected_actor: Cross-tenant: any organization with an outstanding invitation, at whatever role that invitation carries (ADMIN is invitable — the role CHECK is `role in ('ADMIN','MEMBER')`).
findings.exploit:
1. An admin invites victim@corp.com as ADMIN. The invitation row is PENDING.
2. The attacker creates an account for victim@corp.com through the product's own sign-up form (or POSTs /auth/v1/signup with the public anon key). Under mailer autoconfirm, GoTrue stamps email_confirmed_at at creation and returns a session immediately — no link is ever sent or clicked.
3. app.user_confirmed_email() now returns victim@corp.com; organization_invitations_select_own_email admits the row; accept_organization_invitation's `email_confirmed_at is not null` predicate is satisfied and the EMAIL_MISMATCH branch is skipped; a membership is inserted at the invitation's role.

A variant I could not test at all but which follows from the same GoTrue setting: with autoconfirm on, an email CHANGE is also auto-confirmed, so an attacker holding any ordinary account could re-point it at an invited address without ever creating a new one. supabase/config.toml:317 sets `double_confirm_changes = true`, which would normally prevent that; whether autoconfirm short-circuits it is a GoTrue behaviour I did not observe.
findings.evidence:
PARTIAL — this is the one finding I did not reproduce end to end, and I want that stated plainly rather than buried. The sandbox contains only a hand-written auth.users shim; there is no GoTrue in it, and reaching the local GoTrue would have meant writing to the forbidden `postgres` database. Everything below is source and configuration, not observation.

supabase/config.toml:319, under [auth.email]: `enable_confirmations = false`, directly beneath its own comment at :318 "If enabled, users need to confirm their email address before signing in."

supabase/migrations/20260829380000_p11_review_email_confirmation_and_invitation_hardening.sql:34-39, describing the fix: "This holds regardless of what `enable_confirmations` is set to on any environment: an unconfirmed user's email claim is now worthless for this class of authorization no matter how Auth is configured, closing the silent-dependency problem at its root rather than only asserting it should be set correctly elsewhere." The same claim is repeated inside the shipped function's COMMENT at :103-110, so it is carried in the database itself.

What the fix actually does (live body, via pg_get_functiondef, matching :206-210): `select email into v_user_email from auth.users where auth.users.id = auth.uid() and email_confirmed_at is not null;`. It reads a column that GoTrue stamps at signup with zero verification whenever autoconfirm is on. The dependency was moved from `auth.jwt() ->> 'email'` to `auth.users.email_confirmed_at`; it was not removed.

What I DID verify live, and it is worth recording as the boundary that holds: the SQL layer itself is correct. With an auth.users row whose email exactly matched the invitation but whose email_confirmed_at was NULL, accept_organization_invitation returned `EMAIL_MISMATCH | (null)`. The predicate does exactly what it claims. The failure is that the column it reads is not the assertion it is treated as.

The repository's own release report contradicts the migration at docs/plans/P13_RELEASE_READINESS_REPORT.md:577 (finding S3): "GoTrue stamps it at signup with zero verification when confirmations are disabled" — carried in Bucket B, HIGH, must fix before release, status "Documented, not code-fixed."
findings.why_controls_fail: The control is a database column, and the thing it is trusted to mean ("this person proved they control this mailbox") is decided entirely outside the database, by an Auth service setting. app.user_confirmed_email() is a faithful implementation of "return the email only if email_confirmed_at is set"; it simply cannot supply the property the migration claims for it, because that property is a fact about how the column came to be set. The compensating control is a pre-go-live checkbox in docs/runbooks/DEPLOYMENT.md §5 — an unversioned, unattested, out-of-band dashboard setting, which is precisely the class of silent dependency the migration says it closed at the root. And because every environment the repository itself builds has the gate off, no test in this repository exercises the gate through a real signup flow; the one integration test that covers it (tests/integration/organizations-isolation.test.ts:748-900) has to hand-mint a raw JWT to reach an unconfirmed session at all.
findings.impact: Where autoconfirm is on, an invited organization can be entered at ADMIN by anyone who knows the invited address, using only the public anon key. Where it is off, nothing here is exploitable — but the codebase's own account of why it is safe is wrong, which means the next person to reason about this boundary will reason from a false premise. That is the part this release should not carry: not the vulnerability, which is tracked, but the comment in the shipped function that says it was closed.
findings.recommendation: Two separable actions. (1) Correct the false guarantee before shipping: amend the comment on app.user_confirmed_email() — via a new migration, since the applied one must not be edited — to state what is true, that the gate is only as strong as the Auth project's confirmation setting, and cross-reference the DEPLOYMENT.md requirement. A shipped function comment asserting a security property the function does not have is worse than no comment. (2) Make the property real if it is wanted: bind the invitation to something the platform controls rather than to an email string — e.g. record the invited user's auth.users id at invite time when the address already has an account, and require the acceptor's id to match; or gate acceptance on a per-invitation nonce delivered only to the invited mailbox, which is proof of delivery rather than proof of a column. Also add a startup or health-check assertion that the Auth project reports mailer_autoconfirm=false, so the dependency is observed rather than assumed. This finding is recorded in docs/plans/P14_ADVERSARIAL_REVIEW_FINDINGS.json and remains unremediated at cad99adb.

findings.title: /reset-password changes the account password for any live session with no re-authentication and no current password, then signs every other session out
findings.boundary: Account ownership. Converting temporary possession of a session into permanent, exclusive control of the account.
findings.precondition: Possession of a live session for the target account — an unlocked shared workstation, a stolen session cookie, or a session obtained via finding 4. No password, no email access, no second factor.
findings.affected_actor: Own-tenant: the individual user, and through them whatever their memberships reach.
findings.exploit:
1. Attacker reaches /reset-password in the victim's authenticated browser (it is not gated on a recovery-scoped session — app/(auth)/layout.tsx is a presentational container with no session check, and proxy.ts performs no route protection, only a getUser() cookie refresh).
2. Attacker submits a new password. The form (app/(auth)/reset-password/reset-password-form.tsx) has exactly two fields, password and confirmPassword; there is no current-password field.
3. updatePasswordAction accepts any non-null user and calls updateUser({password}).
4. It then calls signOut({scope:"others"}), which terminates the legitimate owner's other sessions.
The owner's original password no longer works and their sessions are gone; the attacker's session persists.
findings.evidence:
file:line, source-derived.

app/(auth)/reset-password/actions.ts:155-165 — `const { data: { user } } = await supabase.auth.getUser(); if (!user) { return error }`. ANY non-null user proceeds; there is no check that the session came from a recovery link, no AAL/amr inspection, no recency requirement.
app/(auth)/reset-password/actions.ts:167-172 — `await supabase.auth.updateUser({ password: parsed.data.password })`.
app/(auth)/reset-password/actions.ts:212-215 — `await supabase.auth.signOut({ scope: "others" })`, with the doc comment at :198-211 confirming this is deliberate ("A password change should end every session the old password could have established"). Correct in intent; it completes the lockout when the caller is not the owner.
supabase/config.toml:321 — `secure_password_change = false`, directly beneath its own comment at :320: "If enabled, users will need to reauthenticate or have logged in recently to change their password." The GoTrue-side control that would independently block this is off in every environment this repo builds.
proxy.ts:30-124 — the whole file constructs a client, calls getUser() at :121 for cookie refresh, and returns; there is no redirect or branching, and config.matcher at :132 matches everything. No route guard exists anywhere.
`grep -rni 'reauthenticat|aal|amr|nonce'` across app/ src/ components/ returns nothing outside tests.

I did not exercise GoTrue, so the claim that updateUser succeeds without reauthentication rests on secure_password_change=false plus the absence of any application-side check — not on an observed 200.
findings.why_controls_fail: There are three plausible controls and none is present. (a) An application-side current-password challenge: absent, and the form has no field for one. (b) A recovery-scope check — this route is reached both from a recovery link and by any signed-in user, and the code cannot distinguish them because it inspects only `user`, never the session's authentication method. (c) GoTrue's own secure_password_change, which exists precisely for this and is disabled in config.toml:321. The rate limiter at :39-48 bounds the number of attempts, which is irrelevant when the first attempt succeeds. The `scope: "others"` sign-out, added in this release as a security improvement, makes the outcome strictly worse for the victim in the attacker case.
findings.impact: Temporary session possession becomes permanent account takeover plus owner lockout, with the product itself performing the lockout step. It crosses no tenancy boundary on its own, which is why I rate it MEDIUM — but it is the natural second stage of finding 4, and on a shared or kiosk workstation it needs no exotic precondition at all.
findings.recommendation: Split the two flows that currently share this route. A recovery-link visit (session established from a recovery token) may set a password without a current one; an ordinary signed-in visit must be a change-password flow that requires the current password or a recent re-authentication. Enable secure_password_change on every Auth project as the independent backstop, and add it to DEPLOYMENT.md's pre-go-live checklist alongside the confirmations setting. This finding is recorded in docs/plans/P14_ADVERSARIAL_REVIEW_FINDINGS.json and in docs/plans/P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md as an open high-risk item; it is unremediated at cad99adb.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Deleting an evidence_files row -- directly, or by cascade from emission_data or organizations -- orphans the storage object permanently; nothing anywhere links the two
findings.boundary: Data-lifecycle boundary between the Postgres metadata record and the Storage object.
findings.precondition: For the direct route, a MEMBER plus the state manipulation of finding 1. For the cascade route, service_role or a DB administrator deleting an emission_data or organizations row (no RLS DELETE policy exists on either table, so an ordinary member cannot take that route).
findings.affected_actor: The account owner (unbounded paid storage no application surface can enumerate) and the security posture -- the orphaned object stays readable to org members through evidence_storage_select_own_org's path-prefix rule while having no metadata row, so it sits outside every audit and retention view the product offers. Also any data subject whose erasure request the organizations cascade appears to satisfy.
findings.exploit: (a) `delete from public.evidence_files where id=<ev>;` via PostgREST, once finding 1's chain has unlocked the delete policy -- the object is untouched. (b) `delete from public.emission_data where id=<rec>;` -- evidence_files rows cascade away, objects remain. (c) `delete from public.organizations where id=<org>;` -- the whole org's evidence_files rows cascade away, objects remain. The only code path that ever deletes a storage object is removeEvidenceFile (src/application/evidence/upload-evidence.ts:561-566), and it is on none of these routes.
findings.evidence:
psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox":
begin;
  evidence_files for E1                             | 1
  storage objects at that path                      | 1
  delete from public.emission_data where id='eeee0000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001';  -> DELETE 1
  AFTER emission_data delete -- evidence_files      | 0
  AFTER -- storage objects still there (orphaned)   | 1
rollback;
begin;
  delete from public.organizations where id='bbbb0000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001';  -> DELETE 1
  AFTER org delete -- evidence_files for org        | 0
  AFTER org delete -- storage objects               | 1
rollback;

Structural: `select conrelid::regclass, conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) from pg_constraint where confrelid in ('public.evidence_files'::regclass,'public.emission_data'::regclass)` -> only `evidence_files|evidence_files_emission_data_id_fkey|FOREIGN KEY (emission_data_id) REFERENCES emission_data(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`. `select count(*) from pg_constraint where confrelid='storage.objects'::regclass` -> 0. `select count(*) from pg_trigger where tgrelid='public.evidence_files'::regclass and not tgisinternal` -> 0.

PARTIAL: the storage.objects rows here are shim fixtures I inserted; the FK/trigger topology is real and is what the finding rests on.
findings.why_controls_fail: There is no control. The evidence_files -> storage.objects relationship is a text path with no referential integrity, no trigger and no reconciliation job anywhere in the repository. removeEvidenceFile is the sole deleter of objects and it also runs the storage delete BEFORE the metadata delete (upload-evidence.ts:561 then :590) -- its own doc comment at line 465 argues that ordering is the safer failure mode, which is defensible for that function but means the inverse hazard (metadata gone, object retained) has no owner at all. The `on delete cascade` on evidence_files_emission_data_id_fkey was chosen for referential tidiness in Postgres with no counterpart in Storage.
findings.impact: Evidence bytes accumulate in the bucket with no record that they exist, still readable by org members via the storage path-prefix policy, invisible to every product screen, and impossible to enumerate or purge through the application -- which also means a deletion request (GDPR erasure, contract termination, the organizations cascade above) does not actually delete the documents. It is the mirror image of finding 1: there the metadata dies and the bytes live; via the removeEvidenceFile ordering, the bytes die and the metadata lives.
findings.recommendation: Replace the implicit link with an explicit lifecycle. Add an AFTER DELETE trigger on evidence_files that enqueues the storage_path for object deletion (an outbox table the service role drains), so the direct-delete and both cascade routes converge on the same cleanup as removeEvidenceFile. Add a reconciliation job that reports objects in the evidence bucket with no evidence_files row and rows whose storage_path resolves to no object, and assert both sets are empty in a periodic check. Re-examine whether `on delete cascade` is right for evidence on a compliance record at all -- `on delete restrict` would force the deletion to be explicit.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: filed_snapshot is immutable against UPDATE for every role including service_role, but a FILED declaration can be DELETEd outright by service_role -- the immutability trigger is BEFORE UPDATE only
findings.boundary: Trusted-boundary scope. service_role is trusted by design, but the filed declaration is the one artifact this schema treats as permanently immutable, and it defends only half the ways it can be destroyed.
findings.precondition: service_role key (server-only, src/infrastructure/supabase/admin-client.ts). Not reachable by anon or authenticated -- an authenticated DELETE returns 0 rows because declarations has no DELETE policy.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant and the regulator: the archived filing record.
findings.exploit: `set local role service_role; delete from public.declarations where id='<a FILED_RECORDED declaration>';` succeeds. There is no BEFORE DELETE trigger and no protection equivalent to app.prevent_declaration_fact_change. Two ON DELETE CASCADE paths widen this: declarations_org_id_fkey (deleting an organization removes all its filed declarations) and declarations_supersedes_declaration_id_fkey (deleting a superseded original removes its amendment chain).
findings.evidence:
psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox":
begin; set local role service_role;
-- UPDATE is defended:
update public.declarations set filed_snapshot = jsonb_set(filed_snapshot,'{totals,embedded_emissions_tco2e}','"1"') where id='aff726e5-9102-4743-b119-5dae6bac3b07';
 --> ERROR: declarations: filed_snapshot, filed_reference and filed_at may only be written by public.record_declaration_filed(), in the same statement that moves status READY -> FILED_RECORDED
-- DELETE is not:
delete from public.declarations where id='aff726e5-9102-4743-b119-5dae6bac3b07';   --> DELETE 1
select count(*) from public.declarations where id='aff726e5-9102-4743-b119-5dae6bac3b07';   --> 0
rollback;

And the trigger genuinely cannot be evaded by service_role:
alter table public.declarations disable trigger declarations_prevent_fact_change_trg;  --> ERROR: must be owner of table declarations
drop trigger declarations_prevent_fact_change_trg on public.declarations;              --> ERROR: must be owner of relation declarations
set local session_replication_role = replica;                                          --> ERROR: permission denied to set parameter "session_replication_role"
create or replace function app.prevent_declaration_fact_change() ...                   --> ERROR: permission denied for schema app
(pg_roles: service_role rolsuper=f, rolbypassrls=t; public.declarations owner = postgres.)
findings.why_controls_fail: app.prevent_declaration_fact_change is attached only as `BEFORE UPDATE ... FOR EACH ROW`. Its own header reasons carefully about rewriting -- "a filed row's own snapshot/reference/timestamp can never be rewritten later by any statement at all, not even another SECURITY DEFINER one" -- and that reasoning holds, but it addresses rewriting, not removal. calculation_results was explicitly hardened to append-only in 20260903190000 by revoking UPDATE and DELETE grants; declarations received the equivalent UPDATE protection and no DELETE protection.
findings.impact: Bounded by the service-role trust boundary, so this is not an authenticated-user exploit. It matters because the filed declaration is the record a declarant would produce years later to re-prove a filing, and an accidental admin-path deletion, a mis-scoped organization cleanup routine, or a compromised server key destroys it with no database-level objection -- while a far less damaging attempt to alter a single number in it is refused loudly. Immutability that permits erasure is not immutability.
findings.recommendation: Add a BEFORE DELETE trigger on public.declarations that refuses deletion of any row with status = 'FILED_RECORDED', and revoke DELETE on public.declarations from anon and authenticated to match calculation_results' posture. Re-examine both ON DELETE CASCADE paths: a filed declaration should survive its organisation row being removed (or organisation removal should itself be refused while filed declarations exist), and a superseded original must not be destroyed by anything that touches its amendment.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: parameter_datasets is hardcoded to [] even though the engine reads the cbam_goods regulatory dataset at calculation time, so no persisted row records which regulatory data the Annex II decision came from
findings.boundary: Provenance boundary: the row's own documented contract vs. what it actually stores.
findings.precondition: Any ACTUAL-method calculation. calculate-line.ts passes an empty array unconditionally.
findings.affected_actor: Own tenant, and any future auditor of a filed declaration.
findings.exploit: Not an attack — a missing record. src/domain/calculations/types.ts defines CalculationParameterDataset as identifying 'one ACTIVE regulatory dataset the calculation engine read (beyond the DEFAULT_EMISSION_VALUES dataset already captured inside the line's own EmissionDetermination snapshot)'. For an ACTUAL determination the engine's Annex II branch is driven entirely by cbam_goods.sector, which is exactly such a dataset and is not inside the determination snapshot. It is read (calculate-line.ts:116-141) and then not recorded. A later re-ingestion of cbam_goods — which is how this project is required to correct regulatory facts, per the facts-as-datasets rule — silently changes what every past ACTUAL calculation would reproduce as, and no persisted row says which version it originally saw.
findings.evidence:
src/application/calculations/calculate-line.ts:290 — `parameter_datasets: [],` (the only value ever passed; there is no other call site).

psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "select distinct parameter_datasets from public.calculation_results;"
 []

cbam_goods carries no dataset_id / version column at all:
select column_name from information_schema.columns where table_schema='public' and table_name='cbam_goods';
 id | trade_code | trade_code_type | record_type | record_level | parent_good_id | sector | description | functional_unit | active_from | active_to | created_at

filed_snapshot.provenance records engine_versions, determination_methods, regulatory_dataset_versions (read from determination->resolution->dataset_version, which only exists on the DEFAULT path) and calculation_result_ids — so for an ACTUAL-method line the snapshot's regulatory_dataset_versions is empty and nothing anywhere names the goods data used.
findings.why_controls_fail: record_declaration_filed's provenance block reads `c.determination -> 'resolution' ->> 'dataset_version'`, which is null for every ACTUAL row, so the gap is invisible there too. record_calculation_result accepts p_parameter_datasets as an opaque jsonb and never checks that it is non-empty or that it corresponds to anything the engine actually read. The type's own doc comment says these datasets are what the column is for; the caller simply never fills it.
findings.impact: A filed ACTUAL-method figure cannot be re-proved years later, which is the stated purpose of the provenance block ('what lets a filed declaration be re-proved the same way years later, rather than being an unattributed number'). It also removes the only structural defence against finding 1: if the goods row identity and as-of date were recorded here, the release_date manipulation would be detectable after the fact.
findings.recommendation: Populate parameter_datasets for ACTUAL determinations with the cbam_goods row actually consulted — at minimum {trade_code, sector, as_of_date, row id} — and have record_calculation_result derive it itself rather than accept it, for the same reason it sets calculated_at itself. Have reproduceCalculationResult read that frozen entry instead of re-deriving. If cbam_goods is to be versioned as a dataset (it should be, per the facts-as-datasets rule), add the dataset_id/version columns and record those.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The DEFAULT determination validator compares regulated numerics via ::numeric, so a whitespace-padded value is accepted into a frozen determination and then throws an uncaught DecimalError out of the engine
findings.boundary: Member -> the stored determination -> every server-side surface that runs the engine for that line.
findings.precondition: A plain MEMBER of the owning org, a DEFAULT-method line, a non-LOCKED/VOID shipment. Direct PostgREST/SQL write (the same posture the P14.1 migration header treats as in scope).
findings.affected_actor: Own tenant only. I found no cross-org reach.
findings.exploit: `update public.shipment_lines set emission_determination = jsonb_set(emission_determination,'{resolution,values,total,value}','"  1.470  "')`. app.emission_determination_matches_regulatory_record's final comparison is `v_record.total_value is not distinct from app.try_cast_numeric(v_resolution->'values'->'total'->>'value')`; Postgres trims whitespace on a numeric cast, so 1.470 = 1.470 and the write is accepted. The engine then calls toDecimal(total.value) — src/domain/shared/decimal.ts:152, which by contract does not re-validate — and decimal.js does NOT trim, so it throws. calculateLine, reproduceCalculationResult, and the why-this-number panel all run that same code path for that line, permanently, until the determination is rewritten.
findings.evidence:
psql, as a plain MEMBER (user 1daa38d3, role MEMBER, org 78fbb4bb):
begin; set local role authenticated; set local request.jwt.claims = '{"sub":"1daa38d3-79b3-433f-aba1-bee81265c691","role":"authenticated"}';
update public.shipment_lines set emission_determination = jsonb_set(emission_determination,'{resolution,values,total,value}','"  1.470  "') where id='29c412d3-1613-4cdb-8352-f36f5418c96e';
UPDATE 1
select emission_determination->'resolution'->'values'->'total'->>'value';
   1.470     <-- accepted, padding preserved
rollback;

(also accepted: '"1.47e0"' -> UPDATE 1)

Real engine, via tsx, DEFAULT determination, net_mass_tonnes 100:
"1.470"      => COMPUTED 147
"  1.470  "  => UNCAUGHT THROW: Error [DecimalError] Invalid argument:   1.470  
"1.47e0"     => COMPUTED 147

app.try_cast_numeric(' 1.5 ') -> 1.5   (Postgres trims)
new Decimal(' 1.5 ')          -> throws (decimal.js does not)
findings.why_controls_fail: src/domain/shared/decimal.ts's own header documents this exact failure class as already fixed — 'a value like "  42  " came back {status: "OK"} from THIS function yet threw a raw DecimalError out of toDecimal()'. parseDecimalString was hardened accordingly, and CANONICAL_DECIMAL_PATTERN is deliberately narrower than decimal.js's grammar so that 'exactly one canonical reading exists for any stored value'. But the DEFAULT determination validator never uses parseDecimalString: it is a second, independent definition of 'is this a valid regulated numeric', written in SQL, and it is wider than the canonical one. The ACTUAL path does not have this problem because it compares as TEXT against emission_data, whose own CHECK enforces `^-?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?$`. The DEFAULT path has no equivalent CHECK on the jsonb column at all.
findings.impact: A member can permanently break calculation, reproduction and the explanation panel for one of their own lines with a single write, with no error message that points at the cause. More significantly, it means a regulated numeric can be frozen into a determination in a non-canonical form that different readers parse differently — Number('  1.470  ') is 1.47, Number('1_470') is NaN, decimal.js reads '1_470' as 1470 — which is precisely the multi-reading hazard decimal.ts was hardened to eliminate at the other entry point.
findings.recommendation: Make the SQL validator assert canonical form, not numeric equivalence: add `and (v_resolution->'values'->'total'->>'value') ~ '^-?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?$'` (and the same for direct/indirect) before the ::numeric comparison, mirroring emission_data_direct_specific_numeric_ck, so the two definitions of 'canonical decimal' cannot drift. Independently, make toDecimal fail as a discriminated outcome rather than a throw at the engine boundary, so a malformed stored value surfaces as a named non-computable status instead of a 500.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: calculation_results is not append-only: ON DELETE CASCADE from shipment_lines lets a plain member destroy a line's entire calculation history
findings.boundary: Member -> the append-only audit record the P14.1 migration claims to have strengthened.
findings.precondition: A plain MEMBER of the owning org and a shipment in DRAFT or READY (shipment_lines_delete_parent_not_terminal excludes only LOCKED/VOID).
findings.affected_actor: Own tenant; the audit trail the regulator would rely on.
findings.exploit: A member calculates a line, dislikes the figure, and deletes the line. `calculation_results_line_id_fkey ... ON DELETE CASCADE` removes every calculation_results row for it. They then re-add the line with different inputs and recalculate. The superseded higher figure is gone from calculation_results entirely, not superseded.
findings.why_controls_fail: The P14.1 migration header states: 'Append-only is also strengthened while we are here. It was previously enforced only by the ABSENCE of UPDATE and DELETE policies, while authenticated still held table-level UPDATE and DELETE grants -- one future permissive policy away from being mutable. Those grants are revoked outright.' The revoke is real and I confirmed it — but a cascading FK delete is not a DELETE on calculation_results by the deleting role, so no grant or policy on that table is consulted. The domain type's own comment ('Never updated -- ... superseded results remain queryable for audit') is therefore not true.
findings.impact: The append-only guarantee that the calculation audit trail rests on is defeated by an ordinary product operation. Partial mitigation, which I verified: audit_events has no foreign key to shipment_lines (only org_id and actor_user_id, both ON DELETE RESTRICT), so the `calculation.computed` event and its embedded_emissions_tco2e payload survive the cascade. That makes this a loss of the primary record rather than a total erasure, which is why I am not rating it a blocker.
findings.recommendation: Change calculation_results_line_id_fkey from ON DELETE CASCADE to ON DELETE RESTRICT and make line removal a soft delete (or refuse to delete a line that has calculation results, the way declarations already refuse to file over drift). If hard deletion of a DRAFT line must stay, at minimum record a `calculation.discarded` audit event carrying the destroyed rows' ids and figures before the cascade fires.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: record_declaration_filed never checks that member shipments belong to the declaration's reporting period, and release_date can be moved without re-deriving reporting_period_*
findings.boundary: Member -> the reporting period a filed emissions total is attributed to.
findings.precondition: A plain MEMBER to move release_date; an ADMIN/OWNER click to file (the filing itself is admin-gated, but the admin has no way to see the mismatch).
findings.affected_actor: Own tenant and the regulator — emissions land in the wrong reporting period.
findings.exploit: Found while reproducing finding 1, and it is the same root cause: shipments carry declared facts that nothing pins. I filed an ANNUAL-2025 declaration whose sole member shipment is stamped ANNUAL-2026, and whose release_date (2025-01-15, set by the member) contradicts its own stored reporting_period_year (2026, derived at creation and never re-derived). record_declaration_filed accepted it and froze the total under the 2025 period.
findings.why_controls_fail: The reporting-period membership rule is presumably enforced when the declaration draft is assembled (compute-declaration-draft-facts / mark-declaration-ready), i.e. at the application layer. record_declaration_filed re-verifies almost everything else the application already checked — line completeness, determination currency, quantity currency, shipment lockability, actor membership, actor admin status — specifically because the P13/P14 rounds established that application-layer gates are not what a compliance record should rest on. Period membership was left out of that re-verification, and the same member who can move release_date can therefore move a shipment's emissions between periods without the filing gate noticing.
findings.impact: Emissions can be attributed to the wrong CBAM reporting period in a filed, immutable snapshot, with the shipment's own release_date and reporting_period_year mutually contradictory inside that snapshot. I am reporting this at MEDIUM and flagging it as adjacent to Area 3 (declarations) — it deserves that area's scrutiny too, since I only probed it incidentally.
findings.recommendation: Add the period comparison to record_declaration_filed's existing member-shipment check: refuse (a distinct result_status, e.g. SHIPMENT_PERIOD_MISMATCH) when any member shipment's reporting_period_kind/_year/_quarter differs from the declaration's. And pin shipments.release_date (see finding 1's recommendation) or re-derive reporting_period_* in a BEFORE UPDATE trigger whenever it changes, so the two can never disagree.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: 'tCO2/t' is deliberately accepted as if it were 'tCO2e/t', erasing the CO2 vs CO2e distinction for sectors whose CBAM scope includes N2O and PFCs
findings.boundary: Producer-supplied unit semantics -> the regulated figure. A CO2-only claim and a CO2-equivalent claim are materially different and are collapsed into one.
findings.precondition: A producer enters an emission_unit whose numerator is 'tCO2' rather than 'tCO2e' — a natural thing to type when the underlying measurement genuinely is CO2-only — for a good in a sector where CBAM counts more than CO2.
findings.affected_actor: The regulator and the filing. Direction is UNDER-report: a CO2-only intensity is filed as though it were the full CO2-equivalent.
findings.exploit: The numerator regex is `/^TCO2E?(?:\/|_PER_|$)/` (calculate-line-emissions.ts:179) — the `E?` makes the 'e' optional by design, and the comment above it states the intent: 'The NUMERATOR must be tonnes-of-CO2e ("TCO2E" or "TCO2")'. 'tCO2/t' is accepted and multiplied through unchanged. For fertilisers (N2O from nitric acid production) and aluminium (PFCs) the CO2-only figure is strictly lower than the CO2e figure, so the shortfall is silently filed. I can state the direction with confidence but not the magnitude: the ACTIVE dataset is entirely CO2e (all 12,540 rows TCO2E_PER_TONNE), so it offers no CO2-only counterpart to quantify against.
findings.evidence:
Real engine, 1000 t, direct 1.5 / indirect 0.5:
"tCO2/t (CO2 only) treated as CO2e" -> COMPUTED 2000   (identical to the tCO2e/t control)
Guard behaviour extracted from source:
"tCO2/t"   massBasisAccepted= true
"tCO2/MWh" mwhAccepted= true

The dataset offers no CO2-only values to compare against:
$ psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "select emission_unit, count(*) from default_emission_values group by 1;"
TCO2E_PER_TONNE|12540

Nothing constrains what a producer may type — the emission_data CHECK constraint list contains no emission_unit entry (full list quoted in the kilotonne finding above).
findings.why_controls_fail: The permissiveness is deliberate and traceable: the DEFAULT path's dataset CHECK allows 'TCO2_PER_MWH' (tCO2, not tCO2e — the source's own naming for electricity), and the shared guard was widened to accept both numerators so that one value would pass. But the guard is shared with the ACTUAL path, where the string is unvalidated free text carrying a real semantic claim rather than a fixed dataset enum. A concession made for one known, controlled value became a blanket acceptance on the uncontrolled side. No test distinguishes tCO2 from tCO2e on the ACTUAL path.
findings.impact: Understatement of embedded emissions for any ACTUAL line whose producer reported a genuinely CO2-only intensity in a sector where CBAM's scope includes other greenhouse gases — notably fertilisers (N2O) and aluminium (PFCs). The declarant has no way to see that a semantic distinction was dropped: the panel and the snapshot both echo the producer's string while the engine has already treated it as equivalent to CO2e. Magnitude is the size of the non-CO2 share, which I could not quantify from this dataset.
findings.recommendation: Fold this into the emission_data.emission_unit allow-list. If a CO2-only unit is to be accepted at all, it must be recorded as such on the snapshot and surfaced in the 'why this number' explanation, not silently equated with CO2e. The narrower immediate fix is to require the 'E' on the ACTUAL path while leaving the DEFAULT path's dataset enum untouched — the two paths do not need the same predicate, and sharing it is what caused this.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Default-value resolution ignores dataset effective dates and the shipment's release date, while good classification is effective-dated — the two halves of the same subsystem disagree about time
findings.boundary: Temporal boundary between a shipment's release date / reporting period and the regulatory dataset version that supplies its numbers.
findings.precondition: A second DEFAULT_EMISSION_VALUES dataset is activated (a new regulatory year, or a correction). Today exactly one is ACTIVE, so no wrong number is produced yet — this is a latent defect that arms on the next activation, which is a certainty rather than a hypothetical for an annual regime.
findings.affected_actor: The regulator and the filing: a shipment released in year N, determined or re-determined in year N+1, receives year N+1's default values.
findings.exploit:
1. findActiveDefaultEmissionCandidates (supabase-regulatory-repository.ts:242-266) selects on dataset_type and status='ACTIVE' only, with `.limit(2)` purely to detect duplicates. It takes no as-of date and never consults regulatory_datasets.effective_from / effective_to, even though both columns exist and are populated.
2. findCbamGoodsByCode, in the SAME adapter (:701-740), DOES take an asOfDate and applies it to cbam_goods.active_from/active_to — with an explicit doc comment on why ('never "today" -- a shipment entered now may declare a past release date').
3. So classification is period-correct and valuation is not. After a 2027 dataset activates, a 2026 shipment re-determined during an amendment (create-declaration-amendment.ts exists and is a supported flow) is classified against the 2026 good and valued against the 2027 dataset.
Already-frozen determinations are safe — the snapshot carries dataset_id and version, and the trigger short-circuits on unchanged determinations. The exposure is re-determination and late determination.
findings.evidence:
The dataset is effective-dated and the columns are populated:
$ psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "select id, dataset_type, version, status, effective_from, effective_to, source_file_name from regulatory_datasets;"
efcd5c92-e7d5-4eef-ba79-d0ea642f6abb|DEFAULT_EMISSION_VALUES|2026-definitive-corrected|ACTIVE|2026-01-01||cbam-default-values-2026-definitive-corrected.xlsx

The resolver query ignores them — the only predicates in the dataset selection are:
      .eq("dataset_type", DATASET_TYPE)   // 'DEFAULT_EMISSION_VALUES'
      .eq("status", "ACTIVE")
      .limit(2)
while the goods query in the same class applies:
      .or(`active_from.is.null,active_from.lte.${asOfDate}`)
      .or(`active_to.is.null,active_to.gte.${asOfDate}`)

Nothing enforces one ACTIVE dataset at the schema level either — the constraints are:
$ psql ... -tAc "select conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) from pg_constraint where conrelid='public.regulatory_datasets'::regclass;"
regulatory_datasets_status_check|CHECK ((status = ANY (ARRAY['DRAFT','ACTIVE','SUPERSEDED'])))
regulatory_datasets_source_type_version_uq|UNIQUE (source_id, dataset_type, version)
(no partial unique index on status='ACTIVE'). The adapter throws on >1, so it fails closed at runtime — but the invariant lives only in TypeScript.
findings.why_controls_fail: The subsystem clearly knows about effective dating — it built the columns, populated them, and applied the same discipline to goods with a comment explaining exactly why 'today' is the wrong date to use. The values path simply never adopted it. Because only one dataset has ever been ACTIVE, no test and no review round could have observed the divergence: every query returns the same answer regardless of date. The DB validator reinforces the single-ACTIVE assumption (it requires `rd.status = 'ACTIVE'` for the claimed dataset), so it will not catch a period-inappropriate-but-active dataset either.
findings.impact: On the day a second dataset is activated — an annual certainty — every re-determination or late determination of a prior-year shipment silently adopts the new year's default values while continuing to classify against the correct year's goods. Amendments to a prior period, which is exactly when this path is exercised, would file numbers from the wrong regulatory year with no indication of the substitution.
findings.recommendation: Give findActiveDefaultEmissionCandidates the same asOfDate parameter findCbamGoodsByCode already takes, and select the dataset whose effective_from/effective_to covers the shipment's release date rather than whichever is ACTIVE. Add the partial unique index on (dataset_type) WHERE status='ACTIVE' so the single-active invariant is enforced where it is relied upon. This does not need to block release if the next activation is gated on it — but it must be closed before a second dataset is ever activated, and that dependency should be recorded somewhere an operator will see it.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: A published default of 0.000 tCO2e/t (Hydrogen / Mali) files a zero CBAM liability, and nothing anywhere flags a zero regulatory default as worth a second look
findings.boundary: Ingested regulatory dataset -> the filed figure. Reported with the scope of my evidence stated plainly: I verified the parse, not the source.
findings.precondition: A shipment line declares CN 2804 10 00 with origin Mali and takes the DEFAULT path.
findings.affected_actor: The regulator, if the source value is wrong: a 100% under-report on that line.
findings.exploit:
The row resolves normally. isUsableTotalValue (resolve-default-value.ts:64-73) requires only status AVAILABLE and value non-null; 0.000 satisfies both. calculateFromDefaultDetermination multiplies quantity x 0.000 and returns COMPUTED with embedded_emissions_tco2e = 0. No blocker, no warning, no note in the 'why this number' panel. The figure is filable.
What makes it worth flagging rather than accepting: it is the ONLY zero in 12,540 rows, and every other country's hydrogen default is 10.820 or higher. A lone zero in an otherwise dense column is the classic signature of a source-side artefact.
findings.evidence:
$ psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "select count(*) filter (where total_value=0), count(*) filter (where total_value<0) from default_emission_values;"
1|0

$ psql ... -tAc "select g.trade_code, g.sector, c.name, d.direct_value, d.direct_raw_source_value, d.indirect_value, d.total_value, d.total_raw_source_value, d.source_sheet, d.source_row from default_emission_values d join cbam_goods g on g.id=d.good_id join countries c on c.id=d.country_id where d.total_value=0;"
28041000|HYDROGEN|Mali|0.000|0,000||0.000|0,000|Mali|43

Every other hydrogen default:
$ psql ... -tAc "select d.total_value, count(*) from default_emission_values d join cbam_goods g on g.id=d.good_id where g.sector='HYDROGEN' group by 1 order by 1 limit 8;"
0.000|1
10.820|79
13.450|2
14.030|10
17.740|1
25.940|1
26.640|2

Mali's other sectors are all normal, so this is not a whole-country parsing failure:
$ psql ... -tAc "select g.sector, count(*), count(*) filter (where d.total_value=0), min(d.total_value), max(d.total_value) from default_emission_values d join cbam_goods g on g.id=d.good_id join countries c on c.id=d.country_id where c.name='Mali' group by 1;"
CEMENT|8|0|0.900|0.980
FERTILISERS|29|0|0.320|2.790
HYDROGEN|1|1|0.000|0.000
findings.why_controls_fail: The pipeline behaved correctly and I want to be precise about that: direct_raw_source_value and total_raw_source_value both hold '0,000' (European decimal comma), and the same row's absent indirect is NULL/UNAVAILABLE — so an explicit published zero and a blank cell are being distinguished exactly as CLAUDE.md requires. The gap is not the parse, it is that no control treats a zero regulatory default as remarkable. There is no ingestion-time outlier check, no test asserting anything about the distribution of values, and nothing at determination or filing time that would make a reviewer look twice at a line whose CBAM figure is exactly zero.
