findings.impact: If the source cell is wrong, hydrogen imported from Mali carries a CBAM figure of exactly zero and a filed liability of nothing — a complete under-report on that line, presented by the product with the same confidence as any other resolved default. If the source cell is right, there is no harm today, but the absence of any outlier check means a future ingestion that produces a spurious zero would land the same way, unnoticed.
findings.recommendation: Verify this single row against the source workbook (checksum 900583811c7e1194799eb9bdbad2d6d7e1100f5a7d80a664c1584a8fce6f9f35) and the published regulation before release — it is one cell. If the source says 0,000, ship it and add a distribution assertion to the pipeline's verification step so a future zero is surfaced rather than absorbed. If the source does not, this is a corrupted regulatory fact in an ACTIVE dataset, which is a BLOCKER, and the correction is a new dataset version plus an activation migration — never an in-place edit.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Transitional-regime shipments can be created for pre-2026 release dates, but no cbam_goods row is active before 2026-01-01, so no line can ever be classified
findings.boundary: Advertised reporting-regime support vs. the effective dating of the loaded regulatory dataset.
findings.precondition: A user creates a shipment with any release date before 2026-01-01. createShipment accepts any calendar-valid ISO date — parseIsoDate checks shape and round-trip only, with no bounds (src/application/shipments/create-shipment.ts:80-93).
findings.affected_actor: The declarant: a whole reporting regime the product models is unusable, and the failure appears as a per-line 'unsupported code' rather than as 'this period is not supported'.
findings.exploit:
1. reportingPeriodForReleaseDate (src/domain/shared/reporting-period.ts:105-142) classifies any release date before 2026 as QUARTERLY transitional, and the shipments/declarations schemas both carry a QUARTERLY reporting_period_kind — the regime is modelled end to end.
2. findCbamGoodsByCode filters cbam_goods on active_from <= asOfDate, where asOfDate is the shipment's release_date.
3. Every cbam_goods row has active_from = 2026-01-01 and none is NULL.
4. Therefore every classification attempt on a pre-2026 shipment returns zero candidates, classifyGood returns UNSUPPORTED_CODE, and the line can never be determined or calculated. The shipment is a permanent dead end.
This fails closed, which is the right direction — but it fails at the wrong place, presenting a period-level limitation as a per-code error.
findings.evidence:
$ psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "select min(active_from), max(active_from), count(*) filter (where active_from is null) from cbam_goods;"
2026-01-01|2026-01-01|0

The schema models the transitional regime fully:
$ psql ... -tAc "select conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) from pg_constraint where conrelid='public.shipments'::regclass and contype='c';"
shipments_reporting_period_kind_check|CHECK ((reporting_period_kind = ANY (ARRAY['ANNUAL','QUARTERLY'])))
shipments_reporting_period_quarter_ck|CHECK ((((reporting_period_kind = 'ANNUAL') AND (reporting_period_quarter IS NULL)) OR ((reporting_period_kind = 'QUARTERLY') AND ((reporting_period_quarter >= 1) AND (reporting_period_quarter <= 4)))))
(declarations carries the identical pair.)

And createShipment applies no date bound — parseIsoDate's only rejections are malformed strings and calendar-impossible dates (src/domain/shared/reporting-period.ts:18-84).
findings.why_controls_fail: The two halves were built against different assumptions and nothing checks them against each other: the period model supports 2023-2025 quarterly reporting, the loaded dataset starts at 2026-01-01. No test creates a pre-2026 shipment and attempts classification, so the combination has never been exercised. The QUARTERLY branch of reportingPeriodForReleaseDate is live, tested in isolation, and unreachable in practice.
findings.impact: A user can build an entire transitional-period shipment that can never be completed, and the only feedback they get is a misleading per-line 'unsupported CN code' on codes that are in fact perfectly supported. No wrong number is filed — the failure is closed — but the product presents a supported-looking workflow that cannot terminate.
findings.recommendation: Decide which is true and make the code say it. If the definitive regime is the only supported one, bound release_date in createShipment with a named rejection reason and say so at the point of entry, rather than letting a user build a shipment that can never be completed. If transitional periods are intended to work, the dataset that supports them has to be loaded. Either way this should not ship as an unreachable branch that reports itself as a bad CN code.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The auth helper functions the entire RLS surface resolves through are checked for existence only: auth.uid() rewritten to a constant still reports POSTURE MATCHES
findings.boundary: Recovery verification boundary, over the function every one of the 55 public RLS policies depends on for its meaning.
findings.precondition: A restore into a target whose auth.uid()/auth.role()/auth.jwt() differ from the source's — a different GoTrue version, a hand-written shim (which is what the review sandbox itself uses), or a repaired auth schema.
findings.affected_actor: Every tenant. auth.uid() determines what app.user_org_ids() returns, which determines what every RLS policy admits. A wrong body silently redefines the entire tenancy boundary in either direction.
findings.exploit:
1. Restore leaves auth.uid() returning something other than the JWT sub — a constant, or NULL.
2. Run the acceptance test. POSTURE MATCHES.
3. Depending on the substituted body, either every tenant sees one fixed organisation's data, or every read silently returns empty and the system looks merely 'quiet'.
findings.evidence:
Isolated mutation on p14rev_a10_authfn (template clone of the fresh rebuild, one statement changed and nothing else):

psql -c "create or replace function auth.uid() returns uuid language sql stable as \$\$ select '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000'::uuid \$\$;"
  CREATE FUNCTION

node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs <sandbox> <p14rev_a10_authfn>
  ... all 14 comparison checks [MATCH], functions 84 rows both sides ...
  [OK] auth_schema_and_helpers_present
  ... all 9 self-checks [OK] ...
  RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES

file:line — the `functions` check at scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:152-167 hashes prosrc but filters `where n.nspname in ('public', 'app')` at :164, so the auth schema is out of scope. The self-check auth_schema_and_helpers_present at :254-274 asserts only that pg_proc rows named uid/role/jwt exist in the auth namespace; it never reads their bodies, arguments or return types.
findings.why_controls_fail: The check's own comment at :255 explains it was rewritten to assert positively rather than vacuously, and it does — but 'the function exists' is a strictly weaker claim than 'the function does what the policies assume'. The policy_definitions check faithfully compares 55 policy texts that all read `auth.uid()`, and then never compares what `auth.uid()` is.
findings.impact: The one function that gives every RLS policy its meaning can be replaced wholesale and the recovery acceptance test reports no difference. This also bears on this review's own foundations: the sandbox certified POSTURE MATCHES runs hand-written auth shims whose fidelity to the hosted auth.uid() this tool never checked, so 'the sandbox matches production' rests on an unverified assumption.
findings.recommendation: Extend the `functions` comparison check to include the auth namespace (or at minimum auth.uid/role/jwt), and add a behavioural self-check that sets request.jwt.claims to a known sub inside a transaction and asserts auth.uid() returns it — a five-line addition that turns an existence assertion into a correctness one.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: auth_user_foreign_keys_present passes with one of the ten foreign keys it names, so --check clears a restore that lost nine of them
findings.boundary: Recovery verification boundary, in the single-database mode the runbook prescribes 'against a restored target before a source is available to compare with'.
findings.precondition: A restore in which some but not all of the product foreign keys to auth.users fail to create — which is the documented behaviour of this project's own dump: BACKUP_RESTORE.md's 'Finding 3' records exactly 'Nine of the ten foreign keys still could not be created'.
findings.affected_actor: Data integrity across audit_events, calculation_results, declarations, emission_data, evidence_files, import_batches, memberships, organization_invitations and sharing_grants — every attribution of an action to a user.
findings.exploit:
1. Restore, losing nine of the ten FKs (the project's own measured outcome).
2. Run `compare-database-posture.mjs --check <dsn>` as BACKUP_RESTORE.md:633 instructs.
3. It reports POSTURE MATCHES, including [OK] on the very check whose message names ten.
findings.evidence:
On p14rev_a10_mut, after dropping nine of the ten:

psql -tAc "select 'remaining product FKs to auth.users: '||count(*)::text from pg_constraint con join pg_class c on c.oid=con.confrelid join pg_namespace cn on cn.oid=c.relnamespace join pg_class r on r.oid=con.conrelid join pg_namespace rn on rn.oid=r.relnamespace where con.contype='f' and cn.nspname='auth' and c.relname='users' and rn.nspname in ('public','app')"
  remaining product FKs to auth.users: 1

node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs --check "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14rev_a10_mut"
  [OK] auth_schema_and_helpers_present
  [OK] auth_user_foreign_keys_present
  [OK] policy_functions_resolve
  [OK] tables_without_rls
  [OK] rls_without_policies
  [OK] tables_without_insert_policy
  [OK] api_roles_hold_their_grants
  [OK] truncate_granted_to_api_roles
  [OK] security_definer_without_search_path
  RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES

The ten FKs, enumerated on the candidate schema: audit_events_actor_user_id_fkey, calculation_results_calculated_by_user_id_fkey, declarations_created_by_user_id_fkey, emission_data_verifier_user_id_fkey, evidence_files_uploaded_by_user_id_fkey, import_batches_created_by_fkey, memberships_user_id_fkey, organization_invitations_accepted_by_fkey, organization_invitations_invited_by_fkey, sharing_grants_created_by_user_id_fkey.

file:line — scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:277-298. The message string at :286 is 'NO product foreign key references auth.users -- expected 10', and the predicate at :297 is `) = 0`.
findings.why_controls_fail: The check was narrowed (comment at :280-285) to fix an earlier vacuous pass on a bare Supabase project, and that narrowing is correct — but the threshold stayed at zero while the message asserts ten. In comparison mode the `constraints` check does catch the drops, so this only bites in --check mode. That is precisely the mode the runbook prescribes for the moment when no source is available, i.e. the real recovery moment.
findings.impact: The check the runbook singles out as the one that 'fails loudly' on the condition that turned the 2026-08-29 drill into a silent loss passes on a database that has lost 90% of the integrity it is asserting. Every user attribution across nine tables can be dangling and the restore is signed off.
findings.recommendation: Change the predicate at :297 from `) = 0` to `) < 10`, or better, enumerate the ten expected (table, constraint) pairs as a VALUES list and report each missing one by name, matching the style of policy_functions_resolve at :301.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The eleven pending migrations are pushed non-atomically and include a pair where the second fixes a security hole in the first, with no automated all-or-nothing verification
findings.boundary: Deployment boundary: the state of the production database between the first and last migration of the pending set.
findings.precondition: `supabase db push` (DEPLOYMENT.md step 4) stops part-way — a network drop, a lock timeout, a statement error, or an operator interrupting the window.
findings.affected_actor: Every producer/operator organisation whose emission data is evidence-gated, if the push stops between 20260903140000 and 20260903150000.
findings.exploit:
1. Push stops after 20260903140000 applies and before 20260903150000 does.
2. 20260903140000 created app.enforce_emission_data_verification_gate() with a hole its own fix commit describes: it keyed the un-verify rule on new.status='ACTIVE' as well as old.status, so a single UPDATE moving both columns walked past it, and the two-statement ACTIVE -> DRAFT -> re-verify variant defeated every gate keyed on old.status='ACTIVE'.
3. Production is left running that version. Nothing in the procedure detects it automatically, because both migrations replace the same function and the difference is only visible in prosrc.
findings.evidence:
73 of the 74 migration files carry no explicit transaction wrapper (`for f in supabase/migrations/*.sql; do grep -qiE '^\s*begin\s*;' "$f" || echo $(basename $f); done` lists all but 20260827110000; `grep -lE '^\s*begin\s*;' supabase/migrations/*.sql | wc -l` -> 1).

Both migrations define the same function:
  supabase/migrations/20260903140000_p14_emission_data_verification_downgrade_gate.sql:50  create or replace function app.enforce_emission_data_verification_gate()
  supabase/migrations/20260903150000_p14_emission_data_evidence_integrity_v2.sql:83        create or replace function app.enforce_emission_data_verification_gate()

Commit e31d3cc, which added 20260903150000, states the defect in 20260903140000 verbatim: '20260903140000 keyed its un-verify rule on `new.status = ACTIVE` as well as `old.status`, so a single UPDATE that moved both columns walked straight past it ... and the VERIFIED -> strip evidence -> VERIFIED chain that migration's own header named was reproducible again.'

DEPLOYMENT.md:525-528 concedes the detection gap: 'For every function the migration touched, compare pg_proc.prosrc, prosecdef and proconfig against the repo file. A partial push is otherwise undetectable.'
findings.why_controls_fail: The only defence is DEPLOYMENT.md step 5, an unaided manual prosrc comparison performed by whoever is watching the window — the same class of human checklist that BACKUP_RESTORE.md:518 explicitly retired for restores ('The acceptance test is no longer a checklist a human reads'). compare-database-posture.mjs would catch it via the `functions` body_md5 check, but only in two-database comparison mode, and a production push has no second database to compare against. --check has no function-body check at all.
findings.impact: A push that stops between two adjacent migrations can leave production running a version of the evidence-integrity gate whose hole was documented and fixed the same day, and the release procedure would not notice unless one person correctly eyeballs 84 function bodies under time pressure.
findings.recommendation: Before pushing, record the expected md5 of every public/app function body from a locally rebuilt database, and after the push run a scripted comparison of pg_proc prosrc/prosecdef/proconfig hashes against that manifest — mechanising step 5 instead of asking an operator to eyeball 84 functions. Independently, verify the ledger count reached 74 before the window is declared closed.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: NEW: any MEMBER can write 39 catalogued audit_events types into their own org's append-only compliance log with arbitrary payloads, including `emission_data.verified` claiming third-party verification — while no trigger audits emission_data writes at all
findings.boundary: Audit-trail integrity within a tenant, and by extension the §21 evidence chain a regulator or dispute would rely on.
findings.precondition: Any MEMBER account, raw PostgREST.
findings.affected_actor: The organisation's own administrators, auditors, and any party relying on the audit log to reconstruct what happened.
findings.exploit: POST /rest/v1/audit_events with any of the 39 catalogued event_type values, actor_user_id = self (enforced), org_id = own org, and a completely free-form payload jsonb. The row is append-only: audit_events has SELECT and INSERT policies only, so it can never be retracted through the API.
findings.evidence:
Live on p14_review_sandbox, as role authenticated with the JWT of a user whose memberships row reads MEMBER, in a rolled-back transaction:
  insert into public.audit_events (org_id, actor_type, actor_user_id, event_type, aggregate_type, aggregate_id, payload)
  values ('22222222-...-0001','USER',auth.uid(),'emission_data.verified','EMISSION_DATA','deadbeef',
          '{"verified_by":"the CEO","verifier_body":"TUV Rheinland","note":"independently verified against site records"}');
  -> INSERT 0 1
  id | event_type | payload
  2b2379ac-... | emission_data.verified | {"note": "independently verified against site records", "verified_by": "the CEO", "verifier_body": "TUV Rheinland"}

The policy, from pg_policy: audit_events_insert_own_org_as_self constrains actor_type='USER', actor_user_id=auth.uid(), org membership, and event_type against a 39-value catalogue — and nothing else. Payload and aggregate_id are unconstrained.

A wall that DID hold: the same insert with event_type='declaration.filed' -> ERROR: new row violates row-level security policy for table "audit_events". RPC-only events are correctly excluded.

And the other half: `select count(*) from pg_trigger t join pg_class c on c.oid=t.tgrelid where c.relname='emission_data' and not t.tgisinternal and t.tgname ilike '%audit%'` -> 0. Nothing writes an audit row when emission_data is inserted or updated.
findings.why_controls_fail: The catalogue constraint (20260829430000) and the actor pin close impersonation and unknown event types, which is real progress — but the audit log's evidential value depends on its ENTRIES being produced by the operations they describe, and here they are produced by whoever wants to claim the operation happened. The design assumes the application layer is the only writer; the grant and policy make every member a writer.
findings.impact: Two directions, and the combination is what matters. Forward: a member can manufacture a plausible verification trail — including a named third-party verifier — to corroborate a forged emissions record. Backward: because no trigger audits emission_data, the forged INSERT in chains C1 and C2 leaves NO automatic trace, so the audit log cannot be used to detect it either. The log can neither confirm nor refute the forgery, which is the worst of both.
findings.recommendation: Route the audit writes that back a compliance claim through SECURITY DEFINER RPCs that also perform the operation, as record_declaration_filed and record_shared_data_consumption already do, and revoke direct INSERT on audit_events from authenticated. At minimum, add a DB-side trigger that audits every emission_data INSERT and status/verification transition, so the trail is produced by the operation rather than asserted alongside it.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: config.toml's configured seed path does not match supabase/seed.sql, so three documents' claim that the CLI applies the seed as the last step of `supabase db reset` is contradicted by the repository's own configuration — and this question sets the true severity of eight other findings (prior #4)
findings.boundary: Operational. What a rebuilt local, CI, or recovery-target database actually contains.
findings.precondition: Running the repository's own documented developer command.
findings.affected_actor: Every developer rebuilding locally, and any operator following DEPLOYMENT.md's 'Rebuilding on a fresh database' during an incident.
findings.exploit: Run `supabase db reset`. If the configured glob is authoritative, nothing is seeded: the base-table grants the file exists to restore are never applied — a state seed.sql:9-11 itself describes as failing every query — and the revoke re-assertions the P14.3 remediation depends on are never applied either.
findings.evidence:
supabase/config.toml:66-73:
  [db.seed]
  enabled = true
  # No seed data exists yet (supabase/seed/ is currently empty); this glob
  # matches the directory without requiring a specific file to exist.
  sql_paths = ["./seed/*.sql"]

And the directory does not exist. `ls -la supabase/`:
  .branches/  .gitignore  .temp/  config.toml  migrations/  seed.sql  snippets/
There is no `supabase/seed/`. The comment's own premise ('supabase/seed/ is currently empty') is false — it is absent.

The three contradicting assertions: supabase/seed.sql:2-4 ('the CLI runs this exclusively as the final step of `supabase db reset`/`start`'), docs/runbooks/DEPLOYMENT.md:561 ('`seed.sql` runs LAST'), and the P14 audit's equivalent claim.

The CI evidence does not distinguish the cases: .github/workflows/ci.yml:315 applies the file explicitly with `psql ... -f supabase/seed.sql`, which alone explains the observed CI behaviour.

UNRESOLVED — settling it requires `supabase db reset`, which this review is forbidden to run.
findings.why_controls_fail: Nothing in the repository tests which of the two is true. The claim is asserted in three documents and contradicted by one config key, and both the assertion and the contradiction are committed at the same SHA.
findings.impact: Whichever way it resolves, the release ships with the mechanism its headline security remediation depends on described in three places by a claim its own config contradicts. It also determines the severity of the eight-entry seed.sql cluster: if the glob is authoritative, that cluster describes CI's state only (CI applies the file by hand) and `supabase db reset` instead produces an unusable database.
findings.recommendation: Set `sql_paths = ["./seed.sql"]` (or delete the key to take the CLI default), then verify by running `supabase db reset` once and checking `select defaclacl from pg_default_acl` — if the postgres/public default ACL is absent afterwards, the seed did not run. Fix the stale comment either way.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: seed.sql's blanket grant re-opens narrow revokes, and the P14.3 remediation is a hand-maintained three-item list with no test behind it (prior #0, #2, #9, #14, #19, #34, #41, #47 — EIGHT entries for ONE defect)
findings.boundary: Dev/CI database posture. NOT production: seed.sql never runs against a hosted project.
findings.precondition: Any future migration adding a revoke-based control, plus nobody editing supabase/seed.sql.
findings.affected_actor: Developers and CI. CI is the gate meant to prove the forgery is unreachable, so a silently-widened CI database is a false green on the release's highest-value control.
findings.exploit: Add any revoke-based control (the established pattern: 20260903170000 and 20260903190000 are both this shape). Nothing edits seed.sql. `pnpm test`, CI and `compare-database-posture.mjs --check` all pass. The next rebuild applies seed.sql's `grant all on all tables|functions in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role` last, and the control is gone.
findings.evidence:
The present-day symptom, measured on the sandbox: seven SECURITY DEFINER RPCs hold EXECUTE for anon that no migration ever granted — accept_organization_invitation, accept_sharing_grant_invitation, create_organization_with_owner, list_org_members, record_declaration_filed, record_shared_data_consumption, sharing_counterparty_org_names — while record_calculation_result, the one the seed re-revokes by name, is correctly `{postgres=X/postgres,service_role=X/postgres}`.

The persisted default ACL means the widening is automatic for future objects, not a one-off.

I DOWNGRADE this cluster from the prior HIGH/MEDIUM for reasons I tested rather than assumed. As role anon on the sandbox: 0 rows from calculation_results, 0 from latest_calculation_results; anon and authenticated are NOLOGIN roles reachable only via PostgREST's SET ROLE; and each of the seven RPCs defends itself internally (four raise on `auth.uid() is null`, list_org_members raises 'Not a member of this organization.' via app.user_org_ids(), sharing_counterparty_org_names returns 0 rows). I also confirmed the protected regulatory tables hold under RLS despite anon/authenticated holding INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE grants on all six — every write verb I tried returned 0 rows affected.

EIGHT of the 50 prior entries (#0, #2, #9, #14, #19, #34, #41, #47) are this single defect, restated across five review dimensions with overlapping evidence.
findings.why_controls_fail: seed.sql:68-76 asserts the coupling is safe because it 'is covered by tests that already caught it once' — true of one of the three controls it names and of none of the future ones. The function branch of its compensating block is keyed on `to_regprocedure('public.record_calculation_result(<11-arg signature>)')`, so renaming or adding a parameter (which PostgREST's named-argument dispatch makes an ordinary change) makes it a no-op with no error. And there is no privilege assertion anywhere in the suite to notice: `grep -rn "has_table_privilege|information_schema|role_table_grants|has_function_privilege" --include=*.test.ts` returns zero across all test files.
findings.impact: Defence in depth on the tenancy-root RPCs is one guard deep instead of two in every freshly built environment, and the dev/CI attack surface is wider than production's — so CI cannot catch a regression in those seven ACLs. The forward-looking risk is the real one: the next revoke-based control, and the next SECURITY DEFINER RPC that correctly relies on its migration's grant list instead of an internal auth.uid() check.
findings.recommendation: Stop coupling. Either narrow the blanket grant to the tables and functions that actually need it, or replace the hand-maintained list with a generated one — re-run the migrations' own revoke statements after the grants, extracted mechanically rather than transcribed. Then add the privilege-assertion test the suite entirely lacks, so any drift fails cheaply.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Neither the filing gate nor the completeness check considers engine_version, so a result produced by a superseded engine is accepted as current and frozen into an immutable declaration (prior #7)
findings.boundary: Platform -> regulator. The reproducibility contract.
findings.precondition: None. No attacker. Any line calculated before an engine bump whose determination and quantity have not changed since.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant and the regulator.
findings.exploit: None required. Mark the declaration READY and file: the superseded figure is summed verbatim into filed_snapshot, and running the on-demand reproduction check on it returns ENGINE_VERSION_CHANGED rather than flagging any disagreement.
findings.evidence:
I read record_declaration_filed's full prosrc. engine_version appears in the body only inside the snapshot-building step — `'engine_versions', (select coalesce(jsonb_agg(distinct c.engine_version), '[]') from current_result c)` — i.e. it is RECORDED and never GATED. member_line_counts compares determination, quantity and quantity_unit only.

On the sandbox: `select engine_version, count(*) from calculation_results group by 1` shows multiple versions present in real data.

src/application/calculations/reproduce-calculation-result.ts short-circuits to ENGINE_VERSION_CHANGED before any comparison, so the reproduction proof is SILENT, not failing, for exactly the rows where it matters.
findings.why_controls_fail: The gate was built to detect a stale DETERMINATION and a mismatched QUANTITY, both of which it now does well. Staleness with respect to the ENGINE is a third axis nobody added, and the one control that could notice is deliberately blinded for those rows. src/domain/calculations/types.ts states in the codebase's own words that pre-1.2.0 rows can carry numbers the current engine would not produce and that 1.2.0 -> 1.3.0 is 'a genuine behavioural change'.
findings.impact: The system's central promise — 'same inputs + engine_version => byte-identical output, re-provable on demand' — is enforced nowhere at the moment it matters. The gap is structural; whether a filed declaration currently disagrees with the shipped engine depends on the data, and I did not attempt to recompute the sandbox's rows.
findings.recommendation: Fold `c.engine_version is distinct from <the current ENGINE_VERSION>` into the same uncalculated_count/INCOMPLETE path the determination and quantity mismatches already use — 'calculated by a superseded engine' should be treated exactly like 'not calculated', which is the pattern 20260903110000 established. And make reproduceCalculationResult report ENGINE_VERSION_CHANGED as a finding rather than a short-circuit.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Append-only on calculation_results is defeated by ON DELETE CASCADE from shipment_lines: a member with no DELETE grant erases calculation history (prior #8)
findings.boundary: Role boundary within a tenant; evidential integrity of a not-yet-filed figure.
findings.precondition: An ordinary member deleting a shipment line on a DRAFT or READY shipment — a permitted product operation.
findings.affected_actor: The organisation's own audit trail.
findings.exploit: DELETE a shipment line (permitted by shipment_lines_delete_parent_not_terminal). Every calculation_results row for that line is removed by the cascade, which executes on the referencing table's behalf and is subject to neither the deleting role's grants nor RLS. Deleting the shipment, or the organisation, cascades the same way.
findings.evidence:
Structurally confirmed on the sandbox. calculation_results.line_id references shipment_lines(id) ON DELETE CASCADE (declared in 20260829180000_p6_calculation_results_schema.sql:38-40, org_id and shipment_id likewise). The 20260903190000 revoke that the header claims 'strengthens' append-only is a table-level grant revoke, which a cascade does not consult — I verified the direct paths are genuinely closed: as authenticated, calculation_results holds only REFERENCES, SELECT, TRIGGER, and `truncate public.calculation_results` and a direct DELETE both fail on permission.

I did not re-run the prior pass's live cascade reproduction; the FK action is unambiguous in the committed migration and I confirmed the grant state it interacts with.
findings.why_controls_fail: 20260903190000 reasoned about DIRECT writes and closed them completely. A cascade is not a write by the deleting role; it is a referential action the engine performs, and no grant or policy stands in its way. src/domain/calculations/types.ts:108-113 states 'An append-only record of one calculation run ... superseded results remain queryable for audit', which is not true.
findings.impact: Bounded and own-tenant: it cannot touch a LOCKED or VOID shipment, so figures already frozen into a filed declaration are unaffected and filed_snapshot is immutable. The loss is the evidential trail behind a not-yet-filed number — and the honesty of the append-only claim, which other parts of the system rely on rhetorically.
findings.recommendation: Change the FK to ON DELETE RESTRICT and require calculations to be superseded rather than orphaned, or soft-delete the line. If cascade must stay, amend the claim in types.ts and in 20260903190000's header so the guarantee is stated accurately.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The determination validator accepts determinations the protected resolver can never produce — but on THIS dataset the numeric harm is zero, which the prior HIGH did not quantify (prior #24, HIGH -> MEDIUM)
findings.boundary: Application validator <-> protected resolver semantics. Own-tenant, raw-API only.
findings.precondition: An authenticated member hand-writing a determination over PostgREST.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant's own record; latent regulator exposure on a future dataset version.
findings.exploit: CLASS A — claim a coarser prefix record for a CN8 line: the validator admits any source_trade_code that merely prefix-covers the line's code, while the uniqueness rule is evaluated for the COARSER code rather than the line's. CLASS B — claim the Other-Countries fallback on a route the origin country lacks: the R7 clause-2 precondition filters own-country records by the line's declared route, so a country whose only usable record sits at a different route becomes invisible and the fallback passes, where the resolver would take EXPLICIT_ROUTE_NO_MATCH and persist nothing.
findings.evidence:
CLASS A, live on the sandbox as role authenticated, in a rolled-back transaction, calling the installed validator directly with two otherwise identical determinations for line cn_code '76109010', origin CN, route null:
   legit_cn8_record | forged_hs6_record_claimed_as_cn8_match
   t                | t
(The forged one names source_trade_code '7610 90', source_row 56 — an HS6 record — while carrying reason 'EXACT_CN8_MATCH'. That single probe confirms prior #27 as well: the reason is never cross-checked against the record's code level.)

WHY I DOWNGRADE — I measured the numeric consequence and it is nil on this dataset:
  divergent prefix pairs (same country, coarser code prefix-covering a finer one, DIFFERENT total_value, both AVAILABLE): 0
  (country, code) pairs with more than one usable AVAILABLE candidate — the AMBIGUOUS case the uniqueness rule exists to catch: 0
  Class B triples available (country's own usable records all at other routes): 1734, of which the Other-Countries value is LOWER than the country's own in 0; the minimum delta across all 1734 is +0.8%.
So today Class A yields the identical number and Class B can only over-report. The prior report said as much in its own text ('today's safety is a coincidence of this dataset's numbers') but assigned HIGH; the measured coincidence is what sets the severity.
findings.why_controls_fail: The validator reimplements the resolver's rules in SQL rather than deriving them from it, and the two have drifted on specificity: resolve-default-value.ts matches trade codes by exact normalized equality and can never return an HS6 record for an 8-digit line, while the validator's prefix admission plus coarse-code uniqueness admits exactly that. Class B's route filter asks a subtly different question from the resolver's own EXPLICIT_ROUTE_NO_MATCH branch.
findings.impact: A persisted determination the protected resolver would never have produced, carrying a number the regulatory data does not support at that specificity. No numeric divergence on the ACTIVE dataset — but the safety is a property of the DATA, not of the check, so any new dataset version can turn this into an understatement route with no code change and no test failure.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate the uniqueness rule at the LINE's code level, not the claimed record's, and require the claimed source_trade_code to normalize-equal the line's cn_code the way the resolver does. Bind resolution_reason to the record's code level. And add a dataset-level regression assertion (divergent prefix pairs == 0, multi-candidate pairs == 0) so the coincidence this validator currently relies on cannot silently stop being true.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: record_shared_data_consumption lets a grantee write unverifiable claims into the grantor's append-only audit log, and the release certification never carried the known gap forward (prior #13)
findings.boundary: Cross-tenant write: grantee org -> grantor org's audit stream.
findings.precondition: Membership of an org holding one ACTIVE, unexpired sharing grant.
findings.affected_actor: The grantor producer organisation, whose audit log is the record they would rely on in a dispute about who consumed their emissions data.
findings.exploit: Call POST /rest/v1/rpc/record_shared_data_consumption repeatedly with any shipment_line_id belonging to your own org — including lines with no emission_determination at all — and any valid (emission_data_id, version) under the granted installation. Each call returns OK and appends a sharing_grant.data_consumed row to the GRANTOR's log, unbounded and unretractable.
findings.evidence:
The function's own body documents the gap: 'KNOWN GAP, WORTH-TRACKING, NOT FIXED HERE (mandatory review, 2026-08-29, live-reproduced): this check does not read sl.emission_determination at all, so it never confirms the line was actually determined from p_emission_data_id/p_emission_data_version via p_sharing_grant_id ... There is also no uniqueness constraint, CAS, or rate limit on this RPC.'

It is SECURITY DEFINER and its INSERT targets v_grant.grantor_org_id — a different tenant's stream. From pg_policy, audit_events carries SELECT and INSERT policies only (no UPDATE, no DELETE), and audit_events_select_own_org is `org_id IN (select app.user_org_ids())` — so the grantor cannot read the grantee's side to disprove the claim and cannot remove the rows.

The honesty half: the P14 audit's 'High-risk accepted items' section lists nine items and this is not among them, though it is a live-reproduced gap flagged in a migration as needing owner attention.

I did not re-run the triple-call reproduction; I verified the function's SECURITY DEFINER status, its target org, and the audit_events policy set that makes the write unretractable.
findings.why_controls_fail: The RPC validates the GRANT (active, unexpired, correct grantee) and the caller's membership, and then trusts the caller's assertion about which line consumed which record — the one fact it exists to record. There is no idempotency key, no rate limit, and no cross-check against the line's own determination.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant append-only pollution of another organisation's compliance audit trail, with no removal mechanism. Bounded: only a genuine grantee can do it, and the events are additive noise rather than data disclosure. Part of the severity here is that a reproduced, documented gap did not appear in the document certifying the release.
findings.recommendation: Read sl.emission_determination in the RPC and refuse when it does not name the claimed (emission_data_id, version, sharing_grant_id). Add a uniqueness constraint on (line_id, emission_data_id, version) or a rate limit. And carry the gap into the release's accepted-risk register rather than leaving it only in the migration body.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: A plain MEMBER can move a READY shipment into a different reporting period, silently changing what an ADMIN's already-frozen declaration will file (prior #22)
findings.boundary: Role boundary within a tenant. Standalone MEDIUM; it is the no-admin ignition for chain C3, which I rate HIGH.
findings.precondition: A plain MEMBER with raw PostgREST access. There is no updateShipment service under src/application/shipments/, so the UI does not expose this — the RLS policy does.
findings.affected_actor: The organisation's own declaration and period report.
findings.exploit: PATCH /rest/v1/shipments?id=eq.<ready shipment> with {"reporting_period_year": <other year>} using the anon key and a plain MEMBER's session.
findings.evidence:
The policy role-gates only the LOCKED transition. From pg_policy:
  shipments_update_own_org_not_terminal | w
  USING:      ((org_id IN (SELECT app.user_org_ids())) AND (status <> ALL (ARRAY['LOCKED','VOID'])))
  WITH CHECK: ((org_id IN (SELECT app.user_org_ids())) AND ((status <> 'LOCKED') OR app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of(org_id)))
The only trigger on shipments is shipments_prevent_org_id_change_trg — no column pin on the period columns or release_date.

Live, rolled back:
  select role as acting_membership_role from memberships where user_id=auth.uid(); -> MEMBER
  update public.shipments set reporting_period_kind='QUARTERLY', reporting_period_year=2033, reporting_period_quarter=2 where id='c2000000-...-0001'; -> UPDATE 1
  ADV-D-2035 | QUARTERLY | 2033 | 2 | READY
findings.why_controls_fail: The policy encodes 'only an admin may lock' and nothing about which columns are still mutable once a declaration has frozen its member set. declarations carries prevent_declaration_fact_change for exactly this class of problem on its own side; shipments has no equivalent.
findings.impact: The lowest-privileged role can change the content of a declaration an ADMIN has already marked READY, and can move a shipment out of the period report (which filters on the shipment's CURRENT period columns) while it stays inside the filed declaration — so the report and the filed artifact silently disagree about the same period.
findings.recommendation: Pin reporting_period_kind/_year/_quarter and release_date against UPDATE once the shipment is READY, via a BEFORE UPDATE trigger mirroring prevent_declaration_fact_change; or require ADMIN/OWNER for those columns. Fixing this alone does not close chain C3 — the filing gate must still check the period.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: HYDROGEN is asserted not-Annex-II by a set literal, with no source read, in the over-reporting direction (prior #25)
findings.boundary: Platform -> regulator, via an unsourced regulatory classification hardcoded in domain code.
findings.precondition: A producer records verified emission_data for a hydrogen installation with a non-zero indirect_specific; an importer determines a 2804 10 00 line ACTUAL.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant, who over-surrenders certificates.
findings.exploit: None — the ordinary workflow. good_sector resolves to HYDROGEN, ANNEX_II_SECTORS does not contain it, and the engine sums direct + indirect.
findings.evidence:
src/domain/calculations/calculate-line-emissions.ts:46-52 — ANNEX_II_SECTORS = new Set(['IRON_STEEL','ALUMINIUM']). Hydrogen therefore takes the summation branch.

The ACTIVE dataset's own signature points the other way — from my sector census:
  HYDROGEN  | UNAVAILABLE | 96   | 0
  ALUMINIUM | UNAVAILABLE | 1632 | 0   <- identical signature, and the platform DOES classify aluminium as Annex II
  CEMENT    | AVAILABLE   | 337  | 326 <- the sectors where indirect IS counted
  FERTILISERS| AVAILABLE  | 2416 | 2416

docs/regulatory/CALCULATION_RULE_REGISTER.md RULE-EE-004 states the Annex II list was 'confirmed to begin with Iron and steel CN codes; the full Annex II code list was not transcribed in this pass' — so 'hydrogen is not in Annex II' is an assumption encoded as a set-membership test.

PARTIALLY EVIDENCED: I cannot read EUR-Lex from this session and therefore cannot prove hydrogen's Annex II status either way.
findings.why_controls_fail: CLAUDE.md forbids hardcoding a regulatory fact and requires ambiguity to surface rather than be silently resolved. ANNEX_II_SECTORS is exactly a hardcoded regulatory classification, and its complement (everything not in the set is not Annex II) is a second, unstated assertion carrying the same weight. The set is a proxy for a CN-code-level list that was never transcribed.
findings.impact: If hydrogen is in Annex II, the declarant surrenders certificates for emissions the regulation excludes. Bounded to ACTUAL-method hydrogen lines; the DEFAULT path is unaffected because the dataset publishes no indirect value for hydrogen at all. The asymmetry with the 2601 12 00 finding is instructive: the same unsourced proxy errs one way for one good and the other way for another.
findings.recommendation: Same as for the 2601 12 00 finding — the versioned Annex II membership dataset. Until then, surface the classification as an explicit, visible assumption on any hydrogen ACTUAL line rather than applying it silently, and record it in the release's accepted-risk register in both directions.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: /reset-password changes the account password for ANY live session with no re-authentication and no current password, then signs the victim's other sessions out (prior #30)
findings.boundary: Session possession -> permanent credential control.
findings.precondition: The attacker has a live session (borrowed or unlocked browser, shared machine, exfiltrated cookie).
findings.affected_actor: One account, which may be an org OWNER.
findings.exploit: Navigate to /reset-password on the real origin, type a new password twice, submit. updatePasswordAction sees a non-null getUser() and changes the password, then calls signOut({scope:'others'}), terminating the genuine owner's sessions. The owner's old password no longer works.
findings.evidence:
app/(auth)/reset-password/actions.ts: :157 `await supabase.auth.getUser()`, :168 `await supabase.auth.updateUser(...)` with the new password, :213 `await supabase.auth.signOut(...)`. There is no old-password field, no AAL/AMR check, no recovery-session check and no reauthentication nonce anywhere in the file. app/(auth)/layout.tsx carries no session or recovery-scope guard.

supabase/config.toml:321 `secure_password_change = false`.

NOT EXERCISED — no Auth service is bound to this sandbox; source and config only. The hosted project's own secure_password_change setting is unknown to me and I deliberately did not probe it.
findings.why_controls_fail: The route was designed for the post-recovery-link flow, where possession of the link IS the proof, and nothing distinguishes that flow from an ordinary authenticated session arriving at the same URL. The GoTrue-side control that would compensate (secure_password_change) is off in the shipped config — and turning it on would break the invite->set-password flow, since the app never sends a reauthentication nonce.
findings.impact: Elevates transient session possession into permanent account takeover plus immediate lockout of the legitimate owner, with the product's own signOut({scope:'others'}) doing the locking-out.
findings.recommendation: Distinguish the two entry paths: require a recovery-scoped session (or the AAL/AMR the recovery link produces) for the no-old-password flow, and require the current password for an ordinary authenticated password change. Then enable secure_password_change and implement the reauthentication nonce.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: BACKUP_RESTORE.md's fidelity table is wrong about the storage schema: the `evidence` bucket and the three storage.objects RLS policies are this application's own access control, in neither the dump nor any check (prior #49, LOW -> MEDIUM)
findings.boundary: Operational/recovery, and the evidence chain.
findings.precondition: A restore into a fresh Supabase project, following the runbook.
findings.affected_actor: The recovering organisation; every evidence upload and download afterwards.
findings.exploit: None. After a restore the `evidence` bucket row does not exist and storage.objects carries RLS with none of this application's policies, so every evidence upload and every signed-URL read fails until an operator notices and re-runs 20260829240000's Part 5 by hand.
findings.evidence:
BACKUP_RESTORE.md:622 lists '`auth`, `storage`, `extensions`, `vault`, `realtime` schemas | NO | the target project provides them.' A fresh project provides storage.buckets and storage.objects as TABLES, but not:
  20260829240000_p7c_evidence_files_schema.sql:264 insert into storage.buckets (id,name,public) values ('evidence','evidence',false)
  :268 create policy evidence_storage_select_own_org on storage.objects ... to authenticated
  :277 create policy evidence_storage_insert_own_org ...
  :286 create policy evidence_storage_delete_own_org ...

The dump is `--schema=public --schema=app` (BACKUP_RESTORE.md:145-146), so none of these are in it. The comparator cannot see them either: it scopes pg_policies to schemaname in ('public','app') at :118 and its three RLS self-checks all filter `n.nspname = 'public'` (:320, :334, :351).

Confirmed on this machine: the sandbox's storage schema carries the tables but ZERO policies.
findings.why_controls_fail: The fidelity table classifies by SCHEMA, and the storage schema is genuinely provider-supplied — but this application created objects INSIDE it, so the schema-level classification is true of the container and false of the contents. The comparator inherits the same schema-scoped assumption. D.3's 'required post-restore steps' name auth.users, the revokes and the ledger, but not this.
findings.impact: A recovery that completes with POSTURE MATCHES and a superficially working application has evidence upload and download entirely broken, with no gate that says so — in a product whose regulatory value depends on retrievable evidence documents. I upgrade from the prior LOW because the failure is total for that feature and no check anywhere can see it.
findings.recommendation: Add storage to the comparator's scope (the bucket row, the three policies, the bucket's size/MIME limits from 20260829510000), add it to D.3's required post-restore steps, and correct the fidelity table to distinguish provider-supplied schemas from application-created objects within them.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The audit's measured default-ACL claim is wrong: `anon` holds INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on every future public table, not read-only (prior #3)
findings.boundary: Release-certification honesty, plus a structural exposure in dev/CI environments.
findings.precondition: A reviewer reading the audit; or a future migration creating a table in public and forgetting to enable RLS.
findings.affected_actor: Anyone relying on the P14 audit as the release's evidence of the grant model.
findings.exploit: A future migration creates a table in public and omits `alter table ... enable row level security`. Every holder of the public anon key gets full SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on it with no policy in the way.
findings.evidence:
The audit document states `| postgres default ACL, schema public | anon=rxtm, authenticated=arwdxtm - no D |`. The measured value is `anon=arwdxtm/postgres` — a=INSERT, w=UPDATE, d=DELETE. The 'no D' half (TRUNCATE, reached by the seed's revoke tail) is correct; the anon half is not.

I confirmed the state the claim describes: every table in public carries `anon=...` with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE among its grants (see the full role_table_grants census in my seed.sql finding), and every table in public currently has relrowsecurity = true, so no such table exists today.

The one automated guard against the shape — `tables_without_rls` in compare-database-posture.mjs — is in the script that nothing runs (see chain C5).
findings.why_controls_fail: The default ACL is written by seed.sql's `alter default privileges in schema public grant all on tables to anon, authenticated, service_role`, minus TRUNCATE. The audit line is what a reviewer would read to conclude anon is read-only by default and that the omission is bounded; it was transcribed rather than measured.
findings.impact: A release-certification document misstates a measured privilege fact in the permissive direction, on the release whose headline defect was a privilege regression. The structural exposure is real but latent and dev/CI-scoped.
findings.recommendation: Correct the line. Narrow the default privileges to what is actually needed. And wire tables_without_rls into CI so the latent exposure has an active guard rather than a documented one.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The comparator is the sole programmatic acceptance test for recovery and is itself covered by nothing (prior #46)
findings.boundary: Operational/recovery. Meta-control.
findings.precondition: None.
findings.affected_actor: Whoever depends on the tool during a recovery, when nobody has time to audit it.
findings.exploit: None — structural. There is no fixture database, no expected-output snapshot, and no negative test that deliberately breaks a posture and asserts the tool notices. Each of its 24 queries is validated only by having been run once by hand against one database.
findings.evidence:
`grep -rn "compare-database-posture" --include=*.yml --include=*.yaml --include=*.json --include=*.ts --include=*.mjs` returns exactly one file: the script itself. It appears in prose in BACKUP_RESTORE.md:520-530 and DEPLOYMENT.md:574 and nowhere in .github/workflows/ci.yml or package.json's scripts.

Its self-checks have now been wrong repeatedly: the auth.users FK check that counted Supabase's internal FKs (fixed in aa394ba), the earlier version that passed on an empty project, and the four independent holes established in this pass — the missing 20260903190000 coverage (proven live), the two exact-zero thresholds, and the name-only `sequences` comparison. BACKUP_RESTORE.md:642 nevertheless states 'the acceptance test is now programmatic and demonstrably catches the exact failure the old one missed.'
findings.why_controls_fail: Nothing stops the next edit from re-introducing an exact-zero threshold or a `relkind='r'` filter, and nothing would notice. Each check encodes a lesson from a real incident and has no regression net.
findings.impact: The one tool whose entire job is to be right during a recovery has its correctness asserted in a runbook rather than tested.
findings.recommendation: Run `--check` in CI against the freshly built database on every run, and add negative fixtures: a database with the P14.1 revoke reverted, one missing an auth.users FK, one with most grants stripped — each of which the tool must reject. That is a small amount of work and it converts the runbook's claim into a fact.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: No test in the repository asserts a database privilege, and the one test titled as if it does asserts something else (prior #39, LOW -> MEDIUM)
findings.boundary: Test integrity. This is the reason the posture findings have nothing standing behind them.
findings.precondition: None.
findings.affected_actor: Every reviewer who reads the suite as evidence that the grant model is enforced.
findings.exploit: None — structural.
findings.evidence:
`grep -rn "has_table_privilege|information_schema|role_table_grants|has_function_privilege" --include="*.test.ts" --include="*.spec.ts"` across the repository returns ZERO matches.

tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts case (4) is titled '(4) grants no INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on calculation_results to anon or authenticated at all', and its comment claims 'The property behind tests 1-3, asserted directly rather than inferred from three refusals: no privilege, so no policy can accidentally re-open the surface later.' Its body calls record_calculation_result as serviceClient (expects OK) and as ownerClient (expects a permission-denied error). That is a behavioural refusal, not a privilege assertion, and no anon client is constructed anywhere in the file.

This matters because supabase/seed.sql's own header cites that case as the test covering the seed/migration coupling.
findings.why_controls_fail: Every proof of the P14.1 write boundary in the suite is behavioural, requiring a live PostgREST, a live Postgres, a seeded regulatory dataset and a signed-in member — preconditions that hold only in the build-and-test CI job and on a fully provisioned developer host. There is no cheap, environment-independent assertion of grant posture that a restore drill, a staging check or the fast-gates job could run.
findings.impact: The suite cannot distinguish 'the privilege is revoked' from 'some other wall happened to refuse this particular request', and says nothing at all about anon. I upgrade from the prior LOW because this is the structural reason the seed.sql cluster and chain C5 have no automated backstop — it is not a documentation defect, it is a missing control.
findings.recommendation: Add a small privilege-assertion test file that queries information_schema.role_table_grants and pg_proc.proacl for the objects the migrations deliberately narrowed, and run it in fast-gates against any reachable database. Correct case (4)'s title to describe what it measures.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Every audit-write failure is discarded at all 35 call sites, and one is reachable by ordinary data volume: declaration.marked_ready is silently dropped at 208+ member shipments
findings.boundary: Application -> audit trail completeness
findings.precondition: For the silent-drop case: an importer marking ready a declaration with 208 or more member shipments. For the general case: any audit write that fails for any reason, on any of the 35 call sites.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant org and any later auditor of its trail — the record is incomplete and nothing anywhere says so.
findings.exploit: 1. Assemble a declaration with 208+ member shipments and call markDeclarationReady. 2. The declarations UPDATE commits; the org's most compliance-significant state change has occurred. 3. recordAuditEvent serializes the payload — reporting_period, the full member_shipment_ids array, line_count — measures 8203+ bytes against MAX_AUDIT_PAYLOAD_BYTES, and returns {ok:false, reason:"payload exceeds the audit payload size bound"}. 4. mark-declaration-ready.ts:202 discards the return value. Nothing is logged, nothing is surfaced, no audit row exists. The declaration is READY with no record of being marked so.
findings.evidence:
Wall 1 threshold, computed with the exact payload shape from mark-declaration-ready.ts:210-214 and an ANNUAL ReportingPeriod:
  204|8047 ok   205|8086 ok   206|8125 ok   207|8164 ok   208|8203 DROPPED   (bound 8192)

Wall 2 refuses it too, so the event can never be recorded by any route — live in p14_review_sandbox:
  insert into audit_events (...) select null,'SYSTEM',null,'declaration.marked_ready','DECLARATION','x', jsonb_build_object('reporting_period', jsonb_build_object('kind','ANNUAL','year',2026), 'member_shipment_ids', (select jsonb_agg(gen_random_uuid()) from generate_series(1,208)), 'line_count', 208);
  ->  ERROR:  new row for relation "audit_events" violates check constraint "audit_events_payload_size_ck"

The discard, at the call site: src/application/declarations/mark-declaration-ready.ts:202 — `await recordAuditEvent(supabase, {...});` with no assignment.

And at every other call site. Enumerated mechanically across src/application/ (excluding tests and the helper itself): all 35 are a bare `await recordAuditEvent(` with the {ok, reason} result unassigned — calculate-line.ts:328, create-declaration-amendment.ts:194, generate-or-refresh-declaration-draft.ts:219 and :272, mark-declaration-ready.ts:202, determine-from-actual-data.ts:684, manage-emission-data.ts:341/:551/:864/:896, resolve-line-emissions.ts:327, upload-evidence.ts:403/:648, manage-installations.ts:276/:400, manage-operators.ts:170/:273, invitations.ts:143/:307, manage-membership.ts:163/:255/:376/:503, manage-sharing-grants.ts:320/:507/:629/:736, create-shipment.ts:138, manage-lines.ts:391/:587/:699, transition-shipment.ts:219, manage-suppliers.ts:166/:265.
findings.why_controls_fail: The P14 change that added `reason` to the return value is documented at record-audit-event.ts:90-113 and is honest about the remaining gap: it deliberately does not log from the application layer (correct, on layering grounds), and records threading a request id through the call sites as a post-release item because "a warning on three of a dozen paths would be worse than none." The consequence is that the reason is returned to callers who all drop it, so the diagnostic improvement changed nothing observable. The size bound itself is well-reasoned — audit_events is append-only and therefore unremovable, so bounding it is right — but the bound was chosen without anyone checking which payloads scale with tenant data. member_shipment_ids does; the sibling draft events correctly record member_shipment_count instead (generate-or-refresh-declaration-draft.ts:229, :282), which shows the smaller shape was already known and simply not used here. In practice this drop is masked today because filing fails first at 197 (BLOCKER above), but fixing filing without fixing this leaves the silent drop as the surviving defect.
findings.impact: The largest declarations — the ones with the most regulatory exposure — reach READY with no audit record of it, and the system cannot tell anyone. More broadly, no audit-write failure anywhere in the product is observable by anyone: not the user, not the operator, not a later auditor.
findings.recommendation: Replace member_shipment_ids with member_shipment_count (plus a digest if the id set must be attestable) in the declaration.marked_ready payload, matching what the draft events already do. Then make the discarded result meaningful: have the Server Actions that call these services check {ok, reason} and log a structured warning with the request id — which is exactly the post-release item record-audit-event.ts names, and which should land before release rather than after, since without it the reason field it added has no reader.
findings.reviewer_note: Reproduced directly by the reviewing session with its own psql/CLI probes, not taken from an agent report.

findings.title: All four emission_data integrity triggers are BEFORE UPDATE only, so the verification provenance an importer freezes into a determination has no INSERT-side enforcement
findings.boundary: Producer org -> importer org: the claim that a shared emissions figure was verified, and by whom
findings.precondition: The already-known INSERT-path blocker (a plain MEMBER can insert an ACTIVE + VERIFIED emission_data row). This finding is what that blocker costs in my area, not an independent way in.
findings.affected_actor: The importer who freezes the snapshot, and the regulator who receives the resulting declaration.
findings.exploit: app.enforce_emission_data_verification_gate() contains a carefully built defence for verifier attribution: on the VERIFY transition it discards the caller's claimed verifier_user_id and overwrites it with auth.uid(), and it forbids verifier_user_id changing in any other statement. Its own comment marks this as the fix for "Finding 2 + Finding 3 (verifier_user_id)". Every branch of it is written against `old.` -- it is a BEFORE UPDATE trigger, and there is no INSERT trigger on the table at all. So on the INSERT path the caller's verifier_user_id is accepted verbatim: an inserted ACTIVE + VERIFIED row can name any user as verifier, including an ADMIN or OWNER who never saw the record. An importer then determines a line from that row, and determine-from-actual-data.ts freezes `verification: {status: "VERIFIED", verifier_user_id: <whatever was inserted>}` into shipment_lines.emission_determination. From that point the value is immutable and travels into calculations, declaration snapshots and exports as verified provenance.
findings.evidence:
$ psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "select tgname||' :: '||pg_get_triggerdef(oid) from pg_trigger where tgrelid='public.emission_data'::regclass and not tgisinternal;"
emission_data_activation_gate_trg :: CREATE TRIGGER emission_data_activation_gate_trg BEFORE UPDATE ON public.emission_data FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.enforce_emission_data_activation_gate()
emission_data_prevent_fact_change_trg :: CREATE TRIGGER emission_data_prevent_fact_change_trg BEFORE UPDATE ON public.emission_data FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.prevent_emission_data_fact_change()
emission_data_touch_updated_at_trg :: CREATE TRIGGER emission_data_touch_updated_at_trg BEFORE UPDATE ON public.emission_data FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.touch_updated_at()
emission_data_verification_gate_trg :: CREATE TRIGGER emission_data_verification_gate_trg BEFORE UPDATE ON public.emission_data FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION app.enforce_emission_data_verification_gate()

All four are BEFORE UPDATE. There is no BEFORE INSERT trigger on emission_data.

The defence that consequently never runs on INSERT, from pg_get_functiondef(app.enforce_emission_data_verification_gate()):
    if new.verifier_user_id is distinct from old.verifier_user_id then
        if new.verification_status is distinct from old.verification_status
            and new.verification_status = 'VERIFIED'
        then
            new.verifier_user_id := auth.uid();

The frozen shape an importer ends up carrying, from shipment_lines.emission_determination->'snapshot' for line 27023f49:
    "verification": {"status": "VERIFIED", "verifier_user_id": "7329fb81-8a00-4db0-818a-183957fd728c"}

emission_data_insert_own_org policy CHECK, from pg_policies -- it constrains only entered_by_org_id and installation ownership, saying nothing about status, verification_status or verifier_user_id:
    ((entered_by_org_id IN (SELECT app.user_org_ids())) AND (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM installations i WHERE i.id = emission_data.installation_id AND i.org_id = emission_data.entered_by_org_id)))
findings.why_controls_fail: The UPDATE path is defended thoroughly and, as far as I could push it, correctly -- the gate blocks un-verifying an ACTIVE+VERIFIED row, blocks ACTIVE -> DRAFT, blocks evidence shrinking, requires ADMIN or OWNER to verify, and overwrites the claimed verifier with auth.uid(). Every one of those protections is expressed as a comparison against `old`, which is a coherent way to write a lifecycle gate but silently assumes rows can only arrive at ACTIVE + VERIFIED by transitioning there. The INSERT policy does not enforce that assumption -- it never mentions status or verification_status -- so the assumption is false, and the entire gate is bypassed by starting at the destination instead of walking to it. This is the same structural mistake the gate's own comment describes fixing for the two-statement ACTIVE -> DRAFT bypass ("park the record at DRAFT, and every gate keyed on old.status = 'ACTIVE' stops applying to it"): the lesson was applied within the UPDATE path but not to the absence of an INSERT path.
findings.impact: An importer's frozen determination can carry a verifier attribution that no verification ever produced, and once frozen it is immutable and flows into the filed declaration. Under CBAM the identity of the verifier is part of what makes an actual-data figure usable rather than a default, so this is provenance the data does not support, asserted to a counterparty and ultimately to a regulator. I am reporting this as MEDIUM rather than higher only because the way in is the already-known INSERT blocker; if that blocker is fixed by constraining the INSERT policy alone, this specific consequence closes with it -- but if it is fixed only for status, verifier_user_id remains forgeable.
findings.recommendation: Add a BEFORE INSERT trigger (or extend the four existing ones to BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE with null-safe handling of `old`) so the INSERT path is subject to the same rules: a row may not be inserted at status='ACTIVE', verification_status must start at UNVERIFIED, and verifier_user_id must be NULL on insert. Whichever remedy is chosen for the known INSERT blocker, verify explicitly that it also pins verifier_user_id -- fixing status alone leaves the attribution forgeable. Because this touches emission_data lifecycle behaviour, follow the project's TDD rule: a failing test that inserts ACTIVE+VERIFIED with a foreign verifier_user_id first.
findings.reviewer_note: Reproduced directly by the reviewing session with its own psql/CLI probes, not taken from an agent report.

findings.title: The build artifact on disk contains the production service-role key, database password and Resend API key at .next/standalone/.env, and the artifact gate does not look for them
findings.boundary: Build output / artifact handling -> production credentials. A directory that is treated as a distributable deploy artifact contains full-privilege, RLS-bypassing production secrets.
findings.precondition: Running `pnpm build` on any machine whose .env holds real credentials. That is the machine state the README prescribes. No attacker action is needed to create the exposure; exposure is realised by any handling of the artifact that is not the Railway/Docker path — copying .next/standalone, archiving it, uploading it as a CI artifact, or simply running `pnpm start`.
findings.affected_actor: Every tenant. SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY bypasses RLS entirely, so it reads and writes every organization's shipments, emission data, declarations and sharing grants. SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD is direct Postgres access to the same. The Resend key permits sending mail as the platform.
findings.exploit:
1. `next build` with output:"standalone" copies the project's .env files into the standalone tree. Verified: .next/standalone/.env is byte-identical to ./.env (cmp -s -> IDENTICAL_TO_REPO_DOTENV) and carries the source file's mtime (Aug 31 08:00), so it is Next copying it, not any script in this repo — scripts/build/copy-standalone-assets.mjs copies only <distDir>/static and public/.
2. .next/standalone is exactly the directory the Dockerfile treats as the deployable unit and the directory `pnpm start` executes.
3. Because Next's standalone server loads env files from its own directory, running the artifact anywhere points it at PRODUCTION with the service-role key — including `pnpm start` on a developer laptop, which reads as a harmless local smoke test.
4. scripts/build/assert-clean-production-artifact.mjs walks this exact tree file by file (`walk(STANDALONE_DIR)`, reading every file as utf8) and passes it, because it only tests for the two bypass tokens.
findings.evidence:
```
ls -la .next/standalone/.env .env
-rw-r--r-- 1 rahil.naik 1049089 1588 Aug 31 08:00 .env
-rw-r--r-- 1 rahil.naik 1049089 1588 Aug 31 08:00 .next/standalone/.env
cmp -s .next/standalone/.env .env  ->  IDENTICAL_TO_REPO_DOTENV
```
Contents characterised without printing values:
```
.next/standalone/.env
  SUPABASE_URL -> URL host=tjwzlbujbsnoacbhzmax.supabase.co
  SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY -> <redacted len=219 prefix=eyJ...>
  SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD -> <redacted len=13 prefix=sno...>
  NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL -> URL host=tjwzlbujbsnoacbhzmax.supabase.co
  NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY -> <redacted len=46 prefix=sb_...>
  RESEND_API_KEY -> <redacted len=36 prefix=re_...>
```
`find .next/standalone -maxdepth 1 -name ".env*"` -> .next/standalone/.env
package.json:"start": "node .next/standalone/server.js"
scripts/build/assert-clean-production-artifact.mjs — const RUNTIME_KEY / SOURCE_KEY are the only strings check #3 searches for.
README:147-148 documents `docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env snowkap-cbam:local`, i.e. deliberately pointing a locally-built container at production with the service-role key.
findings.why_controls_fail: The mitigation exists but is incidental and single-layered: .dockerignore lists `.env` and `.env.*`, so the Docker build context has no .env and the image's standalone tree gets none. I verified that. But that is a property of one deploy path, which is exactly the reasoning dist-dir.mjs itself rejects for the bypass — 'nothing shipped is a property of the current deploy path, not an invariant'. The same standard was not applied here. The purpose-built artifact gate walks this tree and is silent, because it was scoped to one class of contaminant. CI's secret scan is `git grep`-based (ci.yml:109-118) and .env is gitignored, so it cannot see a build output either. Nothing anywhere asserts that the deployable directory is free of credentials.
findings.impact: A full-privilege, RLS-bypassing production credential sitting in a build output that is designed to be copied and run. The immediate realistic harm is not a remote attacker but the operator: `pnpm start` after any build silently runs against production. Any future change to how the artifact is produced or moved — a CI artifact upload, a non-Docker deploy, a support bundle, an image built with a looser .dockerignore — turns this into distribution of the service-role key.
findings.recommendation: Extend scripts/build/assert-clean-production-artifact.mjs to fail on any .env* file inside the standalone tree, and on credential-shaped values (eyJ*, sb_secret_*, re_*) in any shipped file — it already walks every file, so this is a few lines in the existing check #3, and it makes the property an invariant rather than a consequence of .dockerignore. Delete .next/standalone/.env in postbuild as well, so the gate is a backstop rather than the only control. Treat the credentials in the current .env as exposed and rotate the service-role key, DB password and Resend key. Change README:148's documented local Docker run so it does not point a local container at the production project.
findings.reviewer_note: Reviewer re-checked directly: .dockerignore excludes .env and .env.*, .env is untracked, and the Dockerfile runs pnpm build inside the image, so the PRODUCTION image does not contain it. True only for a local developer .next directory. Severity reduced accordingly.

findings.title: The 12540-row gate asserts a SUM across every ACTIVE dataset and never checks dataset identity
findings.boundary: Regulatory-data precondition for the calculation and resolution suites
findings.precondition: More than one ACTIVE regulatory_datasets row, or a single ACTIVE dataset of the wrong version that happens to carry 12,540 rows.
findings.affected_actor: Anyone relying on the CI claim that the suites ran against the 2026-definitive-corrected dataset specifically.
findings.exploit: The query at ci.yml:325 is `select count(*) from public.default_emission_values dev join public.regulatory_datasets rd on rd.id=dev.dataset_id where rd.status='ACTIVE'` — an unqualified aggregate over all ACTIVE datasets. Two ACTIVE datasets of 6,270 rows each sum to 12,540 and pass. So does one ACTIVE dataset of a different version with 12,540 rows. Nothing in the schema prevents two ACTIVE rows.
findings.evidence:
Against the sandbox (read-only):
  $ psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "select count(*) from public.default_emission_values dev join public.regulatory_datasets rd on rd.id=dev.dataset_id where rd.status='ACTIVE'"
  12540
  $ ... -tAc "select tgname, pg_get_triggerdef(oid) from pg_trigger where tgrelid='public.regulatory_datasets'::regclass and not tgisinternal"
  (no rows)
  $ ... -tAc "select indexdef from pg_indexes where tablename='regulatory_datasets'"
  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX regulatory_datasets_pkey ON public.regulatory_datasets USING btree (id)
  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX regulatory_datasets_source_type_version_uq ON public.regulatory_datasets USING btree (source_id, dataset_type, version)
  CREATE INDEX regulatory_datasets_source_id_idx ...
  CREATE INDEX regulatory_datasets_type_status_idx ...
  $ ... -tAc "select conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) from pg_constraint where conrelid='public.regulatory_datasets'::regclass"
  (status CHECK, effective-range CHECK, pkey, source/type/version UNIQUE, source FK — nothing partial on status='ACTIVE')
No partial unique index and no trigger enforces at-most-one ACTIVE dataset.
findings.why_controls_fail: The gate's error message ('the regulatory suites would run against wrong data') claims to verify dataset correctness, but the query verifies only a total row count. It never references dataset_type='DEFAULT_EMISSION_VALUES' nor version='2026-definitive-corrected', the identity the suites' own assertions actually name. The gate itself fails closed on a psql error (verified: `set -e` aborts on a failing assignment, `V=$(false | tr -d 'x')` -> exit 1), so the mechanism is sound; the assertion is just weaker than advertised.
findings.impact: Low in practice — the workflow loads exactly one dataset and the sandbox shows a single ACTIVE row. The risk is that this gate is quoted as evidence of dataset identity when it establishes only a cardinality.
findings.recommendation: Qualify the query by dataset_type and version, and additionally assert `select count(*) from regulatory_datasets where status='ACTIVE' and dataset_type='DEFAULT_EMISSION_VALUES'` equals 1. Separately, the missing single-ACTIVE database invariant is worth a partial unique index in its own right.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: evidence_files.uploaded_by_user_id is not pinned to auth.uid(), so evidence chain-of-custody attribution is forgeable
findings.boundary: Audit attribution within an organisation.
findings.precondition: Any MEMBER of the organisation owning the emission_data record.
findings.affected_actor: The organisation's own members, who can be recorded as having uploaded evidence they never touched; and any auditor reading the evidence trail.
findings.exploit: H7, as producer MEMBER 1111...0001: `insert into evidence_files (id, org_id, emission_data_id, storage_path, original_filename, mime_type, size_bytes, sha256, uploaded_by_user_id) values ('aaaa...000f','2222...0001','5555...b1', ..., '1111...0005');` — attributing the upload to a user in a completely different organisation, on an ACTIVE + VERIFIED record.
findings.evidence: `INSERT 0 1`, then `H7 | aaaa0000-0000-0000-0000-00000000000f | 1111...0005`. The policy, from pg_policy: `evidence_files_insert_own_org | a | with check ((org_id IN (SELECT app.user_org_ids())) AND (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emission_data ed WHERE ed.id = evidence_files.emission_data_id AND ed.entered_by_org_id = evidence_files.org_id)))` — no clause on uploaded_by_user_id, no FK-implied constraint to the acting user, and no condition on the parent record's verification_status.
findings.why_controls_fail: The policy constrains scope (which org, which parent record) but not attribution.
