The comparable control elsewhere in this schema does exactly the right thing and shows the intended pattern: the audit_events INSERT policy pins `actor_user_id = auth.uid()`, and its migration header (20260828150000, lines 49-56) explains precisely why — a bare insert policy 'would let a caller forge an arbitrary actor_user_id'. That reasoning was applied to audit_events and not to evidence_files. The application path (`uploadEvidenceFile`) sets the field from the session, so nothing on the honest path is affected.
findings.impact: Low on its own: intra-organisation, and it does not change any emissions figure. It matters as part of the evidence story — the chain of custody on a compliance artefact is attributable to whoever the writer says, which weakens the record an auditor would rely on when reconstructing who attached what. Worth noting alongside finding 1, where the evidence array is fabricated outright: taken together, essentially nothing about the evidence trail is currently authenticated.
findings.recommendation: Add `AND uploaded_by_user_id = auth.uid()` to `evidence_files_insert_own_org`'s WITH CHECK, matching the audit_events policy pattern the project already established. One line, no application change (the honest path already sets the session user). While there, consider whether `evidence_files_insert_own_org` should also refuse a parent record that is ACTIVE + VERIFIED — the ability to add evidence after verification is a deliberate requirement per the v2 migration, but it is currently unrestricted by role, and it is the mechanism that supplies the substitute file in finding 2's U-H variant.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: maxKeys is presented as a hard memory ceiling but is per-limiter; with 45 limiters the aggregate ceiling is ~0.5 GB
findings.boundary: Process memory of the production container — the same boundary the P11 finding #3/N1 fix claimed to close.
findings.precondition: Enough distinct rate-limit keys to fill multiple limiters. After the get-client-ip fix the key is the address the trusted proxy appended, so this requires that many genuinely distinct source addresses (an IPv6 /64 or a botnet). I could not demonstrate reachability and am not claiming it is currently exploitable.
findings.affected_actor: All tenants, via container OOM and restart.
findings.exploit:
1. rate-limiter.ts:91 sets DEFAULT_MAX_KEYS = 50_000, applied per limiter instance (the Map and the cap are both created inside createInMemoryRateLimiter).
2. The application constructs 45 limiters.
3. Aggregate retained entries at the cap: 45 x 50,000 = 2,250,000. At the ~250 bytes/key the file's own header cites as live-measured, that is ~560 MB, before the per-key number[] timestamp arrays (up to `limit` entries each, 60 for the largest configs).
4. On a typical 512 MB / 1 GB container that is at or over the ceiling — i.e. the documented 'hard memory ceiling' is a hard PER-LIMITER ceiling, and the aggregate was not computed.
findings.evidence:
src/infrastructure/rate-limit/rate-limiter.ts:91  `const DEFAULT_MAX_KEYS = 50_000;`
rate-limiter.ts:176-180 — both the Map and maxKeys are per-instance:
```
const hitsByKey = new Map<string, number[]>();
const maxKeys = config.maxKeys ?? DEFAULT_MAX_KEYS;
```
`grep -rn "createInMemoryRateLimiter(" app --include=*.ts | grep -v test | wc -l` -> 45
No call site passes maxKeys — all 45 take the default. Confirmed in the shipped bundle: `let t=new Map,r=e.maxKeys??5e4`.
The 250-bytes figure is the file's own, rate-limiter.ts:58-76: 'live-reproduced at ~250 bytes retained per distinct spoofed key'.
The claim under test, rate-limiter.ts:68-73: '`maxKeys` (default DEFAULT_MAX_KEYS below) bounds it with simple LRU eviction... This trades a small correctness cost... for a hard memory ceiling'.
findings.why_controls_fail: The LRU eviction itself is correct — I read the compiled version and the insertion-order/delete-then-set logic is right. The gap is arithmetic: the fix was reasoned about as one limiter ('five module-scope singleton limiters' per the header comment, written when there were five) and the count has since grown to 45 without the ceiling being recomputed or the default revisited. What actually closed the unauthenticated OOM path was the get-client-ip.ts fix landing alongside it, which removed the attacker's ability to mint unlimited distinct keys; maxKeys is doing less work than the comment claims.
findings.impact: The stated invariant ('a hard memory ceiling') does not hold at the level it is stated. Practical impact today is limited because key minting is no longer attacker-controlled, but the number is wrong by 45x and the comment is what a future reader will rely on — including anyone acting on finding #5's recommendation, which would raise the distinct-key count per limiter substantially.
findings.recommendation: Recompute the ceiling against the real limiter count and set maxKeys explicitly per limiter rather than taking a 50,000 default 45 times, sizing each to the traffic that limiter actually sees. Update the header comment to state the aggregate, not the per-instance, bound. If the shared-store decision in master plan §41 is taken, this disappears with it.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Nothing constrains replica count or survives restart, so every configured limit is silently multiplied or reset by ordinary platform behaviour
findings.boundary: Deploy configuration -> the enforced value of every rate limit in the product.
findings.precondition: For the multiplication: any horizontal scaling of the Railway service, which is a dashboard action requiring no code change and no review. For the reset: any deploy, crash or platform restart — i.e. routine operation.
findings.affected_actor: All tenants, silently. Nobody is notified that the enforced ceiling has changed.
findings.exploit:
1. railway.json declares no replica or scaling key, so nothing in the repository pins the service to one instance. `grep -nE "replica|numReplicas|scal" railway.json` -> no matches.
2. Scaling to N instances gives an attacker spread across them N times the configured limit on every limiter — sign-in becomes 10N per 5 minutes, sign-up 5N per 10 minutes. The application emits no warning and no startup assertion; there is no way to observe from inside that the effective limit is no longer the configured one.
3. Independently, railway.json sets restartPolicyType ON_FAILURE with maxRetries 3, and every limiter's state is process-local. Each restart or deploy resets all 45 counters to zero, granting a fresh full budget on every limiter at once.
findings.evidence:
railway.json — full deploy block is `{"startCommand":"node server.js","healthcheckPath":"/api/health","healthcheckTimeout":30,"restartPolicyType":"ON_FAILURE","restartPolicyMaxRetries":3}`. No replica or scaling key.
src/infrastructure/rate-limit/rate-limiter.ts:8-14 states the property exactly: 'it does NOT survive a process restart (every counter resets to zero on deploy/crash/scale event), and it does NOT coordinate across multiple server instances... N instances behind a load balancer means the effective ceiling for an attacker spread across them is N times the configured limit.'
No startup assertion, log line, or health-check field anywhere reports instance count or warns that limits are per-process — /api/health returns status, git_sha, four check fields, dataset_version and active_row_count, none of which touch this.
findings.why_controls_fail: This is documented rather than uncontrolled, and the documentation is unusually honest — I am not reporting it as a hidden flaw. The gap is that honesty in a source comment is not a control: nothing prevents the scale-out, nothing detects it, and the credential-stuffing bound the sign-in limiter exists to provide ('worst case ~1 guess per 30s, sustained', app/(auth)/actions.ts:94-96) is stated as if it were a property of the system when it is a property of a single process. Master plan §41 lists a shared store as an open owner decision, so the risk is accepted — but acceptance was recorded against a comment, not against a configuration that enforces the assumption.
findings.impact: The stated security property of every limiter in the product is contingent on an unenforced, unmonitored deployment assumption that a single dashboard click invalidates. The concrete case that matters is sign-in: the anti-credential-stuffing bound is the justification for the 10/5min value, and it silently becomes 10N/5min.
findings.recommendation: Pin the replica count where it is reviewable — declare it in railway.json rather than leaving it to the dashboard. Surface the assumption at runtime: log a warning at startup that limits are per-process, and add an instance identifier to /api/health so multiple replicas are observable from outside. Neither is a fix; both convert an invisible change into a visible one until the §41 shared-store decision is made.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: /api/health is unauthenticated, unrate-limited, and runs four service-role database queries per request while also being the platform healthcheck target
findings.boundary: Unauthenticated internet -> the production database via the service-role client, bypassing RLS and every rate limiter; and -> Railway's traffic-gating decision for the instance.
findings.precondition: None. The route is public by design (Railway's healthcheck must reach it unauthenticated).
findings.affected_actor: All tenants, via database load and via healthcheck-driven traffic gating.
findings.exploit:
1. app/api/health/route.ts sets `dynamic = "force-dynamic"` and has no auth check and no limiter — it is one of only two route handlers with `checks=0` (the other is /api/live, which touches nothing).
2. Each request constructs the service-role client (getSupabaseClient, the protected regulatory adapter's client) and runs checkActiveDefaultEmissionValuesDataset (one query) plus checkProductSchema (three `select id ... limit 1`, one per probe table: organizations, shipments, emission_data). Four queries per request, RLS-bypassing.
3. An anonymous caller drives that at whatever rate they choose. Because railway.json sets healthcheckPath /api/health with healthcheckTimeout 30, degrading the route's own latency is also degrading the signal Railway uses to decide whether the instance receives traffic.
4. The response additionally discloses git_sha, dataset_version, active_row_count and (when degraded) missing_tables to anonymous callers.
findings.evidence:
app/api/health/route.ts — `export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";`, `export async function GET(): Promise<NextResponse<HealthCheckResult>>` calling `getSupabaseClient()`, `checkActiveDefaultEmissionValuesDataset(supabase)`, `checkProductSchema(supabase)`. `grep -c '\.check('` on the file -> 0.
Per-file sweep: `app/api/health/route.ts  actions=1  checks=0`, against `app/api/reports/export/route.ts 1/1`, `app/api/evidence/upload/route.ts 1/1`, `app/api/evidence/[id]/download/route.ts 1/1`.
src/application/health/check-product-schema.ts:28-33 `PRODUCT_SCHEMA_PROBE_TABLES = ["organizations","shipments","emission_data"]` and :79-91 one `.select("id").limit(1)` per table inside the loop. Its own comment at :67-68: 'Cost: one bounded, index-free select id ... limit 1 per probe table (three total).'
railway.json: `"healthcheckPath": "/api/health", "healthcheckTimeout": 30`.
findings.why_controls_fail: The route was hardened for the right failure (P13 §16.11/§32: a deploy reporting 'ok' against a database with zero product tables) and the per-probe cost was explicitly considered and kept bounded — that reasoning is sound and I am not disputing it. What was not considered is the request rate, because the assumed caller is Railway's prober. The three sibling API routes all carry a getClientIp()-keyed limiter, so the pattern exists and this route is the exception. The service-role client also means the queries answer to no RLS policy and no per-tenant budget.
findings.impact: A modest unauthenticated database-load amplifier (4 queries per HTTP request) that also degrades the signal the platform uses for traffic gating and restarts, plus minor deployment-provenance disclosure. Low because the queries are genuinely cheap and bounded and Supabase will shed load before the database does — but it is the one security-sensitive route in the app with no limiter, on the path an attacker finds first.
findings.recommendation: Add a getClientIp()-keyed limiter with a budget generous enough for the platform prober (which hits one path from one address) and small enough to bound anonymous abuse, returning 200 with the last cached result rather than 503 when throttled, so rate-limiting the route never itself trips Railway's healthcheck. Consider gating dataset_version/active_row_count/missing_tables behind an authenticated caller, leaving the anonymous response to status and the four check fields.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: An invitation stored with a non-lowercase email is acceptable under RLS but invisible on the invitee's own screen
findings.boundary: Consistency between the RLS/RPC authorization predicate (case-insensitive) and the application's read filter (case-sensitive).
findings.precondition: An organization_invitations row whose email column is not already lowercase. inviteMember normalizes, so this arises from a raw Data-API insert by an admin, or from any future code path that skips normalization.
findings.affected_actor: The invitee, who is told there is nothing pending while a valid invitation to them exists.
findings.exploit: Insert an invitation with email='A7-MixedCase@Victim.TEST'. The invitee signs in as a7-mixedcase@victim.test: RLS shows them the row (the policy compares lower(email)), and accept_organization_invitation accepts it (it compares lower() too) — but /accept-invitation renders nothing, because listMyPendingInvitations and countMyPendingInvitations both use `.eq("email", normalizedEmail)`, an exact match.
findings.evidence:
Sandbox, scratchpad/a7_p4.sql P10, signed in as a7-mixedcase@victim.test:
  mixedcase-visible-under-rls   | a7222222-...-00000000000d | A7-MixedCase@Victim.TEST
  mixedcase-app-filter-eq-lower | 0        (the exact-equality filter the application uses)
  mixedcase-accept              | OK | a7111111-...-000000000001
Code: src/application/organizations/invitations.ts:527-533 and :576-582 both `.eq("email", normalizedEmail)`.
findings.why_controls_fail: The comment at src/application/organizations/invitations.ts:528-530 justifies the exact filter with "invitations are stored already-normalized by inviteMember, so an equality filter here matches it exactly" — true of that one writer, and nothing enforces it. There is no lowercase CHECK constraint and no normalizing trigger on the column; the unique index is on lower(email) while the stored value is free-form.
findings.impact: An invitee is shown "No pending invitations" plus three wrong explanations, for an invitation that is live and acceptable. Cosmetic in the worst case, a support cycle in practice — the same class of dead end the P14 work on this screen set out to remove.
findings.recommendation: Normalize at the boundary that cannot be bypassed: add `check (email = lower(email))` to organization_invitations (or a BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE trigger that lowercases), and change the two reads to `.ilike("email", normalizedEmail)` so the application predicate matches the RLS predicate either way.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: /auth/confirm signs a signed-out visitor into an attacker-chosen account behind one Continue press, with no identity shown
findings.boundary: The authentication boundary, in the login-CSRF direction.
findings.precondition: Any Snowkap account, from which the attacker requests a magic link or recovery mail for themselves and extracts the token_hash. Plus one click from the victim on a link that looks exactly like a genuine Snowkap invitation email.
findings.affected_actor: The victim, and the organization whose data they subsequently enter into the attacker's tenant.
findings.exploit: Send `https://<app>/auth/confirm?token_hash=<the attacker's own token>&type=magiclink&next=/accept-invitation` — byte-identical in shape to supabase/templates/magic_link.html's real link. The page renders "You have a pending invitation ... Select Continue to sign in", the victim presses Continue, confirmEmailLinkAction calls verifyOtp with the attacker's token, and the victim's browser holds the attacker's session.
findings.evidence: Code only. app/auth/confirm/page.tsx builds the form from unauthenticated query parameters (parseConfirmLink(params)) and renders the identity warning only inside `{user ? ... : null}` — a signed-out visitor sees no identity information at all. app/auth/confirm/actions.ts re-validates shape (token_hash present, type in CONFIRMABLE_TYPES) and rate-limits by IP, then calls verifyOtp on whatever token was supplied. Not live-reproduced (no GoTrue reachable under the sandbox rule).
findings.why_controls_fail: The one control that addresses this — "You are currently signed in as X. Continuing will sign you out ..." — is conditioned on there already being a session, which is precisely the case where the victim would have noticed anyway. For a signed-out victim, nothing on the page names the account the token belongs to, and the rate limiter bounds volume, not intent. Inertness on GET protects the token from scanners; it does not establish whose token it is.
findings.impact: Bounded by requiring a click and by the victim eventually seeing an unfamiliar email in the shell — but in the window before that, work done in the attacker's tenant is work handed to the attacker. Inherent to any token-in-URL landing page, which is why it is LOW rather than higher; the fix is cheap.
findings.recommendation: Show the identity the token resolves to before the press, or after verification show an unmissable "You are now signed in as <email> — not you? Sign out" interstitial rather than redirecting straight to `next`. GoTrue will not disclose the address for an unverified token_hash, so the post-verification interstitial is the practical form.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Three load-bearing comments describe an architecture the candidate no longer has
findings.boundary: None directly — but each comment is the stated rationale a reviewer would use to accept a residual risk, and each is now false.
findings.precondition: None. Reading the code.
findings.affected_actor: The next reviewer, and the operator who acts on the health check.
findings.exploit: Not an exploit. (a) src/infrastructure/supabase/browser-client.ts:59 says app/auth/callback/page.tsx is "this app's ONE real (non-test) caller" and uses that to justify shipping a client that writes non-httpOnly session cookies; the callback page now uses Server Actions and getBrowserSupabaseClient has zero non-test callers. (b) app/team/actions.ts:214 and its 40-line doc comment describe getAppOrigin as "The origin used to build the invite email's redirect URL"; all four templates hardcode `{{ .SiteURL }}`, so the emailed link's host no longer comes from that function at all. (c) src/application/health/check-app-url.ts:25 degrades /api/health on the grounds that a missing APP_URL "emails http://localhost:3000/auth/callback?... to every real user" — no template produces a /auth/callback link any more.
findings.evidence: grep for getBrowserSupabaseClient across the tree returns only src/infrastructure/supabase/browser-client.{ts,test.ts} and one string literal inside tests/architecture/layering.test.ts:519 — no application call site. supabase/templates/{invite,confirmation,recovery,magic_link}.html each contain `{{ .SiteURL }}/auth/confirm?token_hash={{ .TokenHash }}&type=...` and no `{{ .RedirectTo }}`. src/infrastructure/supabase/browser-client.ts:59; app/team/actions.ts:214; src/application/health/check-app-url.ts:25.
findings.why_controls_fail: Nothing checks that a rationale still matches the code it defends. The browser client is dead infrastructure whose only documented justification has evaporated; the getAppOrigin hardening (P11 finding #12) is now defending a value GoTrue's templates ignore; and the health check gates on a condition that can no longer produce the harm it names, which trains an operator to treat that signal as noise.
findings.impact: A reviewer reading browser-client.ts concludes a non-httpOnly-cookie client is architecturally necessary when it is now simply unused and deletable. An operator reading the health check believes APP_URL still controls what real users receive. Both are the kind of stale certainty that makes the next audit round wrong in the same way this one's predecessors were.
findings.recommendation: Delete src/infrastructure/supabase/browser-client.ts (and its test) or add a comment stating it has no call site; rewrite getAppOrigin's doc comment to say what it actually still governs (the redirect_to GoTrue validates, not the link body); and re-derive what checkAppUrl is protecting now that the templates are self-contained — or retire it.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The database determination validator accepts resolution reasons and prefix-matched trade codes the protected resolver can never produce
findings.boundary: The validator is meant to enforce 'the determination must be one the resolver would actually have produced for this line's declared inputs'. On the trade-code axis it is looser than the resolver.
findings.precondition: A member writing a determination directly via PostgREST, on a line whose cn_code has an HS4/HS6 ancestor with an AVAILABLE value for the same country.
findings.affected_actor: The filing, in principle. Zero exploitable instances on the ACTIVE dataset.
findings.exploit: Claim a determination whose record_identity.source_trade_code is the HS4 heading (e.g. '7206') rather than the line's CN8 code, with reason EXACT_HS4_MATCH. app.code_prefix_covers accepts the prefix; EXACT_HS4_MATCH and EXACT_HS6_MATCH are both in the validator's allowed-reason list; the uniqueness and exact-row checks are satisfied by the heading row itself.
findings.evidence:
Validator source (app.emission_determination_matches_regulatory_record):
  if not app.code_prefix_covers(v_source_trade_code, p_cn_code) then return false; end if;
  ... v_reason = any (array['EXACT_TARIC_MATCH','EXACT_CN8_MATCH','EXACT_HS6_MATCH','EXACT_HS4_MATCH','OTHER_COUNTRIES_FALLBACK'])
app.code_prefix_covers is prefix containment on whitespace-stripped strings, whereas src/domain/regulatory/resolve-default-value.ts:31-39 requires exact equality.

Measured impact on the ACTIVE dataset:
  ... select count(*) as forgeable_pairs, min(hs.hs_total/cn.cn_total) from cn join hs on hs.country=cn.country and left(cn.cn_code,length(hs.hs_code))=hs.hs_code where hs.hs_total < cn.cn_total;
  -> forgeable_pairs 0
  Broken out by status: AVAILABLE/AVAILABLE 136 pairs, 0 with a lower HS value; AVAILABLE/REFERENCE_REQUIRED 5,921; UNAVAILABLE/REFERENCE_REQUIRED 22; UNAVAILABLE/UNAVAILABLE 11.
findings.why_controls_fail: The validator was hardened repeatedly (v6 -> v10) against country and route substitution, and each round tightened the invariant toward 'what the resolver would have done'. The trade-code axis was left as prefix containment, and two resolution reasons the resolver cannot emit were left in the allow-list — the same dead HS4/HS6 hierarchy finding 4 describes from the other side. Nothing is broken today only because no HS ancestor in this dataset happens to carry a lower value.
findings.impact: None on the ACTIVE dataset — I measured it. It becomes exploitable the moment a dataset version ships in which any HS4/HS6 row is lower than a CN8 descendant for the same country, which is not a property anything guards or tests.
findings.recommendation: Tighten app.code_prefix_covers to exact equality for the DEFAULT determination path (it is also used for cn_scope, where prefix semantics are intended — split the two uses), and drop EXACT_HS6_MATCH / EXACT_HS4_MATCH from the allowed-reason list until hierarchical resolution actually exists and has a written, cited rule. Add a regression check to regulatory:verify that no HS ancestor value is lower than a CN8 descendant for the same country, so a future dataset cannot quietly open this.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: calculation_results.parameter_datasets is never populated, and a hardcoded regulatory year threshold sits in domain code
findings.boundary: Provenance and the facts-as-datasets rule.
findings.precondition: None.
findings.affected_actor: A later auditor of a filed calculation.
findings.exploit: Read any calculation_results row and try to determine which regulatory dataset versions governed it from the field designed to answer that question.
findings.evidence:
SQL (sandbox): select parameter_datasets, count(*) from calculation_results group by 1;
  {} | 1
  [] | 27
Every row is empty. src/application/calculations/calculate-line.ts:290 passes `parameter_datasets: []` unconditionally. The dataset id/version is recoverable, but only by digging into the frozen determination JSON, and only for DEFAULT determinations.

Separately, src/domain/shared/reporting-period.ts:94: `const DEFINITIVE_REGIME_START_YEAR = 2026;` — a regulatory regime threshold typed into domain code, which CLAUDE.md's facts-as-datasets rule lists among the things ('a markup, a threshold, a price, a benchmark') that must arrive through a versioned regulatory_datasets row.
findings.why_controls_fail: CalculationResult.parameter_datasets is a declared part of the persisted record's contract (src/domain/calculations/types.ts:121) with a documented purpose, and nothing asserts it is populated. The year constant carries a careful citation comment but is still a hardcoded regulatory fact; regulatory_datasets.dataset_type already anticipates a COUNTRIES/EXEMPTIONS-style dataset for facts of this kind.
findings.impact: Weakened audit provenance rather than a wrong number. Worth fixing because the whole design premise is that a filed calculation is self-explaining from its frozen row.
findings.recommendation: Populate parameter_datasets with the dataset id + version for DEFAULT determinations (and leave it explicitly empty, not merely empty, for ACTUAL ones — an empty array should mean 'no regulatory parameter datasets were consulted', which is a claim, not a default). Move DEFINITIVE_REGIME_START_YEAR into a versioned dataset when the next regulatory dataset lands, or record an explicit ADR exempting fixed regime-start dates from the rule.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Re-confirmed, already-disclosed unit defects: tCO2/t is computed as CO2e, and tCO2e/t/yr is computed as per-tonne
findings.boundary: Unit boundary. Listed for completeness because my brief asked about tCO2/t specifically — both are already pinned as recorded defects in the golden fixtures, so the prior work did name them.
findings.precondition: A producer entering emission_unit 'tCO2/t' (CO2 only, not CO2e) or a per-year intensity such as 'tCO2e/t/yr' or 'tCO2e/t-year'.
findings.affected_actor: The regulator and the filing — under-report in both cases.
findings.exploit: Record actual emissions with either unit string and determine a line from it.
findings.evidence:
Real engine (tsx, 1000 t, direct 1.000):
  tCO2/t     COMPUTED 1000
  tCO2/TJ    UNIT_UNSUPPORTED
Golden fixtures already pin both, honestly: 'OPEN OWNER QUESTION: tCO2/t computes, treating CO2 as CO2e ... the difference is material for aluminium PFCs and fertiliser N2O' and 'RECORDED DEFECT: tCO2e/t/yr currently computes as if it were per-tonne ... wrong by however many years the record covers' (tests/golden/fixtures/engine-1.3.0/emission-units.json).
src/domain/calculations/calculate-line-emissions.ts:180 — /^TCO2E?(?:\/|_PER_|$)/ makes the 'E' optional by design.
findings.why_controls_fail: They do not fail silently — both are written down, pinned by fixtures, and flagged as open. That is the right handling of a known defect. But they remain live in a release candidate: tCO2/t drops the entire non-CO2 share of embedded emissions, which for fertilisers is N2O (the dominant gas for nitric-acid-derived products) and for aluminium is PFCs. The dataset itself carries all fertiliser and cement values as TCO2E_PER_TONNE, so the CO2/CO2e distinction is real and the platform's own reference data respects it.
findings.impact: Under-report by the non-CO2 share (unquantifiable from this dataset, but for nitric-acid-derived fertilisers it is the majority of the figure), and under-report by a factor of the number of years covered for the per-year spellings.
findings.recommendation: Both are subsumed by the emission_unit allow-list recommended in finding 5. If the allow-list cannot land before release, the owner should decide explicitly whether tCO2/t is accepted (and if so, whether it should carry a trace annotation saying CO2-only was treated as CO2e) rather than leaving it as an open question inside a fixture note.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: An ADMIN can forge sharing_grants.created_by_user_id, naming any user — including one in another organization — as the issuer of a data-sharing grant
findings.boundary: Provenance of a cross-organization data-sharing authorization.
findings.precondition: ADMIN or OWNER of a PRODUCER_OPERATOR organization (the same standing required to issue a grant legitimately).
findings.affected_actor: The producer organization's other officers, and any user named as issuer. The record of who authorized sharing a producer's emissions data with a third party is attacker-chosen.
findings.exploit: INSERT into sharing_grants with created_by_user_id set to an arbitrary auth.users id. sharing_grants_insert_own_org's WITH CHECK validates the grantor's admin standing, the installation's ownership, the grantee/email shape and status='INVITED' — but omits the `created_by_user_id = auth.uid()` conjunct that its siblings on declarations, import_batches and organization_invitations all carry. app.prevent_sharing_grant_fact_change then pins created_by_user_id forever, so the forged value is permanent.
findings.evidence:
As ADMIN aaaa…0002 of rev-atk:
  insert into sharing_grants(id,grantor_org_id,grantee_org_id,installation_id,status,created_by_user_id)
   values('a8000000-…','a0000000-…','b0000000-…','a2000000-…','INVITED','bbbb0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001');
  INSERT 0 1
  grant created_by=bbbb0000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001 (actor was aaaa..0002)
bbbb…0001 is the OWNER of rev-vic, an unrelated organization.

Compare the policies that get this right:
  declarations_insert_own_org             CHECK: ... AND (created_by_user_id = auth.uid()) ...
  import_batches_insert_own_org           CHECK: ... AND (created_by = auth.uid())
  organization_invitations_insert_...     CHECK: ... AND (invited_by = auth.uid()) ...
  sharing_grants_insert_own_org           CHECK: (no actor binding)
findings.why_controls_fail: Straightforward omission: the policy binds the grant's tenancy and shape but not its actor, and the FK to auth.users is validated outside RLS so any real user id is accepted. The immutability trigger, which is otherwise a strength, cements the forgery. Nothing later recomputes or re-derives the issuer.
findings.impact: The audit answer to 'who authorized sharing this installation's data?' is not trustworthy. An ADMIN can attribute a sharing decision to a colleague or to an outsider. Bounded — the actor must already hold the authority to issue the grant, so this is misattribution rather than escalation — hence LOW.
findings.recommendation: Add `AND created_by_user_id = auth.uid()` to sharing_grants_insert_own_org's WITH CHECK, matching the three sibling policies.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The protected regulatory tables carry INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE grants for anon and authenticated, leaving RLS as the only thing between a member and the ACTIVE dataset
findings.boundary: Defence in depth around the protected regulatory subsystem (ADR-0005).
findings.precondition: None today — RLS default-denies, and I verified that. This is a latent-exposure finding: the precondition is any future change that adds a permissive policy or disables RLS on these tables.
findings.affected_actor: Every tenant and the regulator, since default_emission_values is the ACTIVE regulatory dataset every DEFAULT determination is validated against.
findings.exploit: No exploit today. The concern is the size of the blast radius if a single policy is added or RLS is toggled: relacl on regulatory_datasets, default_emission_values, cbam_goods, countries, production_routes and regulatory_sources is `anon=arwdxtm/postgres | authenticated=arwdxtm/postgres` — INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER, MAINTAIN — while their only policy is `SELECT USING (true)`.
findings.evidence:
Grants (pg_class.relacl):
  default_emission_values | postgres=arwdDxtm/postgres | anon=arwdxtm/postgres | authenticated=arwdxtm/postgres | service_role=arwdDxtm/postgres
  regulatory_datasets     | ... anon=arwdxtm ... authenticated=arwdxtm ...
  cbam_goods, countries, production_routes, regulatory_sources: identical.
Policies: exactly one each, e.g.
  default_emission_values_select_authenticated :: SELECT :: roles=authenticated :: USING: true
Currently blocked, verified live as a MEMBER:
  update default_emission_values set total_value=0 where true;   -> UPDATE 0
  delete from default_emission_values where true;                -> DELETE 0
  insert into regulatory_datasets(...)  -> ERROR: new row violates row-level security policy for table "regulatory_datasets"

The contrast that shows the project already knows the narrower pattern:
  calculation_results | postgres=arwdDxtm | anon=rxtm | authenticated=rxtm | service_role=arwdDxtm
and as a MEMBER: INSERT -> 'permission denied for table calculation_results'. That is a hard grant-level refusal, not an RLS filter.

Related posture note: no table in public has FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY (relforcerowsecurity = f on all 21), and all are owned by `postgres` — so any connection as the owner, and every SECURITY DEFINER function, bypasses RLS entirely.
findings.why_controls_fail: There is no second layer here. For these six tables the grant layer is wide open and RLS is doing 100% of the work, on the strength of an absent policy rather than a present prohibition — a write is refused only because no INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE policy happens to exist. That is a fundamentally different guarantee from calculation_results, where the privilege was never granted and the refusal comes from the privilege system regardless of what policies do. Because the tables are also owned by `postgres` with FORCE RLS off, any owner-role connection (a migration runner, an ops script, a DATABASE_URL path) and every SECURITY DEFINER function bypasses the one layer that is present. ADR-0005 designates this data as protected but that designation is expressed in documentation and process, not in the grant table.
findings.impact: None observed. But CLAUDE.md and ADR-0005 designate this dataset as the protected regulatory foundation, and the difference between 'RLS happens to deny it' and 'the role was never granted the privilege' is exactly the difference calculation_results already draws. A single future permissive policy on default_emission_values would let any authenticated user rewrite the ACTIVE emission factors — the highest-consequence write in the system.
findings.recommendation: REVOKE INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, TRIGGER on the six regulatory tables FROM anon, authenticated — leave SELECT — exactly as calculation_results is already configured. Consider ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on the tenant tables so that owner-role connections (migrations, ops scripts, any future DATABASE_URL path) do not silently bypass every policy. Neither change touches the five protected regulatory migrations, the resolver, or the dataset itself, so neither is an ADR-0005 protected-zone edit.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Cross-tenant existence oracles via unvalidated foreign keys and RLS-vs-constraint error divergence
findings.boundary: Cross-tenant information disclosure (existence only, no content).
findings.precondition: Any authenticated member; ADMIN for the organizations oracle. A candidate id must already be held — these confirm ids, they do not enumerate them.
findings.affected_actor: Any tenant whose row ids appear in a URL, a log, an export, a shared determination snapshot, or a support ticket.
findings.exploit:
Three distinguishable oracles.
(1) emission_data.predecessor_id: a real id (any tenant) is accepted; a nonexistent one raises a foreign-key error naming the table. This is the same primitive that powers Finding 3.
(2) suppliers.linked_operator_id: a member can point their own supplier row at another organization's operator id and the INSERT succeeds; suppliers_insert_own_org constrains org_id only.
(3) organizations existence: an ADMIN inserting a sharing_grant with a real grantee_org_id succeeds, while a nonexistent one fails with 'new row violates row-level security policy' — the difference comes from app.organization_exists() inside the WITH CHECK.
findings.evidence:
(1) Real cross-org emission_data id:  INSERT 0 1  (ACCEPTED: my row claims predecessor=b3000000-…-000b which belongs to org b)
    Random uuid, identical statement:
      ERROR:  insert or update on table "emission_data" violates foreign key constraint "emission_data_predecessor_id_fkey"
      DETAIL:  Key is not present in table "emission_data".

(2) As plain MEMBER aaaa…0003:
      insert into suppliers(org_id,name,linked_operator_id)
       values('a0000000-…','S1','b1000000-0000-4000-8000-00000000000b');
      INSERT 0 1
      ACCEPTED linked_operator_id=b1000000-0000-4000-8000-00000000000b
    (b1000000-… is rev-vic's operator. FK is ON DELETE SET NULL, so the victim deleting their operator silently mutates the attacker's row.)

(3) As ADMIN of a PRODUCER_OPERATOR org:
      grantee_org_id='b0000000-…' (real)          -> INSERT 0 1 / ACCEPTED (org exists)
      grantee_org_id='99999999-9999-4999-8999-999999999999' -> ERROR: new row violates row-level security policy for table "sharing_grants"
findings.why_controls_fail: Postgres validates foreign keys as the referenced table's owner, outside RLS, so an FK confirms a row's existence to a principal who cannot SELECT it. None of these three policies adds a same-tenant conjunct on the referencing column — suppliers_insert_own_org and suppliers_update_own_org constrain org_id alone, and emission_data_insert_own_org constrains only entered_by_org_id and installation_id. For (3), app.organization_exists() is a SECURITY DEFINER helper deliberately called from a WITH CHECK, which necessarily converts a cross-tenant fact into an observable pass/fail. A secondary consequence of (3): an ADMIN can create INVITED grants naming arbitrary real organizations, which those organizations' members will see as unsolicited grants (sharing_grants_select_grantor_or_grantee).
findings.impact: Low on its own — v4 UUIDs are not brute-forceable, so these confirm ids rather than discover them. They matter because ids leak routinely in this system by design: a grantee holds the producer's emission_data_id inside its own frozen determination snapshot and inside record_shared_data_consumption payloads. Combined with Finding 3, oracle (1) is the reconnaissance half of a cross-tenant denial of service. Oracle (2) additionally lets a tenant record a false internal linkage to another tenant's operator.
findings.recommendation: Constrain the referencing columns in the policies themselves: add a same-tenant EXISTS for suppliers.linked_operator_id (operators o WHERE o.id = linked_operator_id AND o.org_id = suppliers.org_id) on both the INSERT and UPDATE policies, and the lineage EXISTS for emission_data.predecessor_id described in Finding 3. For the organizations oracle, accept it as inherent to validating a grantee at insert time, or move direct-grant creation behind a SECURITY DEFINER RPC that returns a uniform result for 'no such org' and 'not permitted' — the same NOT_FOUND-over-a-more-specific-reason posture record_declaration_filed and accept_organization_invitation already adopt deliberately.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Two mutating Server Actions ship with no rate limiter, and the accepted 'N replicas = N x the limit' caveat is pinned nowhere in the deploy config
findings.boundary: Authenticated user -> the app's own cookie/session surface; and separately, deploy configuration -> every rate limit in the application.
findings.precondition: A valid session for the unlimited actions. For the replica issue, only that someone scales the Railway service past one instance, which requires no code change and trips no gate.
findings.affected_actor: The acting user for the unlimited actions (impact is genuinely small). For the replica issue, all tenants -- every configured limit silently multiplies.
findings.exploit:
switchOrganizationAction (action ID 4004fec84d148390dd3484e9d5cd58136164863d38, also in the public bundle) and signOutAction have no limiter. switchOrganizationAction only writes a preference cookie whose value is re-validated against real memberships downstream, so the ceiling on abuse is low; signOutAction calls supabase.auth.signOut(), another GoTrue egress call, though supabase-js short-circuits when no session is present, which bounds it to holders of a real session.

Separately: railway.json contains no replica setting at all. Scaling the service to N instances multiplies every limit in the app by N -- sign-in becomes 10N per 5 minutes per IP -- with nothing in the repository detecting or preventing it.
findings.evidence:
components/shell/switch-org-action.ts -- the complete file contains no createInMemoryRateLimiter and no .check(; measured as `exports=1 checks=0`. app/(auth)/actions.ts:336 `export async function signOutAction(): Promise<void>` calls `await supabase.auth.signOut()` at :341 with no preceding check (that file is exports=3 checks=2).

railway.json in full carries only build and deploy blocks:
  "deploy": { "startCommand": "node server.js", "healthcheckPath": "/api/health", "healthcheckTimeout": 30, "restartPolicyType": "ON_FAILURE", "restartPolicyMaxRetries": 3 }
No numReplicas, no replica field. `grep -rn -i 'replica|numReplicas|horizontal|scale' railway.json docs/architecture/ENVIRONMENT.md docs/runbooks/*.md` returns exactly one hit, docs/runbooks/INCIDENT_RESPONSE.md:192, which tells a responder to CHECK the replica count during an incident -- confirming the limitation is known but pinned nowhere.
findings.why_controls_fail: For the unlimited actions: nothing enforces limiter coverage. There is no architecture test asserting that every exported Server Action reaches a limiter (tests/architecture/ holds only layering.test.ts, auth-confirm-get-is-inert.test.ts, local-auth-fixture-invariants.test.ts and layering-rules.ts), so a new action ships unlimited by default and no gate notices -- which is exactly how the two callback actions in finding 1 were missed. For replicas: src/infrastructure/rate-limit/rate-limiter.ts's header and docs/runbooks/INCIDENT_RESPONSE.md:191-199 both state the N-replica consequence plainly and both treat it as an accepted limitation, but acceptance is recorded only in prose. The deploy config that would make it true is silent.
findings.impact: Small directly. The real weight is that both are symptoms of a missing invariant: nothing mechanically ties 'this is a mutating Server Action' to 'it has a limiter', and nothing ties 'these limits are meaningful' to 'exactly one replica'. Both are the conditions that produced finding 1.
findings.recommendation: Add an architecture test in tests/architecture/ that enumerates every exported async function in a "use server" file plus every app/api/**/route.ts handler and asserts each either calls a limiter or appears on an explicit, justified allowlist -- the same shape as layering-rules.ts's UI_ALLOWED_INFRASTRUCTURE_IMPORTS. That single test would have caught app/auth/callback/actions.ts. Separately, pin the replica count to 1 in railway.json with a comment pointing at rate-limiter.ts's header, so scaling past one instance is a deliberate, reviewable change rather than a dashboard click that silently multiplies every auth limit.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: CI never passes --require-artifact to the production-artifact gate, so a build producing no standalone tree passes it vacuously
findings.boundary: CI quality gate -> deployable artifact must not carry the E2E rate-limit bypass
findings.precondition: A build that exits 0 without producing `.next/standalone` (e.g. a next.config.ts change that drops `output: 'standalone'`, or a dist-dir redirect that fires unexpectedly in the fast-gates environment).
findings.affected_actor: Every tenant: the rate limiters protecting sign-up, invitation and mutation endpoints.
findings.exploit: If `.next/standalone` does not exist, assert-clean-production-artifact.mjs prints `[assert-clean-production-artifact] <dir> absent -- nothing to check.` and exits 0, because `requireArtifact` is false. The fast-gates 'Production build' step then reports success having verified nothing.
findings.evidence:
scripts/build/assert-clean-production-artifact.mjs:83-114:
  const requireArtifact = process.argv.includes("--require-artifact");
  ...
  if (!existsSync(STANDALONE_DIR)) {
    if (requireArtifact) { fail(`${STANDALONE_DIR} does not exist, but --require-artifact was passed...`); }
    else { console.log(`[assert-clean-production-artifact] ${STANDALONE_DIR} absent -- nothing to check.`); }
  }

Invocations:
  package.json:8  "postbuild": "node scripts/build/copy-standalone-assets.mjs && node scripts/build/assert-clean-production-artifact.mjs"   <- no flag
  Dockerfile:54   RUN node scripts/build/assert-clean-production-artifact.mjs --require-artifact                                        <- flag present
  .github/workflows/ci.yml  -- the script is never invoked directly at all (`grep -n "assert-clean" .github/workflows/ci.yml` returns nothing); CI relies entirely on postbuild.

The script's own doc comment at line 54-56 says the flag belongs "where the artifact must exist (the Docker build stage, CI after a build step)" — CI is named and does not do it.

I verified the postbuild hook itself is not the weak link — pnpm 11.24.0 does run it and does propagate failure:
$ (throwaway package with postbuild exiting 1) pnpm build; echo $?
BUILD RAN
POSTBUILD RAN
[ELIFECYCLE] Command failed with exit code 1.
PNPM_BUILD_EXIT=1
findings.why_controls_fail: The tolerant branch is correct and necessary for the E2E build (where the artifact legitimately lands in .next-e2e), and the author extended that tolerance to every non-Docker caller rather than to that specific case. The Dockerfile is a real compensating control for the deployed image, which is why this is LOW rather than higher — but it means the CI-side copy of this gate proves nothing when it matters most, and its 'OK' line is indistinguishable in the log from its 'nothing to check' line only to a careless reader.
findings.impact: Latent. The fast-gates build gate can pass without inspecting anything, and the only enforcement of the bypass invariant would be the Docker build, which runs on the deploy platform rather than in CI.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit step to fast-gates after `pnpm build`: `node scripts/build/assert-clean-production-artifact.mjs --require-artifact`. Leave postbuild's flagless invocation alone so the E2E build keeps working.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: resolveGoodSectorForActualLine silently takes candidates[0] from an unordered query, which is the arbitrary-choice-under-ambiguity the project forbids
findings.boundary: Regulatory-correctness rule (CLAUDE.md: ambiguity must surface as AMBIGUOUS/UNRESOLVED, never an arbitrary choice). Latent today; not currently reachable.
findings.precondition: Two or more TRADE_GOOD cbam_goods rows sharing a trade_code with overlapping active windows and differing sectors. None exist in the current dataset.
findings.affected_actor: Own tenant and the regulator, if such rows ever appear.
findings.exploit: `return candidates[0]?.sector ?? null;` picks the first row of a PostgREST query that has no .order() and a .limit(10). Postgres row order without ORDER BY is unspecified and can change with plan, vacuum, or physical row movement. If two rows for one code disagreed on sector, the Annex II direct-only decision — and therefore the number — would be decided arbitrarily and could differ between the original calculation and a later reproduction of the same row, producing a spurious MISMATCH or, worse, a silently different figure on recalculation.
findings.evidence:
src/application/calculations/calculate-line.ts:141 — `return candidates[0]?.sector ?? null;`
src/infrastructure/regulatory/supabase-regulatory-repository.ts:724-746 — the query chains .eq(trade_code), .eq(record_level,'TRADE_GOOD'), two .or() effective-date clauses and .limit(10), with no .order().

Measured, so I am not overstating it:
psql -tAc "select trade_code, count(*), count(distinct sector) from public.cbam_goods where record_level='TRADE_GOOD' group by 1 having count(*)>1;"
 (0 rows)
psql -tAc "select count(*) from public.cbam_goods where record_level='TRADE_GOOD';"
 170
So the arbitrary pick cannot currently fire. cbam_goods also has no dataset_id column, so a re-ingestion that adds a new row for an existing code (new active_from, old row's active_to set) is exactly how the overlap would first appear.
findings.why_controls_fail: Classification (classify-good.ts) has an explicit AMBIGUOUS_CODE outcome for this situation and the UI has a message for it ('That code matches more than one CBAM good and needs to be disambiguated'). The Annex II lookup reuses the same repository method but discards that discipline, collapsing 0, 1 and N candidates into 'null or the first one'. The function's doc comment acknowledges the 0 case ('an unexpected-data-drift case, not a normal outcome') and does not consider N at all.
findings.impact: None today, measured. It becomes a correctness defect the first time cbam_goods carries two rows for one code — which the project's own facts-as-datasets correction path makes likely rather than exotic.
findings.recommendation: Return a discriminated outcome from resolveGoodSectorForActualLine: zero candidates -> null (current, documented behaviour), one -> its sector, more than one -> an explicit AMBIGUOUS state that calculateLine surfaces as a non-computable CalculationStatus rather than a number. Add .order('trade_code') (or better, an ORDER BY that makes the selection deterministic) to findCbamGoodsByCode regardless. Note this touches src/infrastructure/regulatory/, which is protected — TDD-backed, single-purpose commit, with pnpm regulatory:verify run afterwards.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Products are silently rounded to 40 significant digits with no status, so a regulated numeric can lose precision without any signal
findings.boundary: Regulated-numeric precision contract.
findings.precondition: Inputs whose product exceeds 40 significant digits. shipment_lines.net_mass_tonnes is unbounded text (only `~ '^-?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?$'` and `::numeric > 0`), and emission_data.direct_specific/indirect_specific are likewise unbounded text.
findings.affected_actor: Own tenant.
findings.exploit: A line quantity and a specific-emissions value with enough decimal places together exceed decimal.js's configured precision of 40, and `.times()` rounds HALF_UP to 40 significant digits. The result is stored as if exact. Because the rounding is deterministic, reproduceCalculationResult recomputes the identical rounded value and reports REPRODUCIBLE — the loss is invisible to the integrity check by design.
findings.evidence:
Real engine, via tsx:
quantity            = 1234567890.1234567890123456789012345
direct_specific     = 1.2345678901234567890123456789012345
engine (precision 40) => COMPUTED 1524157875.323883675049535156256668026871
exact  (precision 200) => 1524157875.32388367504953515625666802687090533479957338669120562399025

src/domain/shared/decimal.ts — `DecimalJs.clone({ precision: 40, rounding: DecimalJs.ROUND_HALF_UP })`; toDecimalString uses toFixed() with no argument, which preserves whatever precision survived the multiplication.

Column checks confirming no length bound:
shipment_lines_net_mass_format_ck   CHECK (net_mass_tonnes ~ '^-?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?$')
shipment_lines_net_mass_positive_ck CHECK (net_mass_tonnes::numeric > 0)
findings.why_controls_fail: Nothing in the pipeline bounds the number of significant digits on the way in, and the engine's rounding is not reported as a status. The filed snapshot's `rounding` object explicitly asserts `figures_are_full_precision: true` and `applied: false`, which is not strictly true for any product that hit the 40-digit ceiling.
findings.impact: Low in practice: the ACTIVE default_emission_values dataset carries 3 decimal places and the emission_data rows I inspected carry 2, so I could not construct a realistic case that reaches the ceiling. I am reporting it because the filed snapshot makes an unconditional full-precision claim that the engine cannot unconditionally honour.
findings.recommendation: Either bound significant digits at entry (a CHECK on the length of the numeric strings in shipment_lines and emission_data, sized to the regulation's own precision ceilings — Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2547 Annex II A.1(6)-(8) is already cited in the snapshot's rounding note), or detect precision loss in the engine (compare against a higher-precision clone) and return an explicit non-computable status rather than a quietly rounded number. At minimum, stop asserting figures_are_full_precision unconditionally.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The 'why this number' panel asserts a regulatory conclusion the platform cannot establish, and states it falsely for CN 2601 12 00
findings.boundary: What the product tells a declarant about the basis of a filed figure, vs. what the platform actually knows.
findings.precondition: Any ACTUAL-determined line in the IRON_STEEL or ALUMINIUM sector — i.e. every line that triggers the Annex II gate. The panel is the declarant's primary explanation surface.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant, who is given a confident regulatory justification for a number and cannot tell it is inferred from a sector label.
findings.exploit: app/(importer)/shipments/[id]/why-this-number-panel.tsx:596-610 renders, whenever the ANNEX_II_DIRECT_ONLY step is present: 'This good is in a sector subject to the Annex II treatment, where only direct emissions are taken into account.' The platform holds no Annex II membership data — cbam_goods has no such column, and the engine's own comment says so ('Annex II is a CN-code-level list; cbam_goods carries no Annex II membership field at all'). For CN 2601 12 00 the sentence is not merely unsupported but contradicted by the platform's own ACTIVE dataset, which publishes an indirect value for that good and sums it into total. The panel then names the excluded indirect figure, which makes the claim look independently corroborated rather than assumed.
findings.evidence:
Panel copy, verbatim (app/(importer)/shipments/[id]/why-this-number-panel.tsx:596-610):
  Treatment: direct emissions only
  This good is in a sector subject to the Annex II treatment, where only
  direct emissions are taken into account. The installation also reported
  {annexIiStep.inputs.indirect_specific_excluded} indirect emissions; that
  figure is kept on the record and was not added to this result.

The dataset contradicting it for 2601 12 00 (28 country rows with indirect published and summed):
26011200|Kazakhstan|direct 0.170|indirect 0.170|total 0.340
26011200|Serbia    |direct 0.120|indirect 0.110|total 0.220

And the engine's own admission that it has no such data (src/domain/calculations/calculate-line-emissions.ts:78-82):
  `sector` is a PROXY. Annex II is a CN-code-level list; `cbam_goods`
  carries no Annex II membership field at all, only this coarser sector.
findings.why_controls_fail: The honesty is present in the source comment and absent from the user-facing string. The code knows it is guessing; the panel speaks as though it knows. Every other uncertainty in this product is surfaced with care — UNAVAILABLE, REFERENCE_REQUIRED, AMBIGUOUS, the in-band `rounding` note on filed_snapshot saying the rounding method is unresolved — which makes this one stand out as an omission rather than a house style.
findings.impact: The declarant is told a regulatory conclusion the platform cannot support, in the one place they would go to check whether a figure is defensible. For CN 2601 12 00 they are told something the platform's own dataset contradicts, which means the explanation surface actively conceals the under-report in the first finding rather than exposing it.
findings.recommendation: Fix the underlying gate first (finding 1); this string then becomes true for the goods it applies to. Until an actual Annex II dataset exists, the panel should say what is actually known — that the treatment was applied on the basis of the good's sector, and that sector is a proxy for Annex II membership — in the same register the rest of the product uses for uncertainty.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Two latent resolver/validator disagreements that the current dataset happens to mask
findings.boundary: Consistency between the domain resolver's matching rules and the database validator's independent re-derivation of the same rules.
findings.precondition: Neither is reachable against the ACTIVE dataset. Both arm if the regulatory geography or code coverage changes. I measured reachability rather than assuming it, and am reporting them as latent for that reason.
findings.affected_actor: The declarant — both failures are over-rejection (a legitimate determination refused at write time), not a wrong number.
findings.exploit:
(a) PREFIX vs EXACT. The validator's R7 clause 2 own-country precondition uses `app.code_prefix_covers(dev.source_trade_code, p_cn_code)`, a prefix match, while the resolver's matchesCode uses exact normalized-code equality. A country holding an AVAILABLE record at a SHORTER prefix code, but none at the exact code, would make v_own_country_has_usable true and reject a fallback the resolver legitimately produced.
(b) COUNTRY FILTERS. mapCountry filters `country_type='COUNTRY' AND active=true`; the validator's UNLISTED branch checks only `exists (select 1 from countries c where c.iso2 = p_origin_country)`. A country row that is present but inactive, or typed as something other than COUNTRY, would map to UNLISTED in the application and then be rejected by the validator for existing.
findings.evidence:
(a) Prefix overlaps genuinely exist in the data — HS4 '7207' is a strict prefix of 21 CN8 codes, '761090' of 76109010 and 76109090, and 165 distinct 8-digit plus 5 ten-digit codes are loaded. But the exploitable combination does not:
$ psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "with norm as (select c.name cname, regexp_replace(dev.source_trade_code,'\s','','g') code, dev.total_status from default_emission_values dev join countries c on c.id=dev.country_id), other_exact as (select code from norm where cname='_Other Countries and Territorie' and total_status='AVAILABLE'), cand as (select distinct n.cname, oe.code from other_exact oe join norm n on n.cname <> '_Other Countries and Territorie' and length(n.code) < length(oe.code) and left(oe.code, length(n.code)) = n.code and n.total_status='AVAILABLE' where not exists (select 1 from norm n2 where n2.cname=n.cname and n2.code=oe.code)) select count(*), count(distinct cname), count(distinct code) from cand;"
0|0|0

(b) No row can trigger it today:
$ psql ... -tAc "select country_type, active, count(*) from countries group by 1,2;"
COUNTRY|t|121
OTHER_TERRITORIES|t|1
$ psql ... -tAc "select iso2, count(*) from countries where iso2 is not null group by 1 having count(*)>1;"
(empty — no duplicate iso2, so the validator's unqualified `select ... into` single-row assumption also holds)
findings.why_controls_fail: Nothing fails today — I am reporting these because the validator is deliberately built as an independent second wall that re-derives the resolver's rules, and a second wall that computes a slightly different predicate is a latent source of unexplainable write refusals. The divergences are invisible to every test because the dataset is fully dense across countries.
findings.impact: None today — measured, not assumed. If the regulatory geography gains an inactive or non-COUNTRY row, or if code coverage becomes uneven across countries in a future dataset, legitimate determinations will be refused by the database with a generic validation error and no way for the user or an operator to tell why the resolver and the validator disagree.
findings.recommendation: Align the two predicates: use exact normalized-code matching in the validator's own-country precondition to mirror matchesCode, and apply the same country_type/active filters the application's mapCountry uses. Neither should block release. Both should be closed before any change to the regulatory geography or to code-level coverage, and they are worth a comment in the validator noting that the predicates are intended to be identical to the resolver's.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Two smaller regulatory-hygiene defects: a hardcoded regime-start year, and a NULL functional_unit silently treated as mass
findings.boundary: CLAUDE.md's facts-as-datasets rule, and the 'no value is not a value' rule, at two minor sites.
findings.precondition: Neither produces a wrong number against the current dataset. Reported because both are the pattern this codebase treats as a defect elsewhere.
findings.affected_actor: Future maintainers; potentially the filing if either assumption changes.
findings.exploit:
(a) `const DEFINITIVE_REGIME_START_YEAR = 2026;` (src/domain/shared/reporting-period.ts:97) is a regulatory threshold — the date the CBAM definitive regime begins — hardcoded in application code. CLAUDE.md is explicit that this class of fact must enter through a versioned regulatory_datasets row: 'Hardcode a regulatory number (a markup, a threshold, a price, a benchmark) into application code'. The value is correct; the mechanism is the one the project forbids. It determines which reporting regime every shipment is filed under.
(b) `requiredQuantityKind` (src/domain/shipments/classify-good.ts:110-116) returns `good.functional_unit === "MWH" ? "ENERGY" : "MASS"`. cbam_goods.functional_unit is nullable, so an unknown unit resolves to MASS rather than surfacing as unknown — the same 'absent treated as a value' shape the regulatory resolver is explicitly forbidden from taking. A good with a NULL functional_unit would have its quantity validated against tonnes without anyone deciding that.
findings.evidence:
(a) src/domain/shared/reporting-period.ts:97 and its use at :125:
  const DEFINITIVE_REGIME_START_YEAR = 2026;
  ...
  if (year >= DEFINITIVE_REGIME_START_YEAR) { return { kind: "ANNUAL", year }; }

(b) The column is nullable:
$ psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/p14_review_sandbox" -tAc "select column_name, is_nullable from information_schema.columns where table_name='cbam_goods' and column_name='functional_unit';"
functional_unit|YES
Not reachable today — every row is populated:
$ psql ... -tAc "select functional_unit, record_level, count(*) from cbam_goods group by 1,2 order by 1,2;"
TONNES|HS_HEADING|50
TONNES|HS_SUBHEADING|63
TONNES|TRADE_GOOD|170
(283 rows, no NULL, no MWH.)
findings.why_controls_fail: (a) The subsystem is otherwise disciplined about this — no certificate price, benchmark, CSCF or markup is hardcoded anywhere (I checked: calculation_results.certificates_due and liability_amount are NULL on all 27 rows and nothing in src writes them). This one slipped through because it reads as a calendar constant rather than a regulatory one. (b) The ternary's else-branch is doing double duty as both 'TONNES' and 'unrecognised', which no reviewer would notice while the column is fully populated.
findings.impact: No wrong figure today. (a) A regulatory threshold that decides which reporting regime every shipment falls under lives outside the versioned-dataset mechanism the project relies on for auditability, so correcting it would be a code change rather than a dataset version. (b) If a future goods dataset ever carries a NULL functional_unit, that good's quantity basis is silently assumed to be mass rather than surfaced as undetermined — the precise failure mode the regulatory rules forbid.
findings.recommendation: (a) Move the regime-start year into a versioned dataset alongside the other regulatory facts, or — if that is disproportionate for a single date — record explicitly in the ADR trail why this one constant is exempt, so the next reviewer does not have to re-derive the question. (b) Make requiredQuantityKind total over the three cases: TONNES -> MASS, MWH -> ENERGY, null -> a surfaced unknown, consistent with how every other 'no value' is handled in this codebase. Neither blocks release.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: BACKUP_RESTORE.md tells a recovering operator the schema is 'reproducible by re-running the migration set', which aborts at file 3 of 74
findings.boundary: Recovery documentation boundary. The reader is mid-incident and following the wrong document.
findings.precondition: An operator recovering from BACKUP_RESTORE.md rather than DEPLOYMENT.md — which is the document the recovery decision tree, the dump procedure and the drill all live in.
findings.affected_actor: Recovery time objective. Not a data or authorization boundary.
findings.exploit:
1. Operator reads BACKUP_RESTORE.md:617 ('Schema, policies, functions, triggers, constraints | yes | also reproducible by re-running the migration set') and elects to rebuild from migrations.
2. Applying supabase/migrations in filename order against an empty database aborts on the third file with an error naming a dataset, not a procedure.
3. Nothing in BACKUP_RESTORE.md mentions the Python-pipeline interleave that makes it work.
findings.evidence:
Measured, applying the tracked migrations in order to a fresh database (p14rev_a10, auth/storage shims + pgcrypto/uuid-ossp present):
  ### RC=0 20260826133116_create_regulatory_foundation.sql
  ### RC=0 20260827093000_support_regulatory_geography.sql
  ### RC=3 20260827110000_activate_definitive_regulatory_dataset.sql
  psql:supabase/migrations/20260827110000_activate_definitive_regulatory_dataset.sql:54: ERROR:  Validated regulatory dataset 2026-definitive-corrected was not found
  CONTEXT:  PL/pgSQL function inline_code_block line 18 at RAISE

I worked around it exactly as the CI recipe does — loading regulatory_sources, regulatory_datasets, countries, cbam_goods, production_routes and default_emission_values (12,540 rows) from the sandbox and resetting the dataset to DRAFT — after which the remaining 72 migrations applied cleanly (RC=0 each).

file:line — the claim is docs/runbooks/BACKUP_RESTORE.md:617. The correct procedure exists only at docs/runbooks/DEPLOYMENT.md:539-575 ('Rebuilding on a fresh database'), which BACKUP_RESTORE.md does not reference, and in .github/workflows/ci.yml:199-215.
findings.why_controls_fail: DEPLOYMENT.md was updated on 2026-09-03 with the correct recipe and even states the principle — 'a recipe that exists only in CI is a recipe nobody can follow during an incident'. BACKUP_RESTORE.md's fidelity table was not updated with it, so the recovery document still asserts a capability the deployment document elsewhere denies. The two documents disagree and the recovering operator is reading the wrong one.
findings.impact: An operator who chooses the migration-replay recovery path from the recovery runbook hits an opaque failure three files in and has to discover the pipeline interleave themselves, during an incident. No data or security consequence, purely recovery time.
findings.recommendation: Replace the cell at BACKUP_RESTORE.md:617 with a pointer to DEPLOYMENT.md's 'Rebuilding on a fresh database', stating plainly that the migration set is not self-sufficient and aborts at 20260827110000 without the regulatory pipeline.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: The sequences check compares names only, contradicting its own stated rationale, and pg_default_acl is never compared at all
findings.boundary: Recovery verification boundary.
findings.precondition: A restore in which a sequence's last_value does not match the source, or in which ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES differ. The sequence half is currently unreachable in this schema, which defines zero sequences.
findings.affected_actor: None today for sequences. For default privileges: every table created after a restore, which would silently inherit whatever the restored default ACL says rather than what 20260903170000 and seed.sql intend.
findings.exploit:
1. A future migration adds a sequence-backed column; a restore brings the sequence back at a lower value; the check compares only sequence_schema||'.'||sequence_name, matches, and the first insert after recovery collides on the primary key.
2. Independently: a restore or rebuild whose ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES include TRUNCATE for anon/authenticated hands TRUNCATE to every table created afterwards. truncate_granted_to_api_roles only enumerates tables that already exist, so it reports [OK] until the next migration adds a table.
findings.evidence:
scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:224-233. The `why` at :226 reads 'a sequence restored at the wrong value collides on the next insert'; the SQL selects `sequence_schema || '.' || sequence_name from information_schema.sequences` and nothing else. Confirmed inert today: `node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs <sandbox> <p14rev_a10>` -> `[MATCH] sequences (0 rows both sides)`.

pg_default_acl is not referenced anywhere in the file (no match for 'default_acl' or 'defacl'). Measured state, sandbox vs my fresh rebuild:
  sandbox: postgres | public | r | postgres=arwdDxtm/postgres anon=arwdxtm/postgres authenticated=arwdxtm/postgres service_role=arwdDxtm/postgres
  fresh:   postgres | public | r | anon=arwdxtm/postgres authenticated=arwdxtm/postgres service_role=arwdDxtm/postgres
Both correctly withhold `D` (TRUNCATE) from anon/authenticated; the only difference is the postgres self-entry. Correct today, and unverified by any check.
findings.why_controls_fail: Nothing else covers either. The sequences check is the only place sequences are mentioned in the file, and as written it cannot fail for the reason it names; it is also marked non-critical, so it would not block a recovery even if it did. Default privileges are covered by neither the comparison checks nor the self-checks.
findings.impact: Two stated recovery guarantees are not actually verified. Low today because the schema has no sequences and the default ACLs happen to be correct, but both are silent failure modes that will surface the first time a migration adds a sequence or a table after a restore.
findings.recommendation: Add `last_value` to the sequences check (or delete the misleading `why`), and add a pg_default_acl comparison check. The ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES statements in 20260903170000 and seed.sql are load-bearing security statements and are currently unverified by the tool that is supposed to prove the posture survived.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: 'tCO2eq/t', a standard spelling of the CO2-equivalent numerator, is rejected as UNIT_UNSUPPORTED (prior #10)
findings.boundary: Product usability; fails safe.
findings.precondition: A producer enters an ordinary alternative spelling in the free-text emission-unit field.
findings.affected_actor: Every importer who later determines a line ACTUAL from that record and gets no number.
findings.exploit: None — a data-entry outcome.
findings.evidence: Evaluating the committed predicate `/^TCO2E?(?:\/|_PER_|$)/` in node: "tCO2eq/t" -> false, while "tCO2e/t" -> true and "tCO2e/tonne" -> true. The anchor requires the numerator to end immediately after TCO2 or TCO2E. "tCO2e/kt" -> false likewise.
findings.why_controls_fail: The numerator anchor was tightened to close the kgCO2e/t false-positive and, correctly, rejects anything it does not recognise — but the accepted set is narrower than the standard spellings in use.
findings.impact: Fails in the safe direction (no fabricated number), so this is usability and support cost rather than correctness. Worth reporting beside the denominator finding because both have the same root cause the file itself names: emission_unit is free text and the engine string-sniffs it.
findings.recommendation: Fixed by the same allow-list: enumerate the accepted spellings explicitly and reject everything else at data entry, with a message naming the accepted forms, rather than failing silently at calculation time.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: Views are invisible to every posture check — but the prior finding's headline claim is FALSE at this candidate (prior #44, HIGH -> LOW; the title materially overstates)
findings.boundary: Operational/recovery detector coverage. NOT, as titled, a live cross-tenant disclosure.
findings.precondition: Someone would have to strip the reloption — a hand-repaired view during recovery, or a CREATE OR REPLACE that omits it. I found no documented operation in this repository that does so.
findings.affected_actor: Latent. Nobody today.
findings.exploit: Not currently available. I attacked it three ways and it held.
findings.evidence:
THE HEADLINE CLAIM IS FALSE AS WRITTEN. The prior title asserts '`security_invoker=false` gives every authenticated user cross-org read of all calculation results'. On the candidate:
  select c.relname, c.reloptions, pg_get_userbyid(c.relowner) from pg_class c ... where c.relkind='v';
  -> latest_calculation_results | {security_invoker=true} | postgres

As authenticated with real claims: `select count(*) from public.latest_calculation_results` -> 0, while the base table holds 25 rows as superuser. As anon: view 0, base table 0.
As a write channel: `update public.latest_calculation_results set embedded_emissions_tco2e='0.001'` -> ERROR: cannot update view "latest_calculation_results" / Views containing DISTINCT are not automatically updatable. Same for DELETE. So the view is no route around the 20260903190000 revoke either, despite anon and authenticated holding INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on it.
And pg_dump preserves the option: a schema-only dump of the sandbox contains `CREATE VIEW public.latest_calculation_results WITH (security_invoker='true') AS` at line 3633.

WHAT IS TRUE, and is the whole of the finding: the comparator cannot see views. :73 filters `table_type = 'BASE TABLE'`; :101, :320, :335 all filter `c.relkind = 'r'`; nothing in the file reads pg_class.reloptions. So if the option were ever lost, no check would notice.
findings.why_controls_fail: The comparator's checks were written for tables and the schema's only view carries its security in a reloption none of them reads.
findings.impact: Detector blindness on one object, with no reachable exploit at this candidate. I downgrade from HIGH because the prior report's title asserts as fact a state the candidate is not in, and a reader would reasonably act on that title. Flagging the overstatement matters as much as the finding: this is one of the entries that made the prior pass's severity distribution untrustworthy in BOTH directions.
findings.recommendation: Add a self-check asserting `latest_calculation_results` carries security_invoker=true, and generally read pg_class.reloptions for every view in the compared schemas. Correct the finding's title before it is actioned as written.
findings.reviewer_note: Reported with live evidence by an attack agent; not independently re-run by the reviewing session.

findings.title: create_organization_with_owner leaks a cross-tenant organisation-existence oracle by slug, and permits slug squatting (prior #15)
findings.boundary: Cross-tenant existence disclosure. No row content.
findings.precondition: Any authenticated user with a guessable slug.
findings.affected_actor: Other tenants on the platform, whose existence is disclosed; and prospective customers whose natural slug can be squatted.
findings.exploit: Call the RPC with a guessed slug. A 23505 with the slug echoed means that organisation exists; success means it does not, and permanently claims the slug.
findings.evidence:
organizations_slug_uq is a global UNIQUE (slug) constraint and create_organization_with_owner inserts a caller-supplied slug with no pre-check and no error translation. The two responses are cleanly distinguishable and the error echoes the probed value.

Related and weaker, and I confirmed this one myself in the predecessor-squat reproduction: emission_data_predecessor_id_fkey returns 'Key is not present in table "emission_data"' for a nonexistent id versus success for a real one — the same oracle over emission_data.id, though it needs a UUID rather than a guessable name.
